Preface to the Second Edition.

It is sixty-five years since a most highly esteemed citizen, intellectually as well as socially probably the most unconditionally independent in the Basel of that day, brought out with the bookseller Detloff on the Freienstrasse his Essay on Ancient Mortuary Symbolism. Already for fourteen years retired from his post as full professor in the faculty of law, but as a member of the court of appeal still in full touch with the public life of the city, with the “commonweal,” as people liked to say then, Johann Jakob Bachofen in his forty-fourth year had set foot on an entirely new path of research, on which only today he is stepping out of the darkness of general incomprehension, to be recognized and appreciated by the friends of antiquity as a profound interpreter of the ancient soul.

The book was received with blind hatred and hesitant favor. Its author often appealed to the following extreme condemnation, devoted to him in the Literarisches Zentralblatt: “408 closely printed pages full of the strangest and most fantastic dreamings, which in their profundity at times pass over directly into the realm of higher imbecility. Examples, pp. 29, 81, 180. Who does not think, on reading them, that the author is speaking in a fever? Alongside these wild interpretations the author’s etymological attempts stand worthily. Examples: p. 116 (gynä), 176 (daktylos). A brew that may perhaps intoxicate one reader or another, but will certainly refresh no one.” Against this Dr. Joseph Schauberg of Zurich wrote in 1861 in his Vergleichendes Handbuch der Symbolik der Freimaurerei: “Bachofen, to be sure, often reads too much and too profound a symbolism into the numbers, as the later Pythagoreans did in departing from Pythagoras; but the annihilating verdict that was passed on his work in no. 27 of the Literarisches Zentralblatt for 1860 he certainly has not deserved. Whoever possesses no symbolic and mythological sense and faith is unable to judge such writings justly.” The book was then straightway pushed into the shadow by a larger brother and has since literally led a cloistered life, like a devout Vestal condemned to seclusion from the world, while the far more voluminous Mutterrecht carried Bachofen’s name out into the world, because through its ethnological discoveries it flowed into the then broadly swelling flood of anthropology and

[PDF 6]

general ethnology, and for a time could even pass for the main stream that took all tributaries into itself. It must be said, however, that between the famous second work and the forgotten first there prevails a true twin relationship, as perhaps never before has it been so much the case that in two books, which appeared two years apart and at two different places of publication, each cites the other copiously, so that without a glance at the date on the title page one would have to take either for the later.

If, then, a book is both a bibliographical unique and has been able to prevail with a content much contradicted; if, further, two generations after its appearance it still contains things that are really to be heard only now; and if, finally, this ancient matter, which is called to work a new effect, speaks a language that moves the heart: then it can only be gratifying, and it ought not to be censured as an artificial revival, when the first edition, wholly exhausted and obtainable only in a few antiquarian copies, is replaced by a new one. This business decision becomes, however, a point of honor for a publishing house that has always made it its task, in a particular way, to cultivate in the book trade the literature of the city of Basel, and that would now like to see this work too, published by its predecessors in the firm, honored anew by wider circulation as an outstanding monument of the Basel spirit of research.

When Bachofen wrote this visionary, symbol-psychological first work in his native city, atmospheric, solemn burial places were among its ornaments. In many cases the old city churches were still surrounded by their parish graveyards, or contained them in their choir annexes. In the corners of the city ramparts or at the flanks of old gates there stretched deep-sunken God’s acres, with ivy-covered, half-collapsing masonry that enclosed in an unforgettable way the ineffable mood of consoling transience. And in the courtyard of the unique Minster there is still sought out today, as a hallowed sight, the quadrangle of venerable family tombs, set at the foot of the red towers around a flower garden: the cloister. This cloister, since it adorns the battlement of the city’s Pfalz above the river Rhine at the crest of its incomparable curve, enjoys besides that union of the burial ground with the living, hurrying water in which Bachofen saw an essential relation of primal veneration of the dead: “All necropolises lie beside a body of water. The murmur of the wave seems to rustle the dead man’s eternal praise, as an epigram of the Anthology puts it, and according to Aeschylus in the Prometheus the rippling springs of the

[PDF 7]

sacred streams bewail their affliction.” In this way of regarding things there lies the power, hardly yet come to its full effect, of Bachofen’s Mortuary Symbolism, now stepping out into the world for the second time. Its justification as a scholarly offering can be measured almost with logical consistency. In every age, in every place on earth, as long as human hearts have beaten and beat, there is a feeling that will always be found the same, undiminished; it is the grief of the bereaved for those of their own torn from them. This grief has found its expression on the funerary monuments of the ancients, and so the interpretation of pictorial representations on sarcophagi is to be likened to a particular language that mourning for the dead has created for itself. Because we know exactly what feeling here comes to utterance, and because besides this feeling has remained accessible to us from our own experience, sepulchral archaeology in Bachofen’s hands has been transformed from a mere professional specialty into a systematic observatory, from which deep glimpses can be had into the soul life of the devout paganism that was filled with the experience of images and, mirrored in it, into the labyrinth of our own breast. Those who are able to repeat Bachofen’s deep glimpses, heavy with intimation, which were given to him, will never be many, but they may gladly become more numerous than they are at present. To feel along with what Bachofen’s psychology of symbols opens to us is a privilege that has only just become free. May it be the fate of this second edition that, as substantially more real understanders can be granted to it than, given the circumstances, once to the first, this should also truly be the case.

To the wish of the publisher that I should introduce this work of our fellow citizen, important beyond example, with a preface, I could respond on my part only with the simultaneous request that Ludwig Klages be invited to write a proper introduction that would disclose the meaning and worth of the book. An elective affinity of gift has let him, since his youth, divine the significance of Bachofen for the investigation of the human soul. Without him, of this much I am certain, the revelatory nature of such symbolic research would have remained undiscovered. With the grateful acceptance of his insights, the understanding of Bachofen’s antique dignity as a seer moves far beyond mere reading into the magic circle of a real interpretation of essence. Basel, 25 November 1924 (the 37th anniversary of Bachofen’s death).

Carl Albrecht Bernoulli.

[PDF 8]

On Bachofen.

Even if we did not lack the time for an appreciation of the Mortuary Symbolism, we could hardly comply better with the publisher’s wish, that the welcome new edition of the mighty work be accompanied by a brief elucidation, than by reproducing from our book Vom Kosmogonischen Eros* those sentences from which, three years ago, the decisive impetus proceeded toward the awakening of a rapidly spreading interest, in the widest circles, in the personality of Bachofen and in his significance for the science of religion, never before fully recognized. The passage in question forms the second and concluding part of a retrospective consideration that seeks to characterize the main lines of the study of legend and of the mysteries in the last century and that, from the age of the post-Romantic thinkers, brings out the imperishable merits above all of men like Laistner, Mannhardt, Pfannenschmid, Rohde. Then it goes on as follows.

“However highly one may rate the value as discovery of many of the foregoing works, none of them has brought about a thoroughgoing change in our conception of the ‘primitive’ state of consciousness. It would be saying too much were we to claim that it had attached itself to the two names now to be opened; but this at least we may state, that it is beginning to attach itself to the one of them, and we add as our conviction that it is destined to be completed in the second. Nietzsche’s The Birth of Tragedy signifies the beginning of a new interpretation of the psychic foundations of antiquity, and thus of the whole of prehistory in general, and henceforth must be known and worked through by everyone who wants at all to venture upon the investigation of symbolic thinking and mythic dreaming. Inessential defects of the highly significant work

* Georg Müller Verlag, Munich.

[PDF 9]

are to be seen in the adoption of Schopenhauerian technical terms and in the drawing in of problems of music (especially those of the Wagner hullabaloo), an essential one, on the other hand, in that quite unsharply delimited conception of Apollinism which has prevented the discoverer from noticing its identity of meaning with the ‘Socratism’ so thoroughly familiar to him! — Before, however, Nietzsche, through his magnificent renewal of the knowledge of the metaphysics of the Dionysian, let its antithesis to the day world of the Olympians emerge in the primordial state of the soul, there had been completed in the mind of another researcher what ‘lower’ mythology, and with it the philosophical longing of the whole of Romanticism, sought without however finding it: the insight, namely, that surely in the Mediterranean circle of peoples, but most probably in humanity as a whole, a ‘Chthonism’ of night-consciousness preceded the ‘Uranism’ of day-consciousness and everywhere yielded to the latter only after heavy and in part bloody struggle.

It was J. J. Bachofen (1815–1887) who, with his two chief works, Mutterrecht and Mortuary Symbolism of the Ancients, undertook to interpret the whole prehistory of the West from the standpoint of the struggle between ‘matriarchalism’ and ‘patriarchalism’; who with divinatory certainty laid bare in legends and symbols the substratum of their oldest formative impulses; and who was able to support, with the pillars of unexampled learning, the thesis of the existence of a primordial religion unconcerned with the barriers of time and peoples, whose associated forms of society, concepts of law, usages, customs, and conceptions of the gods stand in the sharpest contradiction to all, but absolutely all, convictions and commandments of the rational bearer of ‘world history’! The matter did not remain without notice. The ethnologists took it up first, and behold: a Morgan, a Kowalewsky, a Lubbock, etc. were in a position to demonstrate among numerous ‘primitive peoples’, as still existing today, precisely those institutions and customs that Bachofen had merely inferred from the cult ideas of antiquity! Ethnology and jurisprudence alike have meanwhile incorporated Bachofen’s concept of mother right. Advocates of communism such as the highly learned Kropotkin sought with its help to forge from the natural history of mankind weapons against the capitalist dogma of property. Passionate controversies flared up over the nature, age, and origin of the family and have, in their turn, contributed substantially to the broadening and deepening of our knowledge of the earliest tribal associations of mankind. But who has to this day even an intimation that in Bachofen the perhaps greatest discloser of that primeval

[PDF 10]

state of consciousness is to be acknowledged, in relation to whose cultic and mythic deposits, one and all, absolutely all doctrines of faith of historical humanity appear in the light of dilutions or decompositions of the primal source!

The author of these lines confesses that the acquaintance with Bachofen’s chief works that fell to him around the turn of the century was his greatest literary experience and decisively co-determined his further life. Of the suggestions that he then passed on to a small group of Munich researchers and writers, some — more or less anonymously — have meanwhile continued to have effect. On the whole and in essentials, however, the philosophy of religion and the study of myth have not yet arrived where a Bachofen already stood in the sixties of the last century. For writings such as, say, Mutter Erde by Dieterich, which, superficially considered, to be sure seem to tread similar paths (without Bachofen, so far as we see, being so much as mentioned!), remain immeasurably behind the works of the pathbreaker in profundity as in breadth of view. — Bachofen supplied for the Romantic idea of polarity, with a body of evidence not remotely exhausted even today, the proof of its origin in the primordial consciousness of humanity. Earth and heaven, night and day, moon and sun, water and fire, left and right, etc., belong together in pairs in a like sense, as body and soul do, and are thought, through the same reciprocal relation, as incessantly renewing the world, like the female receptive and the male generative principle. The unity so polarized is grasped in the symbol of the mother as well as of the child, whose again polar connection sustains the mystery faith of the eternal cycle. Thereby the whole of events itself appears in the image of a maternity ceaselessly rejuvenating itself through uninterrupted giving birth in the child, and accordingly every individual living being enters into a binding relation of dependence not, as Bachofen thought, on woman, but on one and the same mother, or more correctly on the egg, the life cell. From this results an overvaluation of the psychic readiness for conception and pregnancy as against the generative principle, which performs, as it were, merely auxiliary services — an overvaluation whose consequences for the shaping of morals are incalculable. Bachofen demonstrated down to the detail that there existed, quite ‘beyond good and evil’, a ‘natural law’ undisturbed by any arbitrariness of legislation, which safeguarded the most intimate connection both of man with the world and of men with one another. While, however, with his thoughts of the heart he unswervingly pursued in countless interpretations of symbols the

[PDF 11]

goal just indicated — we recall only his disclosure of the primal meaning of all the usages and arrangements in the Greek agon, to which nothing in the whole study of legend is comparable in seer-like clairvoyance —, his thoughts of the head stand under the influence of the religion of the will of Christianity and mislead him into taking the process, documentable partly historically, partly prehistorically, by which spirit, in and for itself utterly alien to images, takes possession step by step of the day side of life, for a self-overcoming and higher development of the primordial state. The same researcher who on the one hand, in words that murmur like subterranean springs, extols the self-enclosed perfection of the maternally embracing Chthonism, in comparison with which everything later signifies only peaceless unrest, manages on the other to misunderstand the irruption of the peace-disturbing counter-will as a transition to a ‘higher stage’ of civilization! This bewildering to-and-fro between heart and head, not in the least conscious to its bearer, was certainly not the least of what stood in the way of the understanding of the great discoverer and of his recognition.

Nevertheless Bachofen succeeded in freeing the image of the primordial soul from the whitewash of the millennia and in letting us divine its inexpressible beauty. To offer the epistemological key to the profundity and truth of this image is one of our own life tasks.”

This is not the place to make visible the points of connection of our own findings with those of Bachofen, or to speak of our, alas, too early departed companion Alfred Schuler, to whose differently natured continuation of Bachofen’s fundamental ideas only his posthumous papers will bear witness. Likewise, as remarked, we must forgo going into the Mortuary Symbolism more closely, and wish in this connection only to remark further that precisely it brings the deepest and most comprehensive contribution to the interpretation of the agonal circus games. — On the other hand, let one more word be permitted about Bachofen’s fame, just now setting in belatedly.

If Plato’s saying of wisdom, “Thyrsus-bearers are many, genuine inspired ones few,” ever held, it holds today. Hardly has a thought of profundity become audible when crowds of the uncalled throng forward to shout it out as if it were their property. One pretends to have long known what one has only just heard, and outbids oneself in exaggerations of its content. The literati fabricate novellas and dramas out of it; the adventurers falsify unscrupulously their reports about regions still somewhat inconvenient to travel, and nine-times-wise

[PDF 12]

history-prattlers are in the happy position of being able henceforth even to dispense with their preschool knowledge, since the pilfered material suffices to serve up to a credulous public, for a decade and a half, entertaining fancies about the course of development of mankind. We live in the age of business, and “full of solemn buffoons is the market place” (Zarathustra). Should Bachofen become “the fashion” (which may all good spirits forbid!), he will soon be buried deeper under his fame than he was before under his obscurity.

Even now the critical voices of solid classical philologists are stirring, warning against Bachofen as a will-o’-the-wisp. We need hardly say that they are incomparably dearer to us than the adulations of the exploiters and parasites who live on the desecration of his legacy. Only, one should never let oneself be wholly determined by a judgment that derives merely from defense, however justified! Whoever today wants to have a say in questions of antiquity, and above all of the early period of spirit, must know Bachofen. And he must not only have read him, he must have checked him to the best of his ability. He will then know that Bachofen, as in view of so immense a field of research cannot be otherwise, has erred in numerous details (especially etymological ones). But he would deceive himself if he held himself entitled to seek the remaining value of his work in intimations, scents, doubtful “intuitions,” or even in mere outpourings of feeling and enthusiasms. Though we cannot prove it at this place, let it nevertheless be said: The findings circumscribed by the above sentences stand rightly; they are not conjectures, suggestions, aperçus, but discoveries, whose luminosity will first fully prove itself when the controversies of the present have long fallen silent.

Ludwig Klages.

Foreword.

The Villa Pamphili, so famous for its magnificent situation outside the Porta San Pancrazio on the old Via Aurelia, has at various times drawn the attention of antiquarians by the columbaria discovered within its bounds. The first finds coincide with Santi Bartoli’s settling in Rome. Of them nothing has been preserved to us but the brief mention that that famous contemporary of Pietro Bellori, so enthusiastic for antiquity, took up into the preface of his work on tombs (Antichi sepolcri, Roma 1679). Of later excavations Niebuhr communicates in the Kleine Schriften 1, 337 a report that leaves us wholly in ignorance of their artistic and archaeological significance. These discoveries had almost fallen into oblivion when the year 1838 set a new one beside them. The columbarium brought to light at that time distinguished itself by the great number and unusual variety of its wall paintings. Nevertheless only slight attention fell to its share. Made aware of it by a brief description by the late Emil Braun in the Bulletino 1838, p. 4 f., I visited the tomb building at the end of the year 1842. The impression that the sight of this place of eternal rest made upon me was all the deeper because, apart from the two columbaria of the Porta Latina discovered a few years before by Cavaliere Campana, I had not yet seen any similar structure. My visits repeated themselves. The proximity of the Vatican, in whose library I then spent many a morning, offered frequent occasion for this. The beauty of the gardens, the magnificent view that they open, the contemplation of ancient works, which lets the centuries that separate us from antiquity vanish for moments at least, and in addition the magic of novelty and the freshness of enjoyment that a first sojourn in Rome in one’s youth affords: all this united to awaken an interest that was assured of lasting into later life. To those visits I owe the first impulse to the study of the ancient world of the tombs, which has since led me twice more to Italy

[PDF 14]

and has found new nourishment in Greece. In my continued reading of the ancient authors I have never failed to attend to everything that they offer on tombs and the tomb cult. Thus there accumulated over a series of years a body of material that brought the wish and the need of scholarly treatment ever nearer. When I had undertaken this for the purpose of several lectures in the Basel Antiquarian Society and had won some applause thereby, I returned with particular fondness to that Pamphili columbarium which had formed for me the point of departure of so enjoyable a study, and which, through some tracings taken on the spot from the wall itself, invited ever renewed contemplation even at a distance. Two of the numerous wall paintings claimed my attention in particular. The one attracted me by the new turn in which it presents the representation, preserved also in the Campana columbarium, of the rope-plaiting Ocnus, the other by the significance that it attaches to three two-colored eggs lying on a tripod. When I laid these two tomb paintings before the Basel Antiquarian Society for contemplation some years ago, they were not yet published, and had become known only here and there through the reproductions, exhibited in the Munich Antiquarium, by the skillful painter Carlo Ruspi. Since then the whole circle of the Pamphili pictures, three excepted, which are withdrawn from the gaze of the public at Munich as well, has been disseminated in lithographic reproduction through the Abhandlungen der königlich Bairischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, vol. 8, pt. 2, and furnished with brief elucidations by Otto Jahn. The appearance of this meritorious publication has at last ripened my long-cherished thought of laying the fruits of my own research before learned friends of antiquity for examination. The three mystery eggs and Ocnus the rope plaiter form the basis and point of departure of two essays on the mortuary symbolism of the ancients, to which I sought to secure, by the detailed treatment of many of the darkest parts of this still so little trodden field and by the tracing back of particulars to comprehensive conceptions of the ancient world, a significance reaching far beyond the domain of the archaeology of art. Over tomb and tomb cult the hurrying centuries and all the innovations that they bring with them have only slight power. Their symbolism, rooted in the oldest views of our race, reaches down unchanged, even if at last no longer understood, into the times of sinking paganism and beyond these into the new year of the world that the incarnation of Christ has opened. Later and earlier generations enter into immediate contact, and with the meaninglessness of separation in time there is joined that of national

[PDF 15]

difference and spatial distance. For the former the egg symbol supplies a most remarkable example; the latter emerges no less surprisingly in the rope-plaiting Ocnus, whom Egypt, Asia, Greece, and Italy know in the same way. The great significance that the ancient world of the tombs gains precisely through this character of constancy and immutability is still further heightened by the insight that it opens to us into the fairest side of the ancient spirit. If other parts of the science of antiquity are able to engage our understanding, the contemplation of the necropolises wins our heart, and is able not only to enrich our knowledge but also to afford nourishment to deeper needs. Where occasion offered, I have not failed to turn my consideration to this side too, and, so far as in me lay, to seek to bring back to consciousness those thoughts whose fullness and loftiness at the place of death only the symbol, not language, is able to set forth. Thereby I have above all done justice to a need of my own nature, but perhaps also come nearer to the highest goal of all research into antiquity, which is to disclose in their lofty beauty the ideas of earlier generations to an age that stands greatly in need of refreshment, than is attainable by a contemplation that clings to the form and surface of things. To collect mere material was not my intention. Collectanea constitute no treatment and give no understanding. If I have touched upon a great number of particulars, it was nevertheless only for the purpose of ascending through them to ideas of wider scope, and of finding the point of connection for much that seems wholly accidental and incoherent. So I have more than once departed from the great highway to look for flowers on side paths, and then, a while later, with fresher courage, to return to the abandoned road. Research has thereby gained in variety without, as I hope, losing in unity. The right connection of the particular and the general is the secret in which all understanding rests. If each is worthless by itself, they form together by their union a whole that satisfies equally both sides of the human spirit, its need for variety and its striving for unity. This is the supreme law by which I drafted the following essays, and by which I should also like to see them judged.

The Three Mystery Eggs.

A Tomb Painting.

Plate 3.

[p. 1]

The tomb painting reproduced on the third plate is perfectly definite and clear in all its details. A company of five youths surrounds a small three-legged table on which three eggs have been laid down. The individual figures appear almost wholly alike, a likeness that is nevertheless saved from monotony by the differences in the fall of the upper garment, in gesture, in the bearing and presentation of the body, and by the skillful grouping of the whole. Barefoot and bareheaded, the ephebes sit distributed on benches and direct their attention to the table standing in the middle, whose three eggs seem to form the subject of an earnest conversation. In this the two figures moved farthest into the foreground, on the right and on the left, take the liveliest part, while the three figures distributed in the background are confined rather to the role of listeners. Least active appears the figure on the right side, removed even in space from the circle of the others, whose addition seems to have been imposed on the artist by the necessity of the number five. Particular attention is drawn by the myrtle wreath that encircles the head of one of the youths, and no less by the burning oil lamp that another carries on the flat palm of his outstretched left arm. These two attributes would put the religious content of the whole representation beyond doubt, were it not already evident enough from the absence of footwear and head covering. The sacred significance of the lamp is quite compatible with the daylight, which allows the outlines of buildings, a temple and a hall, to be made out in the distance. The gathering of the youths takes place by day and under the open sky, and the four-sided, cube-shaped block of stone, the moles nativa1) that is visible in the foreground, shows the open field to be the place of meeting. In this tomb painting ancient art has followed its procedure, grounded in the oldest, symbolic tendency of all representation, of suggesting rather than elaborating the secondary

1) Ovid. Fast. 5, 149.

[PDF 18]

—4—

details, in the most felicitous application. The whole, however, shows in simplicity of composition, art of grouping, symmetry in the distribution of persons and accessories, and in the most measured fusion of repose and movement an adherence to the grandeur and mastery of the perfected style, which lends high artistic interest even to works of art of a later time, and to a wholly handicraft-like, hasty, and careless decoration of the tombs of subordinate classes of the people.

In describing the Pamphili painting we passed over a circumstance that is now to serve as the point of departure of our whole discussion. The three eggs laid down on the table show a peculiarity that has been brought out on our plate 3 in exact adherence to the Munich copy. They are not of a single color, but divided lengthwise, painted white in the upper half, dark in the lower. And this division repeats itself in all three with the same sharpness and definiteness. Were this appearance isolated, it would still have to be retained and explained as a significant feature. But earlier tomb finds show the same peculiarity, and so exclude as impossible the assumption of an optical illusion or of an accident rooted in artistic license. Most decisively there confronts us here a Lamberg vase of the Vienna Cabinet. Since I have seen it repeatedly myself, I can speak with full certainty, and can charge Laborde’s illustration with a lack of accuracy in the detail most important for us. On a pyramidal base consisting of three receding steps sits a naked, bearded Silenopappos. His left hand holds a mighty thyrsus, his right a myrtle wreath, which seems intended for a female figure, clothed in a long transparent chiton, who bears toward him an egg-shaped body. From the middle step there hangs down a fillet fastened in the manner of a garland and forked at both ends. On the same step stands, upright on its rounder end,1) an egg that shows precisely that double coloring. Divided lengthwise, the colors are separated in a sharp line. The right half is dark red, like the fillet, the left light. The agreement of this representation with that of the Pamphili tomb is complete. Beside the egg of the middle step the vase picture shows also

Columella R. R. 8, 5. med. makes mention. Cum deinde quis volet quam plurimos mares excludi, longissima quæque et acutissima ova subiiciet, et rursus cum feminas, quam rotundissima. Hence it may come that the eggs of the Pamphili tomb as well as that of the Lamberg vase are divided lengthwise. A division by the breadth would have emphasized the difference of the sexes.

1) The round end is the female, the pointed the male. Hence the belief of which

a quite small round body, which repeats itself on the topmost step in a pair. A certain determination is not readily possible. But I scarcely doubt that we have before us here nuts, whose natural significance is indeed generally known. However that may be, as to the egg and its double dark and light coloring the evidence of the eye admits of no doubt. — What the monuments represent pictorially, written testimonies also mention. Mercury was represented in pictures with a half-black, half-white pileus. This is attested by Albericus Philosophus, de Deorum imagin. 6., who, though he belongs to the Middle Ages, nevertheless draws on a good older source. — de viro in fœminam et de fœmina in masculum se mutabat, cum volebat: et ideo pingebatur cum utroque sexu. De albis vero nigra et de nigris alba faciebat, quod ostenditur per eius pileum semialbum et seminigrum.1) The same idea is transferred to Mercury’s son Autolycus, whose art of turning black into white and white into black is emphasized by Ovid Met. 11, 314, Nat. 5, 5, Hygin. f. 201. Philostratus tells in the Life of Apollonius 3, 3 that in the swamps of the Hyphasis that philosopher found a woman who from the head to the breast had been black, from the breast to the feet quite white. She was consecrated to the Indian Aphrodite, and as to Apis in Egypt, so to this goddess a variegated woman is born. Particularly significant is what Hyginus f. 4 reports of the Ino of Euripides. She bears twins to Athamas, as does Themisto. Jealousy drives the latter to consecrate Ino’s children to destruction. The twins destined for death are to be covered with black garments, Themisto’s children with white. But Ino chooses the white garments for her own offspring, and puts the black ones on Themisto’s children. So Themisto slaughters her own sons, and then kills herself in despair. The meaning of the double color emerges in this narrative with full certainty. Black belongs to the realm of shadow, white to that of light. The significance continues in the ficus nigra and ficus alba, and here it is all the more noteworthy the higher the position that the fig tree occupies in the ancient nature religions, especially in the phallic cult of Dionysus. According to Veranius de verbis pontificalibus the ficus alba belongs to the felices arbores, the ficus nigra, according to the ostentarium Thuscum or arborarium, to the infelices.2) The opposition of white and black can be traced on a great number of funerary vases, in the most various

In an inscription in Fornerius, rer. quotid. 2, 27 we read: mortuum me quoque funerari jussi rebus lugubribus quibus vivos paravi lecto stragulis forensi penula, nigris omnibus. Hence the black ground color of so many funerary vases, and the black funerary ware of the Chiusine tombs, which adorns our museums in such great number. In other places white is raised to the color of mourning. Of Spartans, Messenians, Romans the ancients attest that the women wear white garments for mourning and that the body of the deceased is dressed in white.4) To Aristodemus his daughter appears clothed in black, and brings him white garments with a golden crown. In this he recognizes the foreboding of his destruction. When here the color of light is brought into connection with death, it is not the destruction of the body but the passage of the soul to life in the realm of light that is the guiding conception. “The corpse is adorned in this way,” says Plutarch, “because one cannot do so with the soul, and yet would gladly send it forth pure and shining, since it is now, after hard and manifold struggle endured, released from its bonds.”

We are no longer here, therefore, in the domain of purely corporeal life, but confront that higher mystery idea which sees in the death of the body the precondition of the passage of the soul to a higher state. In this sense the white color combines quite preeminently with lustration, as indeed the Erinyes in Aeschylus, after Orestes’ atonement, have laid aside the black color and exchanged it for the white; likewise

From the combination of all these testimonies and monuments it results as wholly beyond doubt that the double coloring of the eggs of our tomb painting is not only no accidental circumstance but, on the contrary, a most significant one. Its meaning can be subject to no doubt. The alternation of the light and the dark color expresses the constant transition from darkness to light, from death to life. It shows us tellurian creation as the result of eternal becoming and eternal passing away, as a never-ending movement between two opposite poles. If this idea deserves our highest attention on account of its inner truth, one must at the same time admire the simple expression of the symbol. By the mere opposition of the light and the dark color an idea is brought to view the whole depth of which it seemed to the greatest of the philosophers of antiquity

May we not assume that the conversation which stirs the five ephebes of our tomb painting to such lofty earnestness and such lively participation was concerned precisely to unveil this side of the egg symbol? Certainly no subject is so fitting to the earnestness of the tomb as this one. Certainly no question is brought so near by death as that about the relation of the two poles between which all tellurian existence moves. Certainly, however, no symbol is more suited to raise the spirit beyond the limits of corporeal existence to the intimation of its own rebirth than that of the egg, which encloses life and death within itself, joins them both into an inseparable unity, and lets everything that has become invisible step forth anew into the light.1) That is indeed the lofty dignity and the fullness, rich in intimation, of the symbol, that it admits and even itself stimulates different stages of conception, and leads on from the truths of physical life to those of a higher spiritual order. Yet I do not wish to set up fictions, nor to let myself be carried further away in lending to our tomb company thoughts to which it has perhaps always remained a stranger.2) — I shall deserve better thanks if I here communicate, in its main outlines at least, a conversation that is handed down to us by an ancient author. As on our picture the egg forms the center of the conversation, so in Plutarch Senecio, Alexander, Sulla, and Firmus also make the egg again the subject of a conversation that touches upon the highest questions concerning the origination of the cosmos, as well as of material creation. I am far from the assumption that the artist to whom we owe our picture had precisely that conversation before his mind, and that he sought to depict that symposium pictorially with his brush.

From the physical standpoint this question is among the insoluble. For every egg presupposes a hen, but just as surely every hen a preexisting egg. Negant (Aristoteles, Theophrastus multique Peripatetici) omnino posse reperiri, avesne ante an ova generata sint, cum et ovum sine ave, et avis sine ovo gigni non possit,3) so that the birds of Aristophanes, too, in their parody of the mystery doctrine, trace themselves back to the primal egg as its eldest birth.4) It is otherwise from the religious standpoint. In religion the egg is the symbol of the material primal ground of things, the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. Of all that Firmus adduces for his assertion, the following is especially important. “Ἀείσω ξυνετοῖσι τὸν Ὀρφικὸν καὶ Ἱερὸν λόγον, ὃς οὐκ ὄρνιθος μόνον τὸ ᾠὸν ἀποφαίνει πρεσβύτερον, ἀλλὰ καὶ συλλαβὼν ἅπασαν αὐτῷ τὴν ἁπάντων ὁμοῦ πρεσβυγένειαν ἀνατίθησι. Of the rest,” he continues, “I must keep a pure mouth, for it is far too mystical. But I venture to assert that among the many kinds of animals that the earth contains, not a single one is excluded from origination out of the egg, but that rather the egg brings forth the countless in the doctrines of the Bacchic mysteries of Greece contains the oldest theology, leading back first of all to Egypt. The high antiquity of this Aristotle himself acknowledges repeatedly in the passages cited by Creuzer, Symb. 4, 28. It may likewise be granted that the Orphic poems, as they have come down to us, and the sources from which Damascius drew, may have originated in a late period. Nevertheless the doctrines laid down in them lose nothing of their truly Orphic character, because only what contained Orphic doctrine could successfully be given out as Orphic. In saying this I do not at all concede, moreover, that the form of the songs is really of as late an origin as people seem inclined to assume, although a succession of Orphic schools will have exercised manifold influence on their final shape.

flying and swimming animals, land animals like the lizards, amphibians like the crocodiles, two-footed ones like the hen, animals without feet, like the serpent, and many-footed ones too, like the locust.1) Ὅθεν οὐκ ἀπὸ τρόπου τοῖς περὶ τὸν Διόνυσον ὀργιασμοῖς, ὡς μίμημα τοῦ τὰ πάντα γεννῶντος καὶ περιέχοντος ἐν ἑαυτῷ, συγκαθωσίωται.”

Let us pause here for a moment. Firmus appeals to the significance of the egg in the Bacchic mysteries. Here it is the symbol of the all-birth-giving being that contains everything within itself. We may lay full weight on this explanation, because Plutarch, so pious and so worthy in his religious views, himself belonged to the initiates, as he expressly reports to us. The same high position and significance is held by the egg in Orphic doctrine, and for that reason it is also sacred to the Pythagoreans, those reformed Orphics. It forms the true center of the Orphic-Bacchic mysteries, and of that Ἱερὸς λόγος which the initiates know and to which the Ἀείσω ξυνετοῖσι — alludes. It is that πρωτογενὲς ᾠόν, ἐν ᾧ σπερματικῶς τὸ ζῷόν ἐστι,2) as Proclus writes in Timæum 3, 130 according to Orphic doctrine. How perfectly this significance agrees with the symbolic meaning of the double color I scarcely need to indicate. The material primal ground of things, which out of itself brings forth all life into the light, encloses both, becoming and passing away. It bears within itself at one and the same time the light side and the shadow side of nature. The Orphic primal egg is half white, half black or red, just as Typhon, too, the destructive force, is represented as red.3) Indeed, these colors pass into one another as constantly as life and death, day and night, becoming and passing away. They exist, then, not merely side by side but within one another. Death is the precondition of life, and only in the same measure in which destruction advances can the creative force become active as well. At every moment becoming and passing away go on side by side. The life of every tellurian organism is the effect of a combined double force, the creative and the destructive. Only so far as the latter takes away can the former replace. No idea has found, in the ancient

We recognize it in the rope of Ocnus-Aucnus, which the she-ass again and again devours; in the web of Penelope and of Tarchetius’s daughter,1) which is unraveled again every night; in the unoutwittable thieves of the Egyptian legend of Rhampsinitus, and in the game of dice with Demeter, in which the king alternately wins and loses:2) pictures of the eternally vain labor of nature, which knows how to bring about an eternal rejuvenation of the race only with the help of eternal destruction. We find it again in the ring of Gyges, which makes the unity of the two opposing potencies of natural force quite vivid through the unity of the ring, turned now inward, now outward.3) The same thing recurs in the conceptions of two contending horses and ravens mentioned above; in the ἑτερημερία4) of the Dioscuri, who have sprung from the same egg and in their antithetical union repeat the significance of the alternation of colors. On a line with them stands the Elean pair of brothers, the Molionidae. Sprung from one egg, they drive united the same two-horse team, inseparable as death and life, flying along unattainably swift as eternal becoming and passing away.

However incorrect the etymology set up here may be, since Palici belongs with Pales, Paris, Palilia, palus, phalæ to the stem Pal-Pel, the explanation of the matter that is attached to it is nonetheless telling. The twin pair of the Palici steps forth out of the realm of shadow into that of light, in order to return from the latter to the former, and with every sowing and every harvest to begin the cycle anew. As a twin pair they correspond entirely to the Dioscuri and the Molionidae, and their duality must also be conceived as ἑτερημερία, or an alternating emergence into the daylight and disappearance again. As the light side and the shadow side of nature they stand beside one another like the two Lares, the sons of Mania, like Romulus and Remus, whose union is conceived according to the same religious idea; thus Romulus in the myth in Plutarch parall. min. 32 is thought of as a true Pyrander (31), but in his dismemberment, like Zagreus, as Dionysus Isodaites, and hence represents the light side of natural force, as Remus and his empty θρόνος represent the corresponding night side. — The half black, half white hat of Hermes corresponds especially well to his double nature, by virtue of which he dwells alternately in the heights of light and again in the sunless spaces of the underworld. Like the Castors, the sons of Oedipus rule alternately.1) On their altar the flame divides into two columns blowing eternally in opposite directions.2) The Silenus captured in the rose garden proclaims to Midas the secret of the spring of sorrow and of that of joy.3) “The ceaselessly flowing stream of origination will never stand still, any more than the stream of destruction flowing against it, Acheron or Cocytus, however the poets may name it.” So Plutarch writes to Apollonius,4) and in many passages the ancients bring out the same idea as the fundamental law governing all tellurian creation. “Everywhere in mysteries and sacrifices, among Greeks as among barbarians, it is taught, says Plutarch de Is.

Therefore Isis grants freedom to the captive Typhon. She knows that the constant mixture of the two potencies is indispensable. Typhon may indeed be overcome, but not cleared out of the way. The struggle goes on eternally, and as often as Typhon is taken captive, he tears himself loose again and fights with Horus. “Horus, however, is the world surrounding the earth, in which origination and destruction alternate with one another.”1)

From this is explained the frequency of the pairs of brothers, who appear now as eternally warring with one another, now as amicably united, mostly as twins. They are in fact both at once, two opposites united as one. They are enemies, they fight one another eternally, like life and death, becoming and passing away, and thereby preserve for creation its eternal youthful freshness. They thus press on together toward the same goal, like the Molionidae; indeed, the swift flight of the team arises precisely from the fact that the white and the black horse direct their effort toward one goal. How different this conception seems from that which emerges in the reciprocal murder of the sons of Oedipus. And yet they are only two different sides of the same fundamental idea that find expression here, and that recur in a third form in the many examples of involuntary fratricide. The twin union of the two forces is especially characteristic of their relation. Twins in the same sense are Sleep and Death, of whom the latter represents dying, Sleep the reawakening to life.2) “Homer attests it when he says:

And in another place:

They are the two forces that govern creation, devour one another, yet ever lead life back from the darkness to the light. The two Attines, on many gravestones, which Dr. Haak2) has so beautifully elucidated, attach themselves to the same idea, which also reemerges in the double scourge of the two Keres of death.3)

The alternation of the two colors has been emphasized by the ancients in many ways and under various images as the fundamental law of tellurian life. From Plutarch’s beautiful letter of consolation to Apollonius on the death of his son I single out the following passages of old poets:

“The turning of the wheel brings one felloe up first,

And alternately now the other as well.”

“The race of mortals goes, like the realm of plants,

Ever in a circle. The one blooms up to life,

While the other dies and is mown down.”

Two sayings which have all the more significance because the images of the wheel and of the circle ever running back into its beginning, used in them, do not rest on arbitrary poetic invention but are taken from the oldest symbolism, in particular that of the world of the tombs. “The human race,” says Plato in the Laws 4, p. 721, “and the whole of time are of one nature. The former runs on with the latter and will endure beside it, and is in this way immortal, in that it always leaves behind children and the children of those children, thereby remains at all times one and the same, and through constant becoming has a share in immortality.”4) How this idea recurs in the Orphic Χρόνος ἀγήρατος with the double head and the egg we shall illuminate later. In Euripides, Andromache 418, we read: πᾶσι δ᾽ ἀνθρώποις ἄρ᾽ ἦν ψυχὴ τέκν᾽, which Apollonius in Philostratus V. A. 2, 15 generalizes thus: πᾶσι δὲ ζῴοις ἄρ᾽ ἦν ψυχὴ τέκν᾽. “Children are for the dying man a saving renown. Like cork they float on the surface of the water, while the net lies hidden below on the bottom.” The idea of the eternal alternation of colors in this world I find again in Plutarch’s work on the inscription Εἶ in the temple at Delphi. Let the correctness of the explanation put forward there remain undecided; the idea laid down in it is independent of that. “If I am to give my opinion about that inscription, that syllable is a self-standing address and greeting to Apollo, which in the soul of him who utters it at the same time awakens a conception of the power of this god. Apollo receives each of us who comes to him with the words: Know thyself! a greeting certainly no worse than the usual one: Χαῖρε, Rejoice. To this we then answer him with the expression Εἶ, you are, and thereby bring him the right, unfalsified, unique greeting, due to him alone, which is taken from his existence. For basically we can lay no claim at all to existence, but every mortal nature hovers always between origination and destruction, and gives only a phantom, a dim and uncertain opinion of itself. If one now strains one’s understanding to grasp it fully and completely, it fares with the understanding as with water that is strongly compressed. For just as the latter, by pressing and squeezing, runs away and is wholly lost, so reflection goes astray when one pursues all too distinct conceptions of any being subject to accidents and changes, now toward its origin, now toward its destruction, without being able to catch hold of anything lasting or truly subsisting.”1) “Is there any time when death is not in us? Living and dead, says Heraclitus (ὁ σκοτεινός, in harmony with his doctrine of the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω), waking and sleeping, young and old are always one and the same, for this is only transformed into that, and that again into this. Just as one can form animals out of the same clay and smash them, and so keep doing one thing after the other, so nature too formerly produced from the same matter our forefathers, afterward our fathers, then ourselves, and will also develop others after others. The ceaselessly flowing stream of origination will never stand still, any more than the stream of destruction flowing against it, Acheron or Cocytus, however the poets may name it. The first cause, then, which shows us the light of the

These two potencies, whose antithetical union sustains the life of creation, are set before our eyes in the two-colored egg. It contains within itself the whole natural force, lets everything come forth into the light3) and takes everything back again into its maternal womb. Through the double force of the twins that it encloses it secures immortality for creation, ut cupide generatim sæcla propagent, shows us in change itself the lasting element, and so corresponds entirely to those primal mothers Aphrodite and Demeter, who in their nature unite life and death as potencies lying within one another, and who, half white, half black, like the Indian Venus, belong to the realm of death no less than to that of light.4)

This conception, then, which belongs to so many symbols and myths, underlies all ancient religion, and from which one learns less about the nature of the gods than about the physical relations of creation,1) to see this conception so greatly pushed into the foreground in the Bacchic mysteries cannot be surprising, if we keep in view the nature of this cult, resting wholly in matter, and the high position that the female-material principle of nature occupies in it in its tendency toward fecundation. The two-colored egg as the center of the Dionysian religion shows us the highest law that governs the transient world as a fate inborn in female matter. Plutarch’s dialogue is repeated by Macrob. be thought of as divided not along its length but across its breadth into the two color halves. The one corresponding to the earth is black, that of heaven light. Thus we found the Indian primal mother white above, black below. The division itself is the work of the force that pervades the egg. It takes place with the help of a hair. Thus in Plato’s Symposium p. 190 the human being who originally, as in the Chaldaean teachings of Berosus,1) united both sexes is cut into two halves, “as when one cuts fruits in order to preserve them, or when they cut eggs with hairs.”2) According to the Persian doctrine3) Horomazes encloses 24 gods in the egg, and Arimanius as many. The former sprang from the purest light, the latter from darkness, opposed to the former in everything and engaged with him in eternal war. The 24 gods begotten by Arimanius break through the egg, and hence comes the mixture of good with evil, of whose struggle the life of the universe consists. Here too we have before us, in another mode of expression, the half black, half white egg; here too the doctrine of Heraclitus, who makes strife the father, king, and lord of all things, and rejects Homer’s principle in Il. 18, 107.4) In the custom of the Persian kings of drinking water mixed with wine from a golden egg one readily recognizes the fundamental religious significance, by virtue of which water as the bearer of all tellurian generation, and wine as its most beautiful product, combine quite naturally with the egg, the content of all material force.5) The conception of the egg as mundi simulacrum, of its two halves as heaven and earth, appears only as a development of that fundamental significance in which we first found it. As the material-female ἀρχὴ γενέσεως the egg bears within itself not only the germ of all life, but is also matter itself, and as the former manifests itself in tellurian generation, so the latter articulates itself into the two great constituents of the universe, earth and heaven, whose circular form is derived from that of the egg and recognized again in it. Thus not only is every tellurian organism contained in the egg σπερματικῶς, but heaven and earth also lie within it μὲν Θαλάτθ, Ἑλληνιστὶ δὲ μεθερμηνεύεσθαι θάλασσα, κατὰ δὲ ἰσόψηφον σελήνη. She is thus the material primal mother conceived as primal water and moon.

still unseparated and actually joined side by side. In both relations the egg is preeminently the elementum of the material world, the principium universitatis, or Moth,1) the maternal primal slime, destined, at a further stage of development, to bring its whole content, still hidden now, to the light. In this unfolding the black half becomes earth, the white half heaven, the former the female-material, the latter the male-incorporeal potency. But as they once rested within one another, so now in their separation they long for constant reunion. “Hence the love of human beings for one another is inborn, in order to restore the original nature, to make one out of two, and to heal human nature.”2) In this longing of the two halves of the egg for reunion is rooted the origination of all things, and the stream of becoming that begins with it, against which the equally strong stream of passing away flows eternally. The power that leads back together what was cut apart is that god born from the egg whom the Orphic doctrines call Metis, Phanes,3) Ericapaeus, Protogonos,4) Heracles-Chronos,5) Eros,6) the Lesbians Enorches,7) the Egyptians Osiris,8) the cock that is hatched from the egg, like the birds in Aristophanes, the serpent-shaped Asclepius, whom the impostor Alexander in Lucian represents as born of an egg, Dionysus, who, as a vase painting depicts him, in unbridled lust of becoming breaks through the shell, and brings to its first revelation that which was hitherto hidden, (ἔτι κνόμενον ἐν τῷ ᾠῷ) the mystery of generative masculinity. Thus the egg is in every relation the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. It encloses within itself all parts of the material world, heaven and earth, light and darkness, the male and the female potency of nature, the stream of becoming and of passing away, the

Isocrates in Helenes encomio 26. Ausonius: Hos genuit Nemesis, sed Leda puerpera fovit. Herod. 2, 112. Serv. Aen. 2, 601; 6, 130. Schol. Od. 2. 298. in Buttmann p. 374. Much effort has been made to bring agreement into the various accounts that meet us here. Such an attempt is found in Adrianus Junius, animadvers. libri sex. 1, 15. Perizonius on Aelian V. H. 4, 5. Spanheim on Callimach. Hymn. in Dianam 232. In this way one misjudges the nature of myth, which delights in presenting the same idea ever anew in a thousandfold turns and combinations. In the birth of the Dioscuri and Tyndaridae from the same egg, and in the equation of the mortal Leda and the immortal Nemesis (Lactant 1, 21.) the fundamental idea shows itself, according to which gods and human beings spring from the same matter, and earthly woman is the mortal image of the great tellurian primal mother. Leda nourishes and tends the offspring of Nemesis; Helen is now regarded as Leda’s daughter, that is: every child is really the offspring of the primal mother, earthly woman only at that place a foster mother, an idea that recurs in many myths. The same relation joins the father with the male natural force; he is its representative, as the myth also emphasizes in the Schol. on Apollon. Rhod. 1, 146. Thus Helen says in Eurip. Hel. 16–22. Tyndareus is my father, but it is told that Zeus begot me. In line 471 she is called ἡ τοῦ Διός, v. 473. ἡ Τυνδαρὶς παῖς. Thus Pentheus in Nonn. Dion. 44, 168: I descend from sun and moon, not from Echion and Agave. This identity of the mortal and the immortal is brought out still more clearly by the fact that Zeus

In the Orphic-Bacchic mystery egg the initiate recognizes not only his own origination but also that of his god, and from this he draws that better hope which holds out to the mortal the lot of the god related to him and sprung with him from the same egg, and gives him the certainty that earthly birth too can break through to the immortality of the higher world of light.

On our tomb painting the initiate is adorned with a wreath about his brow. It is, to be sure, neither an ivy wreath nor a laurel wreath, such as the Bacchic initiations and Dionysus’s manifold connection with Apollo seem to require.2) But definite testimonies name the myrtle wreath as the mark of initiation. So in particular Aristophanes, Ranæ 330.3) The myrtle crown is also represented on the vase painting of the Vienna Cabinet mentioned above, and the myrtle branch on another in Raoul-Rochette mon. inéd. XLIV. A. p. 222. These two monuments are all the more noteworthy because both show the egg in connection with the myrtle. This connection is carried on in the lustrating force common to the egg and the myrtle. A deeper connection, however, shows itself in the fact that the egg as well as the myrtle belongs to the female conception of the great principle of nature. For the myrtle is consecrated to Aphrodite-Venus, the primal mother of all tellurian creation.4)

We recognize, then, in the two prominent objects of the Pamphili tomb painting, the eggs and the myrtle wreath, the tracing back of initiation to the material primal motherhood, from which Dionysus too, διμήτωρ,5) has sprung. The phallic god, directed toward the fecundation of matter, is not what was originally given; he proceeds, rather, himself out of the darkness

and Tyndareus lie with Leda in the same night, whence from the same maternal womb the one comes forth immortal, the other mortal. Tzetz. Lycophr. 88. p. 13 Potter. To such a conception the absolute separation of the world of the gods and the world of human beings was quite foreign: they rather constantly overlap, are materially alike, and sprung from one egg: a view that one must first wholly appropriate if one wants to be qualified and entitled to a judgment on ancient history.

of the maternal womb into the light; he stands to female matter in the relation of a son, and, after breaking through the shell of the egg, reveals the mystery of phallic masculinity hitherto hidden there, at the sight of which even the mother rejoices as at her daemon.1) On this rests the high position that woman occupies in the Bacchic religion, which expresses itself in the adoption of women’s clothing by men as well,2) attested of the Dionysian mysteries, as also in the redemption of his mother Semele-Thyone from the underworld,3) and in the 14 Γεραῖραι.4) One might well often have had occasion to put to oneself the question how it comes about that in the religion of the generative god, bull-shaped and phallic in his innermost nature (πολύσπορος ζωοδοτήρ), not so much the male as rather the female principle of nature stands so much in the foreground, and that in his mysteries not, as at his festival,5) the phallus, whose cult he founds, but the female egg, the female myrtle, and, I add, Minerva’s gift the oil, as well as Demeter’s animal the pig,6) appears as the center of cult and symbolism. The reason is no longer doubtful to us. Of the two sides of nature, the female-material and the male-generative, the former is the one originally and alone present, the one given in principle. Matter harbors the force in its womb, and as sons of the egg (ᾠογενεῖς)7) the gods of phallic nature step forth into the light out of its enclosure. At the head of things stands, then, material woman, and Dionysus like Osiris trace their own origin back to matter, conceived as tellurian or lunar, as primal mother of all things, the Rerum naturæ prisca parens. The man veiled in woman’s garb repeats this relation, no differently from the cista, which harbors the phallus made of fig wood, the tacita secreta cistarum. The force is hidden in darkness, as it performs its work in darkness. What meets the eye is the female matter that carries the phallus within it, whose existence is proclaimed by the generation emerging from the lap of the earth. So Achilles dwells among the Scyrian maidens in women’s clothes until the Tyrrhenian trumpet, which calls the generative bull forth from the waves,1) brings him too and his masculinity to appearance.

2.

This much, then, is established: our tomb painting shows us the egg as the center of the Bacchic mysteries, and thereby the deceased as an initiate of Dionysus. In the same significance other funerary monuments attach themselves to it. I recall first the vase of the Vienna Cabinet already discussed. Another is communicated by Creuzer in the illustrations to the Symbolik und Mythologie, pl. 8. Liber and Libera sit on a hill. To the latter a Silenus holds out the egg, whose significance emerges still more through the connection with the ἱερὸς γάμος of the divine pair, and with the likewise Bacchic-Aphroditean symbol of the hare, distinguished by the generative drive and fertility. Accompanied by grossly sensual representation, the Bacchic mystery egg appears on one of the three tomb paintings of the Pamphili columbarium, whose separate enclosure seemed advisable. Before a man who lies stretched out on the ground, turpius excitata natura, there stands, with her back turned to him, ἀνασυραμένη τὸν χιτωνίσκον,2) a female figure. On the patella that she holds before her lie several eggs, whose significance in this connection can be subject to no doubt. The two monuments named contain a double expression of the same idea. The union of Liber and Libera is repeated in human fashion in the phallic tomb painting. There the sexual union of the immortal god, here its image in the mating of the mortal man. With both the egg is connected, which gives origination to the god as well as to the human being. Both times it is attributed to woman. Thereby she appears in her maternity awaiting fecundation. Dionysus has put an end to the Amazonian, man-hating life of woman, and restored her

to her natural destiny, marriage and giving birth. Captivated by the god’s glory, woman longs for union with him. The relation of enmity dissolves into that of love. Inspired, woman follows the phallic god and fights his battles. Him she wishes to serve, and thereby to fulfill the material destiny of her nature.1) This has found its expression in the egg that she carries. Here it is the symbol of marriage and fecundation. What the egg harbors in its dark womb, the interpenetration of the male and the female potency of nature, that steps forth in Liber and Libera, separated into two independent beings, side by side. Marriage leads it back anew to union. In Liber and Libera this is evidently conceived as a marriage of siblings, as in Isis and Osiris, in Hera and Zeus, in Janus and Camisa. Natural force in its double sexual potency is only one and the same. We recognize the Platonic idea of the original unity of the two sexes, which now, after separation has occurred, strive for constant reunion, so that the two halves, driven by the feeling of their incompleteness, may unite again into the original wholeness.2) This constant return of the separated potencies to the original unity, as it is given in the egg, forms the innermost content of the Dionysian religion and of its mysteries. Apart from female materiality the phallic god cannot be conceived at all.3) Matter, which as mother gave birth to him into the light, now becomes his consort. Bacchus is called at once son of Aphrodite and her spouse.4) Mother, consort, sister run together into one. Matter assumes alternately all these characters.5) In Kore, Demeter returns, in Libera, Ceres. To Kore-Libera Bacchus stands in the same relation as to Demeter-Ceres. He is the fecundator of both, the husband of both. This destiny he fulfills as much in the depths of the earth as in the uranian world. He is the chthonian and heavenly sower of matter, his consorts earth and moon. So Demeter appears beside him at once in the depths of the earth and in heaven,6) Libera at once as Persephone and as Semele,7) Ariadne at once

tellurian and uranian.1) Woman follows all the stages of the Bacchic nature. Inseparably bound to him, she becomes both his chthonian and his uranian consort. The sexual union is always the Dionysian fundamental law, γάμος its realization. Conceived in a more sensual way on the tellurian stage, it attains on the uranian the higher purity of exclusive marriage, to which Psyche, after her mating with the dragon, the dweller in lightless spaces, at last breaks through. The lawless sexual mingling in the moist depths of the earth, as swamp life presents it, rises to the chastity of conjugal union, which has a cosmic model in the exclusive relation of the sun to the moon that follows it.2) The former now appears only as a point of passage for woman to the higher condition, in which alone she finds her peace. Thus the fable of Psyche, which likewise belongs to the mysteries, presents the relation of the two stages to us. Thus we see it again in our two funerary monuments. The grossly sensual representation of the Pamphili painting, which is repeated in still more lascivious fashion on two others, presents that lower stage of the sexual union conceived in a purely Aphroditean way, while Liber and Libera bring to view the life that has broken through to the purity of marriage. In this elevation the egg becomes the symbol of conjugal consecration, and of that τέλος which every γάμος bears within itself.3) From this the number five is explained, which appears in the company of the ephebes on our third plate. I have already pointed out above that the number five of the youths cannot rest on artistic caprice, since this would rather have led to the omission of the figure on the right side. Its addition shows that what was at stake here was the representation of a sacred number. The five is designated by the ancients as marriage. It has proceeded from the male Trias and the female Duas, and therefore counts as the representation of the conjugal union of the two sexes. It is the numerical expression of that ἱερὸς

γάμος, which joins Liber and Libera. Since we shall return to the significance of the quincunx at a later place in this work, it suffices to document it here with a single testimony. In treating the question why the Romans burn five cerei at their weddings, neither more nor fewer, Plutarch Q. R. 2 expresses himself as follows: “Among all the odd numbers the five is best suited to the wedding celebration. For the three is the first odd number, but the two the first even number; and from both, as from man and woman, the five arises through union.”1) The newly married therefore need five gods, just as the Cerealian aediles carry five cerei, and five children count as the highest female birth, and five worlds as the highest conceivable number of worlds. That the Pythagoreans held the odd number to be male and the even to be female is attested by Plutarch Q. R. 102, and this conception certainly came to them from the Orphic doctrine, which attained new currency in their school. In all of nature the most depends on the five, so that even the wise themselves call counting πεμπάζειν.2) The number five of the youths can accordingly no longer appear enigmatic or without meaning. It shows us the female egg in that higher significance as the symbol of the sexual community consecrated by conjugal union, and thus forms the counterpart to the three other representations on the same tomb, which with the greatest emphasis bring to view the lower, Aphroditean and lawless fecundation, condemned by the mysteries.

I proceed with the enumeration and consideration of those funerary monuments in which the egg occupies a prominent position.

In the united collections at Munich there is found a beautiful marble fragment, which may well originally have belonged to a larger representation. If the statement that it comes from Pompeii is correct, we may think of the relief decoration of a funerary column. We see the upper half of a youthful female figure in a rich pleated garment and short sleeves fastened by four clasps. From the luxuriant hair, which a mighty headband holds, two tightly twisted locks develop on either side of the head, reaching down over the neck to the breast. Mighty wings, calmly closed, contribute most

to the effect of the whole. The beauty of the countenance is heightened and ennobled beyond human measure by the deep seriousness which the possession of the initiations alone is able to impart. Between the thumb and the other fingers the right hand, held forward, carries an egg. What the closed fingers of the left hand may have held can no longer be made out with certainty on the lower half, which is still preserved. A torch is the most likely thing to think of. That we have before us the image of the personified Τελετή seems to me beyond doubt. The Victoria-like formation of the wings is not rare on initiation vases and tomb paintings—one need only think of the winged genii hovering amid garlands in one of the Campana tombs at the Porta Latina. It seems to have had its origin precisely in the connection of the mysteries with the female egg principle. In Aristophanes, aves 693–704, the birds issue from the egg as the oldest birth, a representation that belongs to the mystery doctrine and not to free poetic invention. Nemesis, the egg mother, is called by Hygin Poet. Astr. 8 avium generi iuncta. Her Smyrnaean image was formed with wings, a remnant of animal shape that Phidias, when he made his Rhamnusian Mother Upis,1) rejected.2) Aphrodite-Syria,3) so closely akin to Nemesis, issues, according to the Asiatic conception, from an egg that doves hatch. She too could therefore be conceived in the form of a bird, as indeed Semiramis-Aphrodite, the Bacchic daughters of Anius, and the Aphrodito-Julian Ctesylla take on the form of a dove.4) Especially instructive are the Lycian egg mothers, who on the so-called Harpy Monument of Xanthus5) appear not only winged and with bird’s feet, but very distinctly with the egg-shaped body, with strongly prominent maternity in the formation of the breast and in the expression of their virginal countenance. Here the connection of the egg with the wings, the origin of the winged form from the nature of the egg, and the relation of both to the Bacchic mysteries come clearly to light. From this is explained the connection of the wings with Telete, and her special relation to the initiations, whose center is the egg, and whose foundation is the female principle of nature.6) In Telete the mystery mother herself is brought to representation. What these tomb inscriptions express as the hope of the initiate takes bodily form in the figure of Telete, who can therefore be designated as a spiritualization of the material mystery mother, as a personification of the higher component of the initiations themselves. Of the two blessings which the Cerealian initia confer on mortals, earthly material well-being and the higher hope in death,4) it is the latter that predominates in Telete. Εὐθηνία, the blessing of abundance and bodily welfare, is the gain that the initiations confer for the duration of life; Ἐπίκτησις, the higher acquisition, the adventitium lucrum, is what opens the fairer prospect for the time after death. In Telete the latter comes to representation, while Εὐθηνία, as the lesser, material good, recedes more into the background.

This idea, which has been rightly recognized in the famous marble fragment from Thurea and its inscriptions,1) finds its application in the Munich relief as well, and is here especially emphasized in the egg, the wings, and the frontal crown.

The following monument came into the Karlsruhe Museum with the Maler collection. We have before us a bronze candelabrum of about one meter in height.2) Etruscan provenance is shown especially by the style of the male figure on whose head the shaft of the candelabrum rests; the hair, arranged above the forehead in a row of parallel locks, the short, closely fitting garment without folds, reaching from the left shoulder to the right knee, the two shod feet set parallel, give the whole figure a hieratic bearing and significance. In full accord with this is the egg resting on the fingers of the outstretched right arm. In the composition of the whole the Karlsruhe candelabrum comes closest to the one published by Micali, storia, Milano 1836, on pl. XL. 5. Three feet, on each of which a duck rests,3) correspond to the three tortoises that form the base in Micali. The topmost point of the shaft shows here and there the image of a swamp plant unfolding into several leaves.4) I cannot refrain from tracing the three prominent components of our monument, the ducks, the egg, and the swamp plant, back to a single idea. And this again is drawn from the center of Bacchic thought. Reed and duck belong to swamp life, in which the mystery of a creation developing out of the waters without human aid meets the eye of the observer daily. The same elemental significance rests in the egg. Duck, reed, and egg thus combine into a unified view. In place of the duck other water animals might also be chosen. The Micali candelabrum shows tortoises instead of it. Other vase paintings give geese and swans, whose Bacchic significance is grounded in their relation to the generative force of the tellurian waters. In the same quality rests the significance of the frogs, whose connection with the Bacchic cult must be present to all readers of Aristophanes’ Ranæ, which on several smaller Isis tablets appear united with water and swamp plants

, which sing their hymns eternally to the Lycian egg mother Leda-Latona in the Lycian swamp lake, and which finally in the Batrachomyomachia appear as Peleiads (from πηλός), just as Achilles the Peleiad, formed like them from the water-soaked swamp earth. The more precise account of this I give in the treatment of the Ocnus symbol, which forms the subject of the following tomb painting. There the religious significance of the swamp reed, the veneration consecrated to it, and its relation to the female principle of nature will also be discussed. By the sprouting lotus Isis recognizes the adultery of Osiris, her brother and consort, with Nephthys. The Ioxids have retained the maternal custom of venerating reed and wild asparagus as sacred. Sari, the Nile reed, is called the hair of Isis. With long-flowing hair, like swamp plants, the thighs of Homer, begotten in adultery, are covered in Heliodorus. For swamp generation is the image of the lawless, extramarital sexual mingling, as agriculture is that of the Cerealian-conjugal life.1) Thus the idea of tellurian generation from the waters rests in reed and duck, and therefore they form a fitting accompaniment of the primal egg, which bears within itself the germ of all life. For this reason they also share with it the Bacchic relation to the mysteries, which the tomb paintings preserved by Santi Bartoli bring out in the most varied ways through the inclusion of nymphs, reed tufts, reed crowns, and swamp waters. In swamps Dionysus is preeminently worshipped. In the Lernaean swamp the phallus is erected to him. Ἐν Λίμναις his service was celebrated, like that of Osiris at Sais. Hence he himself is called Λιμναῖος, Προσύμνος in the nocturnal celebration at the Alcyonian Lake with phallic rites.1) The frogs in Aristophanes 210 f. sing to him thus:

λιμναῖα κρηνῶν τέκνα

ξύναυλον ὕμνων βοάν

φθεγξώμεθ᾽, εὔγηρυν ἐμὰν ἀοιδάν

κοάξ, κοάξ,

ἣν ἀμφὶ Νυσήϊον Διὸς

Διόνυσον ἐν Λίμναισιν ἰαχήσαμεν

ἡνίχ᾽ ὁ κραιπαλόκωμος

τοῖς ἱεροῖσι χύτροισι

χωρεῖ κατ᾽ ἐμὸν τέμενος λαῶν ὄχλος.

Ducks, tortoises, frogs belong to the swamp, from which the reed shoots up as the visible witness of the invisible force. They all point back to the female principle of nature, and therefore combine quite naturally
