in connection with the baccatum monile, Helen’s bridal veil, which her mother Leda gave her and which Achates, as Aeneas’s envoy, is charged with delivering to Dido. Helen, Dido, Leda all bear the same erotic character, which rests on the veil as on the necklace of Eriphyle. Its meaning on funerary scenes is now clear. To the charm of bridal ornament woman sacrifices all her happiness, and the terrible lot of death that attends births cannot suppress in her the voice of nature. Thereby she fulfills the commandment of the Dionysian religion. Amphiaraus returns to the earth, Polynices takes his place and becomes the fecundator of Harmonia. Only of bridal rapture shall the woman think; no thought of fate and the future, no pity, no sorrow may deter her from the fulfillment of her material destiny. Let Niobe’s grief, let Thetis’s deception be reserved for her, let her recognize too late that no beauty and no maternal care can give immortality to the perishable child of the womb, whom Isis and Demeter seek in vain to deify in the fire, and let a song quite other now reach her ears than that which resounded in the laughing joy of the wedding, when, adorned with Harmonia’s necklace, she received the good wishes of her companions: yet she must adorn herself with the loveliness of the Charites and yield to the whisperings of Peitho. She is to cast off the Amazonian life of the man-hating maiden, and through union with man fulfill the τέλος θαλεροῖο γάμοιο, the goal and crown of female upbringing. As Ariadne from Dionysus, so she is to receive the crown from the hands of man, through which, as one initiated into the god’s rites, she attains a higher existence. I have often asked myself what meaning those Amazons can have who are represented as guardians on both sides of the entrance of a Lycian rock tomb. Now the deeper relation of this scene has become clear to me. Overcome by the higher force of Bellerophon, they renounce their man-murdering wild martial ardor and return to woman’s natural vocation. Well disposed to everything male, they now gladly bear the rapture and pain of motherhood. From the virginal, sorrowless time they pass over to marriage, and gird their brows with the band of suffering. From their womb ever new nourishment is born for all-consuming death. Full of grief over the destruction of what is generated, they now stand at the threshold of the tomb, an embodiment of the idea of death, and seem to dwell on the thought of how the man-hating Amazon life would have spared them all this grief. Felices, si sine prole fuissent. But the destiny of woman demands otherwise; she must not shun even grief, if the Aphroditean commandment of Dionysus is to be fulfilled. With death

[PDF 86]

— 72 —

the Cretan Gorgo and the Cyprian Leucomantis atoned, because they scorned their lover and took more pleasure in his destruction than in the enjoyment of his love.1) Therefore on many a funerary vessel Amazonian combats are joined with their counterpart, the Dionysian wedding celebration. Enmity dissolves into love, hatred of man into longing for masculinity, and the consecration of marriage closes the abyss that separates the two members of the opposition. The majority of the funerary representations taken from the Amazon myth, belonging partly to vase paintings, partly to sarcophagus sculptures, bring out this transition from hatred to love, and thereby gain that deeper relation to the fundamental idea of the Dionysian religion which, through the adoption of Dionysian emblems such as the ivy leaf, has received a definite expression, though one outwardly little prominent, and therefore seldom noticed and still more seldom understood.

Thereby it is also placed beyond all doubt that all these representations have a quite definite meaning of initiation. The pure physical idea is joined by the mystery idea, in which the former receives its higher transfiguration. Here again it is the better hopes of the initiates which raise the spirit above the sad lot of death that attends all earthly generation to the intimation of its higher destiny. The curse that clings to Harmonia’s bridal ornament is not the last idea that speaks from those representations. Dionysus becomes for woman not only the founder of her material-sensual life; he is also her redeemer. The fulfillment of the material destiny appears only as a passage to a higher perfection, in which the sorrow over the inescapable lot of all that is born from woman’s womb finds sure dissolution. If the idea that the putting on of the bridal ornament lays the ground for endless suffering can leave behind only despair, in the mysteries, on the contrary, it appears as the way to attain lasting union with the god. The woman who renounces virginal abstinence and becomes a mother,2) heedless of the lot that awaits her births, fulfills the commandment of the Dionysian religion. As in life she thereby attains that higher beauty which distinguishes the bride from the Amazonian warrior, so now in death there falls to her that highest exaltation, the lasting union with the god of life, to whom

Through him she reaches the regions of the stars, where Ariadne’s crown never again withers.1) From this point of view those scenes of bridal adornment that so frequently appear on initiation vases acquire a higher meaning. They no longer concern the mortal man alone, but the god himself, to whose embrace the mother now attains.2) The beauty of the dying Amazon is recognized in its full sublimity only now by Achilles, her conqueror,3) and likewise Perseus marvels at the charms of the beheaded Gorgon.4) The girl is destined to be a mother, not an Amazon. In marriage she fulfills her higher vocation, and whatever sufferings she and her race may fall prey to, as a mother she will nevertheless press through in death to the fullest development of her beauty. In this sense those sarcophagus representations are to be understood which show us man and woman under the image of Achilles and Penthesilea. In the same sense, Harmonia’s necklace. Marriage preserves woman from both degenerations of her sex, from man-hating warlike passion and from unregulated hetaeric love of men. Marriage alone brings her repose; in it alone can woman unfold the whole beauty of her nature, and at last in higher regions attain lasting union with the male god, as Psyche, after the wanderings of sensual-tellurian life have been endured, is united with Eros, and Helen at last, joined with Achilles on the lunar island of Leuke, leads a rapturous existence raised above all unrest and mutability. Through marriage Dionysus becomes the redeemer of the woman consecrated to him. Nor may the lot of death that attends her children keep her from fulfilling her destiny. If Thetis at first laments the destruction of her glorious son, her sorrow is at last turned to joy by the posthumous fame that his virtue has won for him. If she has vainly tried everything to adorn Achilles’s body with the same immortality that she herself enjoys, she now realizes that this is allotted not to the body but to the soul alone, and can be won only through virtue. In these ideas we find the higher resolution of those sad reflections that attach to Harmonia’s bridal ornament. In the domain of material life only misery and lamentation follow it. Every wedding song turns into a dirge, and though all the immortals glorify the wedding feast of Peleus by their presence, as the gods also bring gifts to the weddings of Harmonia and Ariadne, yet unending sorrow is reserved for Thetis. The same lot is allotted to every mother; the laughing joy of the wedding night will one day reach her ears in gloom. Is she therefore to withdraw from the destiny of her sex? The commandment of Dionysus demands otherwise of her. The phallic god wishes her to wear the bridal ornament and thereby to prepare herself for union with himself. Two stages of life run side by side here, as in all mysteries: that of the lower world of becoming and that of the higher world of being. The closest union links the two. They pass constantly into one another: if at birth the soul descends into the realm of change, into which the genius leads it, so at death it returns to that of being. If at birth it takes on the garment of the body, so at death it lays aside its burden again. The constant transition from black to white has this higher relation in itself too. The two colors

designate not only tellurian becoming and passing away, but also the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω, the entry into matter and the return from it. On this higher stage what appeared black on the lower stage of sensual life becomes white. In place of the black color of mourning, which corresponds to the tellurian conception, white is chosen, which represents the higher mystery idea. In Dionysus both stages are united. He lives at once in the dark tellurian sphere and in the higher sphere of light: there subject to change, here unchangeable. Those initiated into his rites share in the same double nature. Their corporeal existence stands in indissoluble connection with the incorporeal, and only through the fulfillment of the material destiny can the higher be won. For woman this connection of corporeal with extracorporeal existence has a twofold significance, on account of her preeminently material earthly nature. To the female sex the Dionysian cult offers the fulfillment of its highest hope. It is calculated above all for the nature of woman. It promises not only satisfaction to sensuality, but makes of this also the foundation of a better hope. In one idea both flow together, the satisfaction of the material and of the supersensible needs. Love becomes religious feeling, motherhood the fulfillment of the twofold, the corporeal and the psychic, destiny. To every stage of female nature Dionysus gives its due. He founds the spiritual life of woman not on suppression but on the regulated satisfaction of her material being, and so becomes in the fullest sense the god of initiation of the female sex. To every mother he offers Ariadne’s crown, and secures to her eternal duration in the region of the shining stars of heaven. Through the Dionysian consecration of marriage the curse that clings to the bridal ornament is removed. Through childbearing woman attains union with her god.1) Man is by nature the image of Dionysus; woman, however, requires for her exaltation man and sexual union with him.2)

clay in the tombs back to that earthen coffin in which Dionysus lays to rest on Naxos the Ariadne whom Theseus had yielded to him, and in connection with this we demonstrated in the terracotta the union of all those physical elements that form the material basis of the Bacchic idea. In this, too, it appeared to us as the perfect expression of the Dionysian religion: in uniting female matter with the male force it leaves the preponderance to the former. The same relation now recurs in the moon, and Dionysus belongs to the lunar region as well. Hitherto we have found him on two levels of the cosmos: first in his union with tellurian matter, which, as the bearer of the male force, he permeates in the form of the chthonian waters and the chthonian fire; then again as the shining sun, as the heavenly phallus, akin to the Apollonian luminous nature, yet, as the materially generating Helios, subordinate to the metaphysically pure nature of Apollo. Now he presents himself to us in a third form. He reappears as Lunus Deus, as νυκτοφαής and σύνδρομος μήνης, who leads the nocturnal round dance of the shining stars of heaven,1) and who, like Ariadne’s crown, takes up among the stars those initiated into his rites. In this Lunus nature he leads the tellurian and the solar potency back to unity. All the components of his physical being are united in the moon, as they are in burnt clay. According to the ancient, and especially the Orphic, view, the moon occupies a middle position between earth and sun. Material like the earth, and therefore designated as ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη or as the Olympian earth,2) it is called the purest of the earthly bodies and the most impure of the heavenly ones. It lies on the boundary of two worlds, the tellurian, in which Becoming dwells, and the solar, in which Being dwells, and unites in itself the nature of both. From the sun it borrows its light; with the earth it shares its material nature. Like the earth, it is a true γῆ; mountains, rivers, and cities are to be found on it,3) but it is not an

For this reason it also forms the boundary between the world of being and the world of becoming. Beneath the moon everything is perishable, caught up in eternal waxing and waning, like the moon itself; above it everything is imperishable, incorporeal like the light of the sun, and subject to no change. Thus the lunar region divides the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω; in it the incorporeal assumes body, the corporeal incorporeality. There the descending and the ascending beings meet; there dwells ψυχή, as σῶμα corresponds to the earth, νοῦς to the pure light. For the nature of man is composed of three constituents, like the κόσμος. ψυχή is the middle stage, purer than σῶμα, more impure than νοῦς; through a first separation σῶμα, through a second ψυχή is stripped away, and only then does νοῦς partake of its spiritual purity of light.1) In this union of two natures, the tellurian and the solar, lies the origin of the hermaphroditic lunar nature. The heavenly earth unites both sexes in itself. Man and woman at once, it is the former in its luminous nature, the latter in its materiality: female receptive in relation to the sun, and sending forth what it has received, in rays of fecundating light, male toward the earth. In this union of both sexes the male appears indeed as the higher, because it springs from the sun, but the female, through materiality itself, as the preponderant. Therefore Luna is more frequent than Lunus, and even Deus Luna2) is in use; therefore ψυχή is female, νοῦς male, σῶμα without sex; therefore in the Thespian mysteries of Eros, in whose mimic representations the fable of Psyche and Amor, as Apuleius relates it, has its root,3) Psyche is always conceived in woman’s form; therefore also in the mystery doctrine of the palingenesis of man the proposition was adopted that the male soul always rises again first in a female body. In the Carrhaean sanctuary of the θεὸς Μήν the teaching was preserved even under the Roman emperors that in the house of him who invokes the moon as Lunus the man will rule, while conversely with Luna is bound up the rule of women.4) We derive

This conception of the lunar world intervenes, guiding and explaining, in all parts of ancient mythology.1) But it corresponds so perfectly to the physical foundations of the Dionysian religion that we are entitled to grasp the latter itself as the cultic expression of the developed conceptions of the lunar world. The three constituents of the Dionysian being, earth, water, light, recur in the moon too, united into one. As the moon occupies between earth and sun a middle stage joining the two, so Dionysus also has an equal share in tellurian and solar nature; purer than the earth, he is yet more impure than Apollo, a material Helios. The moon unites both sexes in itself, and so does Dionysus, who joins to a male-phallic nature the female softness of bodily forms.2) In the moon female materiality rules over male nature, and so in the Dionysian mysteries and the Oschophoria the men also assume women’s clothing.3) Hidden, the phallus rests beneath the exterior of woman. But wherein the moon displays the Dionysian nature most clearly is the intimate union of both sexual potencies, whose longing for union attains in the heavenly earth a never-ending fulfillment. love for woman, his desire for generation and fecundation, woman’s longing for the god, from whose masculinity she expects the fulfillment of her destiny, the aversion to solitary life that expresses itself in the female festal retinue and in the ever united appearance of generation-hungry fauns and satyrs with Bacchae reeling in their senses: all this is realized in the moon. Into the moon Osiris enters,1) longing for female matter, to which he descends as the ray of the sun falls down upon the moon. Following the phallic trait of his nature, he gladly renounces the solitary majesty in which Apollo, like the sun, is best pleased. Through Luna he becomes Lunus. He does not wish, alone on an unapproachable height, to enjoy his own majesty and to perish in barren, Narcissus-like self-contemplation. Mene he seeks, to her he descends, sinks into her material nature, circles about her constantly, an inseparable companion, σύνδρομος Μήνης. In this nature his being, subordinate to Apollonian purity, reveals itself most clearly. No desire for generation can draw the Apollonian god down from the solar height in which he sits enthroned forever in metaphysical clarity. Apollo never becomes Lunus. He belongs to the world of being and has no part in that of becoming. He does not enter into its change, but looks from an unapproachable height upon the ever-rising, ever-sinking waves of creation, ruled by the fate of nature, which Phaethon and Bellerophon are unable to escape. To the Dionysian stage belongs Achilles also, belongs the Cretan Talos. As in his double nature of fire and water, so Achilles corresponds to the Dionysian idea of the deity also in his elevation to Lunus and in his kinship with Apollo, in whose sanctuary he, like Dionysus, finds admission in a subordinate position. An enemy of the Amazons, against whom he renews the combat even on Leuke, drawn by irresistible longing toward woman, and, against his mother’s warning, wrestling for Hemithea on Tenedos, he first attains his wishes on the shining lunar island. There, as Philostratus, Heroica 19 describes it, the most beautiful of men, united with the most glorious woman, leads an eternally blessed life of rapture, and satisfies that love which on earth the dying queen aroused in him in a moment when death frustrated its fulfillment. As Lunus he now circles his beloved, swift-footed in the heavens, as on earth the hurrying stream of the never-resting water. So vase paintings represent him. As Lunus he is related to the fire phenomena of the material aether, like Dionysus. As Lunus he is also hermaphroditic

as the statue on the Sigeum represented him.1) The Cretan Talos shows a similar nature. The guardian of the island, he circles it protectingly; every night he completes his course, and in moonlit nights one hears his splashing when he bathes his bronze limbs in the sea. His highest origin he has in the sun. As Lunus, Helios himself has entered into the moon; separated from it, he appears himself in his solar nature, like Achilles and Dionysus, yet in the phallic materiality of his being unable to press through to Apollonian purity of light. The Lunus nature of Dionysus finds confirmation and completion in the lunar relation of the women joined with him. They are all lunar women, Demeter-Ceres, Ariadne-Aridela, Aphrodite, Athena,2) Artemis. A higher elevation than that to lunar nature has not been granted to female materiality. If the incorporeal force of man appears in a threefold stage, and is completed only in the elevation to the sun, woman, on the contrary, remains standing at the lunar stage. Removed from the chthonian earth, she returns in the heavens as lunar woman, and even in this elevation she preserves that materiality of which receptive maternity can never divest itself. She is always the birth-giving earth, always γῆ, be it the tellurian, be it the heavenly- Olympian. Though Athena in her motherless birth from the head has pressed through to a higher stage of spiritual conception, her physical foundation is yet always the double earth, and in the material Dionysian religion this nature alone comes to the fore. The moon unites all the qualities of the Dionysian woman. As Penia, ever pursuing new fecundation, it follows the course of the sun eternally, and borrows from its golden light the silver sheen with which it shines. Erotic is the innermost core of its nature. It stands by lovers, and by lovers it is implored for help.3) Therefore, precisely, the Amazons so greatly misjudge the nature of the goddess whom they serve. Therefore Hippodamia’s girdle is loosed, in the light of the full moon, by the hero who leads her over to her maternal destiny,4) as indeed all generation of the earth thrives

The force of water and of fire embrace each other in the nocturnally moist light of the queen of heaven, whose ray, when it falls on a cow in heat, gives the god Apis his origin. The idea of female fertility has found its highest expression in the egg-birth of the lunar women, and this idea of the σεληνίτιδες γυναῖκες is doubly important to us because we have recognized the lunar nature of the women of Dionysus. Neocles of Croton says that the Helen egg fell from the moon; from a silver egg, the image of the moon, the Molionidae, λευκίππους κούρους, ἰσοκεφάλους, ἐνιγυίους, came forth, writes Ibycus, and quite generally that Neocles adds: τὰς γὰρ σεληνίτιδας γυναῖκας ᾠοτοκεῖν ἁπάσας. Athenæus 2, 50. Eustath. Od. 11, 298. Herodotus of Heraclea adds that the moon-men who come forth from those eggs are fifteen times larger, a number whose significance we shall return to later. Plut. Pl. phil. 2, 30. In these eggs the moon reveals its material maternal nature, in which it appears as ἑτέρη γῆ οὐρανίη. It is itself Aphrodite’s womb, itself the egg, which like Luna, hermaphroditic, unites in itself the force of both sexes and encloses the germ of all visible creation. When the myth relates that the egg from which Aphrodite-Syria- Semiramis comes forth fell from heaven into the Euphrates, was rolled ashore by fishes, and hatched by doves, here too we must think first of the moon, and the connection of fishes and doves is to be taken as an indication of the double force of moisture and warmth, necessary for generation and united in the udæ ignes of the moon.1) So the lion that the solar hero Heracles slew at Nemea, where the egg-born Molionidae too, the Eleans named after their mother, were struck by the same arrows, fell from the moon into the Peloponnese, as Aelian H. A. 12. 7 and Plutarch de facie in orbe lunæ c. 23 report. The lion, however, unites in itself the same double potency of fire and water, so that, like so many other symbolic animals, notably the horse and the ox, it belongs not only to the sun but equally to the tellurian waters and their generative force, and bears the phallus, with which a Florentine terracotta represents it,2) in this double relation. Lions’ heads pour from their mouths the fecundating jet of water,

The fall of the moon egg from heaven may have led to that custom, which the Turks still keep today, of not laying the egg on the ground in sanctuaries, but of hanging it up. If it was therefore referred to the Leda egg, to which the lunar woman Helen owes her origin, the fundamental idea, with all the arbitrariness of the reference, was yet quite correctly rendered, and as Helen, so also the pair of sisters Hilaira and Phoebe bear the lunar character in their names as in their descent from Apollo, and in the silphium that covers the sacred trapeza display clearly the relation to tellurian fertility. On taeniae hang the eggs of the dream vision mentioned above, from the bedstead, and the six ostrich eggs of the Grotta d’Iside at Vulci show hollows, evidently destined for hanging on threaded ribbons. On this rests the custom of adorning the Bacchic initiation egg too with ribbons. Santi Bartoli communicates in his Pitture, on plate 4, a wall painting found in the baths of Titus, whose center is formed by the youthfully beautiful god with all the signs by which art traditionally is accustomed to express the posture of repose, with the thyrsus in his right hand and a garment thrown wholly apart in front. From the right a female figure approaches the god, presenting on the palm of her right hand the large egg richly wound about with taeniae. On the left, turned away, a second blows the double flute. The relation of the taeniae to the tomb cult is well known. It has its ground in their connection with the female side of nature.

At Megalopolis, beside the sanctuary of the mother goddesses, in which the initiations are celebrated, stands another, of Demeter and Kore, which only the women may enter throughout the year. The base on which the images of the gods stand is surrounded on all sides by the rich adornment of taeniae. A taenia winds around the pair of horns of Io on a funerary terracotta from Sicily, now in the Karlsruhe Museum, which I publish from a new drawing in the appendices to my Mutterrecht. Io’s lunar nature, inclined to love, which receives the many-eyed starry heaven as its guardian, is expressed plainly in her horns and no less in her name, which in Argive signifies the light. Thus the connection of the taenia with the egg acquires a deeper meaning. It meets us on vase paintings in the following form as well. A Vienna vessel shows a funerary column resting on a base; the wave ornament, τὰ κύματα, adorns the base, the column a double taenia, white above and black below, which is wound around the stele at a height of two thirds of the whole. On the top of the column lie four white, ovoid bodies, in which, with more certainty than in similar vase scenes, three smaller eggs and one of double size are unmistakable. The Bacchic character of the whole representation is plainly recognizable in the attributes of the figures distributed on both sides: the radiate crown of the woman, the sphere, the weaving implement furnished with rungs like a ladder, the mirror, the patella. The picture is unpublished. It bears the number 5,255 in the Vienna Cabinet. What idea we are to recognize in this binding with ribbons cannot be said with certainty. Most to be recommended is the connection with the conception of the weaving of the great nature mother. Above we cited the Egyptian χειρόμακτρον of Demeter and the laciniæ mentioned by Apuleius, and in Juno Lacinia too we must recognize such a weaving Hera. The veil of Helen has the same significance; as a woven piece it bears within it the tellurian-Aphroditean nature. To these are joined the fillets, which, precisely as products of weaving, belong to the mother goddesses, and which, through their combination of the alternate appearing and receding of the threads, acquire a special relation to the tombs. Hence, too, their significance in the mysteries. As signs of initiation they appear in countless scenes; among the mystery symbols they occupy a high rank, and they are joined in this especially to the egg and the myrtle, that like these they stand in the closest relation to the female side of nature.

This relation of the lunar world to the Dionysian religion explains to us a feature of the Pamphili tomb painting that evidently belongs to its essential components. It is the burning lamp that appears on the hand of one of the ephebes. It deserves the more consideration the more rarely it occurs. Its relation to the mysteries is put beyond doubt by comparison with another monument. Raoul- Rochette, monuments inédits pl. 78, p. 409, gives the illustration and description of a vase painting that on its principal side, in a double row of figures, represents the union of Apollonian and Bacchic cult and the reception of a mystes1) still in childhood into the Dionysian initiation. In the upper field Apollo himself forms the center. On his left appears Athena; on his right, listening attentively to the conversation of the first two, a second female figure, leaning with her arm on the mystic cista, in whom we are to recognize Demeter or Kore. Behind her, closing the painting, stands a four-sided column bearing a small burning lamp. On the reverse of the vessel, probably Apulian, there appears as a counterpart a funerary column resting on a broad base and wound with black-and-white taeniae, its summit crowned by a kylix. Of the two female figures who, in hovering posture, surround the stele on the right and on the left, one carries a mirror and a bunch of grapes, the other the wreath and the egg-shaped body that so often appears, whose consistent interpretation as a tympanum is met by considerable difficulties. The Bacchic relation of the whole cannot therefore be in the least doubtful, and for that very reason the burning lamp too can bear no other character. Its purely symbolic significance follows from the fact that on the vase painting it is not meant to serve any particular action. It has its purpose in itself, and the same holds for the Pamphili tomb painting. Jahn assigns it here an external purpose. It is supposed to serve the ὠοσκοπία, a special kind of divination that foretells from the appearances of an egg held over the fire.2) Had this been the artist’s subject, he would have set forth his idea in a very enigmatic and imperfect manner. Why should he not then have preferred to show us the action itself, and to bring the egg in the hand of one of the youths near the flames? But what altogether excludes the idea of the ὠοσκοπία is not only the likewise symbolic number three of the eggs, but above all the double color

which they show, and whose mystic significance appears incompatible with the performance of a particular action. Had this so essential a particularity not escaped the interpreter, he would scarcely have ventured his conjecture. I therefore hold fast to the purely symbolic significance of the double-colored eggs, and of the burning lamp as well, and I point out that the latter receives a new confirmation from the broad daylight that surrounds the scene of our tomb painting. Temple and colonnade, which appear in the distance on the right and on the left, are a hint, fully sufficient for the more suggestive than elaborative manner of ancient art, that we have before us a company of ephebes gathered under the open sky. The lamp, then, serves no more than the burning candles on the altars of our churches the purpose of lighting a dark space; it can therefore have only a purely symbolic significance, inwardly akin to Bacchic cult. The way to understanding it has been prepared by our discussion above. As Lunus, Bacchus is νυκτοφαής, νυκτέλιος, λαμπτήρ. In union with the moon he attains the fulfillment of the generative desire innate in his phallic nature, which always yearns for female matter and prefers entering into it to the majesty of the solitary, enthroned star of day. His festivals are therefore always and necessarily nocturnal celebrations. Thus in Livius 39, 13 the Italic Bacchanalia are described to us. Thus the Bacchanalia are true Pervigilia Veneris, which begin with the first appearance of the stars and end with their setting, like all Aphroditean-Sacaean festivals, whose character is borne also by the festival of the flute players dressed as women, celebrated at Tibur.1) As the moon aids lovers in the fulfillment of their wishes, so the night in which it reigns is destined for the accomplishment of love’s business, and the light of the lamp is its companion.2) When Epicurus would withdraw the night from Venus, Menander objects that it befits her best of all the deities, which is why the deductio of the Roman bride too began with the rising of the stars. “Menander perhaps thought in this,” remarks Plutarch, Symp. 3, 6, where he takes his point of departure from Epicurus’s Symposium and the inquiry conducted in it, “that the pleasure of love must be enjoyed only behind the curtain of night, so as not to chase modesty from the eyes by embraces by day, or to make the inclination to voluptuousness bold and shameless through all-too-vivid and persistent recollections that kindle the desires ever anew.” The same ethical relation is attributed by Diodor 4, 15 to the nocturnal celebration of Sabazius, οὗ τὴν τε γένεσιν καὶ τὰς θυσίας νυκτερινὰς καὶ κρυφίους παρεισάγουσι διὰ τὴν αἰσχύνην ἐκ τῆς συνουσίας ἐπακολουθοῦσαν, and Athenaeus stresses as a special proof of Etruscan moral decay that they took Epicurus’s rule as their guide in this point too.3) But the nocturnal character of the Bacchic celebration has its ground in the first instance not in a moral precept but rather in the Lunus-Luna nature proper to Bacchus and Ariadne. Considerations of the former kind are in general little in keeping with that phallic religion. Not morality but immorality is the necessary result of a religion that chooses for its physical foundation the impulse of matter toward union and generation, and makes the material egg the center of its mysteries. The Roman Bacchanalia show how greatly the sensual meaning triumphed over the supersensible one, and the scenes of so many tomb paintings, much that recalls the ancient practices and the mystery doctrine. To the initiate all the thoughts expressed here were familiar.

The lamp is met with more often in authors than on monuments. Not only at Athens, but likewise at Syracuse and in other Greek cities,1) this eternal lamp stood at the Hestia altar of the Prytaneum.2) “In Greece,” relates Plutarch in Numa 9, “where likewise (as at Rome) such a sacred fire is maintained, as e.g. at Delphi and at Athens, not virgins but widows who no longer wish to marry have the charge of it. If this sacred fire ever goes out, as the sacred lamp is said once to have gone out at Athens under the tyrant Aristion, and at Delphi when the temple was burned by the Persians, and at Rome in the Mithridatic and civil war the fire vanished together with the altar,3) then, it is said, no new fire must be kindled from another, but an entirely new and pure one must be caught from the rays of the sun.” It was also fetched, however, from Delphi, or from Delos, whence the ship brought it to the Lemnians every year. After the battle of Plataea the Delphian god gave the Greeks the instruction “that a temple should be built to Zeus the Liberator, but no sacrifice made until all the fire in the temples of that region, which had been desecrated by the Persians, had been extinguished and pure sacred fire kindled anew from the common hearth of Greece at Delphi.” Thereupon the Greek generals went around and had all fire extinguished. To Plataea, however, it was brought by Euchidas, who completed the way there and back in a single day and had covered the thousand stadia before sunset. When he sank down dead, the citizens of Plataea buried him in the sanctuary of Artemis Eucleia.4) — Plutarch gives in Numa 10 and Qu. rom. 96 the description of the cave in which the unchaste Vestals ended their lives. Plutarch gives his thoughts on this in the 75th Roman Question. “Is this done perhaps because the Romans honored light as related and akin to the eternal, inextinguishable fire? Or is this too a symbol that nothing animate, if it is not harmful, may be killed or destroyed? For fire is like an animal, since it needs nourishment, moves of itself, and in being extinguished, as if it were being killed, utters a voice. Or is this custom meant to teach us that we must destroy neither fire nor water nor other necessary things of which we have enough, but, when we have used them, must leave them also to others who need them for use?” — Isis joins the series of the great nature mothers who bear the lamp among their attributes. In her procession the lucerna ardens is carried in front. Apuleius met. 11, p. 261. Quorum (sc. antistitum sacrorum) primus lucernam præmicantem claro porrigebat lumine, non adeo nostris illis consimilem, quæ vespertinas illuminant epulas, sed aureum cymbium, medio sui patore flammulam suscitans largiorem. And further: Magnus præterea sexus utriusque numerus, lucernis, tædis, cereis, et alio genere ficti luminis siderum cœlestium stirpem propitiantes. It can therefore not be surprising that in the mythical narratives centered on the Egyptian king Mycerinus, the builder of the so-called pyramid of Rhodopis, the lamp plays a very prominent role. At Sais, where the great lamp festival was celebrated in honor of Athenaia, Herodot (I, 129–134) saw in the royal palace, in an ornamented chapel, the life-size image, made of wood, of a cow lying on its knees, whose body was covered with a purple cloth, while its neck and head were thickly gilded. Between the pair of horns rests the sun disk, likewise of gold. Every day perfumes of the most various kinds are offered to it, and throughout the night a παννύχος λύχνος is set before it. In an adjoining chamber there stood twenty female statues, likewise of wood, whose hands had fallen off from age. Herodotus saw them lying at the feet of the statues. Once a year the cow is led out of the sacred chamber into the light; this takes place at the festival when they mourn the death of Osiris. Works of art confirm the Herodotean description. A Venetian relief, whose illustration Gronovius and Wesseling add to their editions, shows the recumbent cow, the body cover, the image of the sun, the incense vessels, and, carried by two boys, the burning lamp, adorned at the end opposite the flame with the head of Isis covered by the ox-scalp. From the tombs of the Theban necropolis the authors of the description de l’Egypte, antiquités 2, p. 169, communicate a corresponding

wall painting. We see here the burning lamp in connection with the cult of Isis. For that cow is the animal consecrated to Isis, omniparentis terræ fæcundum simulacrum, as its being led around, like the incense offering and the covering of the head with the ox-scalp, attests for her cult.1) The predominance of the maternal principle appears in the twenty naked female statues, and especially in the myths that attached themselves to them. They were said to have been the king’s concubines. Tellurian matter is thus conceived here in Aphroditean hetaerism, and this conception continues in the story of the king’s sexual mingling with his only daughter.2) If in all these features the luminous side of the life-giving female primal principle comes forward, others reveal the relation to death that Venus-Libitina too, the giver of life, bears within her.3) At the festival of Osiris’s disappearance the cow of Isis is led seven times around the temple. Mycerinus himself was said to have been buried in her body; according to another version he had buried in it his daughter, snatched from him by death. Both accounts show us the maternal womb of matter as the place of death,4) and thus confirm that double nature of the primal mother which Plutarch recognizes so rightly and emphasizes so definitely.5) To both sides of material maternity the lamp stands in relation. Like Isis herself it is an image of life and of death, a representation of the life-giving, eternally self-consuming and thereby eternally self-renewing natural force. In a second narrative the burning lychnos appears once more, and quite with the same meaning. Herodot 2, 133 relates: “After the death of his daughter another misfortune befell the same king. He received an oracle from Buto,6) that he had only six more years to live and would die in the seventh. Distressed at this, he sent to the goddess and reproached her that his father and his father’s brother, who had closed the temples and not troubled themselves about the gods, but had ruined the people, had for so long a time

lived, and he, who was after all a God-fearing man, should die so soon. Then he received a second oracle: precisely on this account his life would be shortened, for he had not done what he should have done. For Egypt was to be unfortunate for 150 years, and the two who had been kings before him had noticed this, but he had not. When Mycerinus learned what was now once for all irrevocably decreed for him, he had a great number of lamps made, and when night came he lit them, and drank and was of good cheer, continued this day and night, and roamed about in the swamp lands and in the woods wherever he could find a place suited to pleasure and joy. This he did to give the oracle the lie, by making twelve years out of six, since the nights had become days.” The religious idea of this second Mycerinus myth lies plainly in the open. All its individual features are explained by the cult of a nature mother conceived as hetaeric, whether we call her Latona or Isis, and by the opposition of this cult to the religion of the shepherd kings, hated by the native Egyptian population. The service of the great material mother appears restored, who rules in the swamps around Buto, crosses the waters in the papyrus boat, is held sacred by the animals of the watery depth, out of innate generative desire seeks everywhere the vanished phallus of Osiris, is crowned by Horus with the ox-scalp on account of her wanton nature, and in the form of a swallow, on the swampy shore of Byblus, circles longingly the Osiris column in the palace of Malcander and Astarte.1) As priestly king of this goddess Mycerinus appears. In swamps and in moist forest thickets he roams about. There he has his pleasure and joy. Here the work of tellurian generation thrives most luxuriantly. But the most vigorous life consumes itself most quickly. Not a long existence, as he expected it as the reward of his εὐσέβεια, does Isis grant him; rather the goddess of swampy Buto announces to him a swifter destruction of it. In six years he will live through twelve; with the seventh a new generation begins. In this religious system the night side of nature comes especially to the fore. Swifter and more violent is the annihilation in hetaeric swamp generation, where the natural force continues its work of generation without interruption day and night. In the fate of Mycerinus death reigns all-powerful. Isis appears in it preeminently as the destroyer of life. As she did the daughter, so she consigns the father to swift destruction. Her cult image becomes a coffin. In hetaeric life both lie so close together, the highest enjoyment of material existence and its highest transience. The swiftly fading

rose is the characteristic attribute of the hetaeric Aphrodite. At the highest intensification of sensual enjoyment Aphrodite-Rhodopis becomes the ever-threatening mother of the grave. The lamp, image of her life-giving maternity, becomes a grave light. As its glow invites to the enjoyment of love, so it now falls on the place of death. On funerary columns the lychnos is hung up,1) an image of self-consuming life, which expires the more swiftly the more violently the flame blazes.

Especially instructive is the connection of the lamp with Psyche. In the myth of Amor and Psyche the burning lamp is assigned a role that enlightens us about its position and significance in the mysteries. For it cannot be doubted that neither Apuleius nor Aristophontes invented the fable, but that it was rather, as considerably older works of art irrefutably demonstrate, in existence long before their time. The fantastic garb in which it appears with them, and whose overloading in wordy elaboration of details Fulgentius Mythol. 3, 6 already censures, may well count as later, novelistic embellishment: the main elements surely rest not on arbitrary invention but on genuine tradition. Its root is itself to be sought in mystery practices and sacred representations.2) Psyche is led by the divine beauty of her body, more than by conscious decision, into the aberrations of sensuality and into the mire of matter. As Aphrodite’s slave she has to pass through a long series of penances and trials, and even to go through the terrors of the underworld. At last, seized by Stygian sleep, motionless, a soulless corpse, she receives, awakened by the touch of an arrowhead, the cup of immortality, and, in union with Eros, the tranquil enjoyment of all that blessed bliss which she had sought in vain in Aphrodite’s service. Two stages of female existence appear here, like the double row of figures on so many vase paintings, comparable to the two parts of Goethe’s Faust: the female soul first in the service of Aphrodite, dominated by matter, led by every step on the fateful path to ever new, unexpected sufferings, finally into the deepest abysses of the mire of matter — but then rising to a new, more vigorous existence, passing from Aphroditean to psychic life. That lower stage bears the tellurian, this higher the uranian character. From the chthonian earth

Psyche is raised to the heavenly one. We recognize that Helen who, yielding to Aphrodite’s natural law, finds no end of sufferings and wanderings until at last, on the luminous lunar island, the most glorious of women, united in eternal union with the most glorious of heroes, she finds the repose that not the tellurian but only the heavenly Eros is able to give. Down there all is unrest, suffering, deceptions as unexpected as solutions are inexplicable: here repose, eternity, and security of enjoyment, the magic of transfiguration, such as the stillness of the moonlit night pours over the dwellings of men, noisily astir by day. There the impurity of tellurian matter, the serpent and the reed, which find their origin in the mire of dark depths, the witnesses and symbols of the unregulated mating of water and earth; here the butterfly that has broken through from the chrysalis of matter to the light, seeking light and having become a partaker of the light; there the purely material, here the uranian Aphrodite; there hetaeric, here conjugal union; there σῶμα, here ψυχή; there the lightless matter of earth, here the purified heavenly earth, the moon, the purest of the tellurian bodies. In Psyche Aphrodite herself ascends to the lunar stage, the highest that the materiality of woman can attain. At her side appears Eros as Lunus. Amor and Psyche are united by the same bond that encircles Lunus and Luna, Achilles and Helen. The kiss that unites them is the basium, which the husband gives the wife, not the suavium, which the friend gives the hetaera.1) The purity and chastity of love that has attained its final fulfillment is expressed in the group of the figures embracing for the kiss with a perfection that no lyric depiction can attain. And yet it would be altogether contrary to the ancient artistic idea to think here of a depiction of purely spiritual love. We have before us not this but earthly love raised to the highest purity. As the moon is the purest of earthly, the most impure of heavenly bodies, so Psyche too takes the same middle position on the boundary of two worlds. She joins the materiality of the one with the purity and tranquil clarity of the other, compels the body to participation in the light, the light to connection with the body, and so holds herself equally far from the immateriality of the one as from the impurity of the other. σῶμα and νοῦς come in Psyche into indissoluble union, and so give origin to a being that raises matter to the farthest limit of ennoblement of which it is capable. To this stage the idea of sexual love is not foreign. But it has put off the Aphroditean-hetaeric character and taken on that

of chaste conjugal union. Psyche’s sufferings and final redemption are themselves only a consecration of marriage, which leads the sexual life of woman out of the swamp depths of impure matter, in which it finds its destruction, over to that path of light by which it can become for her the starting point of a higher psychic existence. In this attainment of her highest and last vocation Psyche unites in herself those two concepts that seem to exclude each other, and yet in so many myths appear in the most intimate union, that of the highest motherhood and that of perfected virginity. And in this too she stands again on the same stage as the moon. Eternally fecundated, it is at the same time eternally virginal, as mother virgin, as virgin mother. With the moon the concept of marriage and sexual mingling is necessarily joined. It is by its nature the union of both potencies, by its nature hermaphroditic, by its nature Lunus and Luna, Eros and Psyche. It seeks the light, as the light never ceases to sink itself into it. The fulfillment of this highest longing has found its expression in the symplegma, in the kiss on the mouth, in the meeting glance. In this first kiss, sealing the marriage bond, “to which Cypria herself adds a fifth part of her own nectar,”1) the cosmic law that governs the uranian bodies seems to receive its fulfillment among men, and the harmony of the higher and the lower world to be restored. As the moon can do nothing through itself but, ever following the sun, borrows from it the light with which it shines in quiet glory, so woman can attain only in conjugal union with man to that higher beauty through which her materiality is able to bind to itself the more spiritual nature of man. We see what relation connects these Eros mysteries with the Dionysian religion, and to what stage of the Dionysian nature they correspond.2) Now the lamp too will acquire for us a deeper relation. By the light of the lamp filled to the uppermost rim with oil Psyche recognizes the divinely beautiful form of her nocturnal visitor, whom her sisters had represented to her as a hideous dragon. The sword that was to give the monster death sinks from her arm. Restlessly the flame flickers, while the girl with growing curiosity enjoys the forbidden sight of the glorious form, of the beautifully curled golden hair, of the many-colored pair of wings, lightly

trembling at the outermost tips, and carelessly scratches her thumb with the arrowhead. Then from the lamp itself a drop of burning oil drips onto the right shoulder of the god, as though it itself were driven by longing to mingle with the lord of all fire. But Eros, awakening from deep sleep, avenges the girl’s disobedience by flight. Sinking exhausted to the ground, she sees the beloved torn from her at the very moment when she had recognized his glory. So the incident with the burning lamp forms the true turning point in the course of the trials which Aphrodite imposes on Psyche, who rivals her in beauty. In place of the sexual enjoyment covered with darkness there appears the longing for the possession of the god recognized in all his glory. To the bodily wound is joined the deeper suffering of psychic pain. For wounding is the principle of love, as Plutarch profoundly emphasizes. As the plowshare opens the earth, and the force of man opens woman’s maternal womb by wounding it, so too in the psychic domain the arrow of Eros pierces the girl’s heart by wounding it, and her whole being is flooded by the painful, ever-growing longing for union with the heavenly bridegroom once beheld and ever present before her eyes. In the restlessly flickering flame, in the glowing oil that strives to join itself with Eros, Psyche herself is prefigured. The nocturnally dark mingling with the dragon1) forms the content of a lower stage of sexual life. It is tellurian swamp mating, which rules in the moist depth of the earth. It is the mingling of Isis and Osiris in the lightless maternal womb of Rhea. Under the bushel stands the burning light, as the great courtesan Lamia reveals her purely tellurian hetaeric character by putting her eyes in a bag. The removal of the modius, the seizing of the burning lamp, denotes the break of a new day, the transition to a new state, the beginning of new sufferings that bring about the final redemption. Psyche seeks the light, as the moth, whose wings she bears, is drawn by an irresistible urge to the flame. In place of tellurian moisture there appears the higher stage of fire, in place of darkness and chaos that of light and order, in place of unregulated hetaerism the longing for elevation to conjugal union. The tellurian stage of pure materiality is followed by the lunar, on which matter itself takes on the nature of light and thereby penetrates to a higher purification. In the oil-filled burning lamp this lunar-psychic stage of the female being has come to symbolic representation.

It corresponds to it perfectly. As the moon is purer than the earth but less pure than the sun, so too the burning oil is a combination of materially tellurian matter with the light, and thereby a union of the purely tellurian and the purely solar principle into an intermediate stage of existence mixed of both potencies. As, further, in the moon the material nature of woman predominates over the immaterial force of the sun and draws this down to itself for entry into matter, so also the fire in combination with the oil takes on a preponderantly material nature. The oil itself, like the olive tree from which it comes, is brought into connection with the female natural principle. Thus Athena,1) thus Damia and Auxesia are recognized in the olive tree.2) Olive tree and palm make possible Latona’s delivery;3) petroleum is ascribed to Medea. When Codrus had died, and his sons Neleus and Codrus were contending for the rule, the oracle promised the rule to him who should first sacrifice ἔνθα ὁ σίαλος τὸν σίαλον τρίβει. Neleus recognized the fulfillment of the oracle when he saw two olive trees move and rub against one another. He brings the sacrifice and rules over Attica.4) The relation of the pig to Demeter and to material earth, however, belongs to the best-known remnants of the old animal symbolism, for which I cite only Ovid’s saying terræ plenæ victima plena datur. In Vesta’s sacred flame lies a similar connection of the oil with the female natural principle, and the preeminent purity of this liquid, which the ancients emphasize,5) as well as the calming influence to which even the wild waves of the sea submit, may well have seemed to many a special expression of the calmly chaste nature of that deity who unites in herself the concepts of motherhood and virginal chastity. In keeping with this significance of the oil, the living sensibility that Apuleius ascribes to it, as well as the prohibition against extinguishing the flame, seems wholly to correspond to the spirit of the old nature religion.6) The same desire for union with the beautiful Eros, the lord of all fire, whose sting drives Psyche, penetrates also the hot liquid. Psyche appears herein herself as a great nature mother, attesting her fertility in the gift of oil, no

less than Athena, Auxesia, and Damia, the goddesses of marriage of tellurian-lunar nature, to whom the maidens dedicate hair, cloak clasps, and small earthen drinking bowls. Proofs of this relation to the fertility of the earth are laid down in individual, very essential features of the Psyche myth. As her kinship with the river reed assigns to her the lowest stage of tellurian generative desire, so she appears, in that labor which she performs in Demeter’s temple, in the sorting of the seeds which the ants, omniparentis terræ agiles alumni, undertake for her, finally in the fetching of the golden sheep’s wool, as the all-bearing Ceres, as the giver of the higher blessing of agriculture, and in the sleep of death from which the touch of Eros awakens her the fate of the seed grain is represented, and the resurrection, mediated by its death, to a new, fairer life. Thus Psyche’s whole being is dominated by the idea of material fertility. She shares with Aphrodite, with Ceres, with Juno the maternal nature that longs for ever new mating with the all-awakening Eros. But she rises above this tellurian stage, on which she is able to give origin only to the plants of the land, to the unwept lower creation, to the higher maternity to which man, the crown of earthly creation, traces back his origin and his continuance. In comparison with this higher perfection of femininity, her relation to the swamp plants and to the golden fruits of the fields appears as a lower region of materiality, as a subordinate function of the female sporium, which first in human marriage and in the begetting of true children (hence joined with Eros in confarreatis nuptiis) fulfills its highest vocation. Thus Psyche is indeed at all stages of her existence the material mother, never divested of the material character, always tellurian-lunar, never penetrated beyond the lunar region to solar-spiritual existence; but yet she has risen above purely tellurian life and the pain of the eternal alternation of becoming and passing away that rules in it, to the heavenly life, where she now, on the boundary of two worlds and uniting both in herself, wedded to the light-bringing Eros, leads in never-ending bliss a sensual-supersensible existence. In the burning oil, which suddenly lights up the darkness hitherto prevailing and, by the unveiling of the higher human beauty, never before beheld, in man and woman, awakens the longing for eternal possession, this pairing of matter with the light, of the tellurian with the solar potency, of moisture with warmth, in a word that union of two worlds recognized in the moon, is brought to pictorial presentation.

The citation and examination of the ancient testimonies on the occurrence of the lamp in the cult of the great nature mothers, of Vesta-Hestia, of Pallas

[PDF 113]

— 99 —

Athena, of Demeter, Themis, Isis, Psyche-Aphrodite puts us in a position to appreciate the thoughts that attach to its appearance in the Bacchic mysteries, and which the sight of it was also capable of suggesting to the ephebes of our tomb painting. As the egg leads from truths of a physical-material kind to reflections of a higher nature, its double color from the laws of the world of becoming to the hopes of a world of being: so too to the mystery lamp attaches a whole sequence of stages of ideas which rise from the deepest regions of the life of nature to the highest of a purified psychic existence. The sensually material always forms the foundation. Though it can be subject to no doubt that the mysteries and their symbols had a higher spiritual content, which alone explains the longing of so many distinguished men to share in its better hopes through initiation, it is nevertheless equally certain, on the other hand, that this spiritualized meaning formed not the lowest but the highest stage of the doctrine, a stage to which probably only the smallest number of the initiated were able to rise. Nature has taken language upon her lap, and has likewise taken religion and its symbolism. As little as the history of a word begins with its figurative meaning, so little can the higher idea of the mysteries be chosen as the starting point of development. The spiritual has built itself up on the broad basis of matter, the spiritual truth on the physical one. In the latter the likeness of the former is recognized. He who, of deeper spirit, was able to discover it in the image has become the benefactor of the human race. In all human things the sensual forms the foundation; to this the spiritual attaches itself. First a material and then a psychic body;1) first the coarse garment of the body, which Aphrodite weaves, then a finer, more artful one, the work of Athena. First the tellurian, then the lunar, last the solar stage of pure νοῦς of eternally changeless being. That is the sequence of stages of the mystery idea, that the fundamental view of Orphic doctrine in general. Through a series of gradually progressing unfoldings all that is created, and with and in it at the same time the creative principle, has passed. From the formless to ever more perfect form, from darkness to light, from tellurism to cosmic order, from the somatic to the psychic and spiritual, from the motherhood of matter to the fatherhood

Hidden under the bushel3) it shows us material warmth working invisibly in tellurian matter and, joined with the moisture of the depth, developing germ in the darkness of the maternal womb of the lower creation of earth. To this lowest stage corresponds the lightless mating with the dragon, to which female matter surrenders itself purely somatically. But the modius is lifted away, and illuminating, the rays of the lamp fall into the deep darkness that hitherto covered matter. With this man steps out of the harmony of creation in which he had lived before unconsciously. He has beheld the forbidden, and has carried away restless longing for the denied enjoyment instead of the former unconscious pairing. Without enjoyment, but also without suffering, is the sexual embrace with the dragon in the lightless spaces of the earth. Had woman never renounced this, never lifted away the lid that hid the lamp, she would never have lost the freedom from care of the lower creation. But Psyche is seduced to seeing; she wants light instead of darkness. The forbidden deed becomes the source of unspeakable sufferings, but also the beginning of a higher existence in which the lower creation has no share. To the first material awakening corresponds the burning lamp that emerges from the covering of the modius. At this stage it still has a purely material meaning. It shows us woman in her sensual-erotic excitement, given over to the pain of a not yet purified desire for satisfaction of bodily pleasure. It calls to mind the Aphroditean unregulated sexual love with all its aberrations. It is here the lamp of the wanton Latona, which

conquest of sensual desire can woman press on to repose and to lasting happiness. Only when purified does Psyche attain eternal union with the god who had withdrawn himself from her purely sensual glow. In the place of the restless, eternally seeking, never fulfilled desire there now enters the blessedness of lasting possession, freed from every torment; in the place of Aphroditean unchastity, that of Cerealian chastity and maternity. Tellurism yields to uranian existence, the somatic to the psychic, the swiftly fleeting pleasure to the certainty of untroubled duration. In calm evenness burns the lamp that before, flickering restlessly, let the glowing drop of oil fall to the earth. At this height the oil flame is the image of Psyche raised to lunar nature, of womanhood that has pressed through to luminous nature. Material, like the moon, she has nevertheless attained the highest degree of purification of which matter is capable. As such a pure flame the eternally burning fire of Vesta-Hestia is conceived. Every unchastity destroys its higher nature and leads it back into the dark depths of impure matter. Marriage, on the other hand, does not violate it. Virginity and maternity stand in exact connection, while hetaerism negates both. Hence the guardians of the pure fire of Vesta are at the same time servants of the phallus, from which the chaste, virginal nature mother awaits her fecundation;1) hence the fire of the Greek prytaneia likewise becomes generative, and every hearth of the state is conceived as the center of material prosperity on the foundation of the chaste, Cerealian-conjugal life.

To a still higher stage of purity woman cannot raise the flame. It is not granted to the materiality of her nature to rise above the lunar stage of existence and to press through into the realm of immaterial light. Every further elevation proceeds from man. The light of the sun has entered into the moon and descended to female matter. Thereby it has itself taken on corporeal nature. Above the moon, on the other hand, it stands alone; at its highest source it enjoys exclusive masculinity, full purity, and unmixed clarity. There it is a monad, while in the moon it becomes a Trias; there it is unmixed being, here it has entered into the change of the world of becoming, which moves in threeness. The moon points, by its luminous nature, to the highest stage of the purely solar region. The derived silver gleam leads the idea back to the primal source that lies in the sun. This highest stage the Dionysian religion has ascended only by the hand of the Apollonian and within it. Dionysus is always of material, phallic nature, a material Helios, and for that reason

is conceived as Sol in infero id est nocturno hemisphærio. Apollo, on the other hand, has pressed through to the monad, finally removed from union with matter, the source of light in its unmixed originality, and is therefore opposed, as Sol in supero, id est in diurno hemisphærio, to the nocturnal Dionysus.1) Thus separated from Apollo, Bacchus nevertheless enters into union with him, and whither he could not rise through himself, thither he lifts himself through Apollo. The latter draws him up to himself, and transfigures and purifies in his own nature the impure luminous nature of Dionysus. The lamp follows the same elevation. Its material fire points back to Apollo as its pure primal source. Through Apollo himself it becomes the image of the purest immaterial sunlight. This last elevation is the consummation of the mystery idea, and the greatest spiritualization of which the impure material fire of the earth was capable. Now the lamp steps forth from its connection with nocturnal festivals and takes its place beside the Apollonian-Bacchic light of day. So we see it on the funerary vase mentioned above, which unites Apollonian and Bacchic religion, so on our Pamphili painting, where sub sole clarissimo the Bacchic initiates gather to contemplate the three mystery eggs. If here the eggs are images of the material life that is destined for reawakening in the uranian world, and so belong wholly to the lunar stage of the cosmos,2) then at the sight of the burning lamp the spirit presses on yet one stage higher, and by the flame that eternally strives upward arrives at the primal source of light, at the region of Apollonian-metaphysical being, of the pure νοῦς stripped of all material admixture. If in the eggs the female natural principle prevails over the male, then, on the other hand, fire at the highest stage of purity is essentially of male nature. Still subordinate to matter in the moon, and therefore at the lunar stage an attribute of the female deities, it becomes in the solar sphere an expression of masculinity, and shows us force in its elevation above matter. Motherhood, which rests in matter, yields to fatherhood, which has its seat in the force of the sun. Apollo purifies the matricide, and annihilates the primeval law of the female-material powers. Into his Delphic sanctuary no woman has entry, any more than into that of the light-hero Heracles, combatant and enemy of women.3) Harmonia’s necklace is offered to him, and thus from the curse

At Delphi, at the Apollonian hearth, the Greek cities fetched it after the defeat of the Persians. From Delos it comes every year to the island of Lemnos, as Philostratus, Her. 19, attests. For in contact with matter it has lost the purity that it always preserves at the primal source of light. The three stages of the cosmos, earth, moon, sun, are repeated in fire as well. Materially impure as the Vulcanian-chthonian flame, purer in the moon, but even here still perishing in matter, it attains in the sun its greatest clarity and complete incorporeality.1) If Prometheus stole the spark in the fennel stalk from the Vulcanian flame of Mosychlus, Sappho on the contrary has him kindle the torch at the wheels of the sun’s chariot, and thus designates the highest elevation to which it is man’s task to press through.2) The material flame is to be purified; through a second death the pure νοῦς, which dwells in the solar region, is to emerge from Psyche’s mixed nature.3) Of the three means of purification of the Dionysian cult, water, fire, air,4) fire, if conceived materially, is the middle one; lower is water, which belongs to the dark tellurian region, higher the air, which belongs to the ethereal region, the dwelling place of Bellerophon, Phaethon, and Achilles. as to what last and highest idea attaches to the mystery lamp. It is the same that lies before us in the resolution of the Prometheis, in which the ancients themselves wished to recognize the revelation of the mystery doctrine. Here and there the same progress from materiality to immateriality, from impurity to the state of highest purification. Here and there the transition from motherhood into the father right of light. Here and there the unrest of the awakening consciousness as the beginning of a struggle that leads, through the severest trials, to the victory of the spiritual solar principle over the power of matter, and raises to communion with the gods the man wrested, in hard struggle, from the maternal principle of matter. The undertaking of this struggle and its carrying through is the goal of human existence. To the mystes who attains the highest degrees of initiation, it is brought near as the highest spiritualization of the idea of initiation. Through darkness to light, through matter to spirit, from earth to heaven, through the motherhood of matter to the fatherhood of the sun: that is the consummation of the Dionysian religion, to which it presses through in its union with the Apollonian cult.

The male solar nature now seizes the female-material egg as well. I remarked above that it is not granted to maternal matter to press through beyond lunar nature into the immaterial-solar. To divest herself wholly of matter she cannot. She remains, like Helen, like Psyche, like all the great nature mothers, behind on the lunar stage, and returns as the nocturnally shining Luna, as the uranian earth, in the heavens. All the more noteworthy is it, then, that in some conceptions of the ancient religions the maternal principle too draws to itself the solar nature and appears divested of that materiality on which, in its innermost being, it rests. Athena, the maternal principle, which as chthonian and as uranian earth forms the material foundation of material life, which by the light of the nocturnal lamp weaves with consummate artist’s hand the coarser garment of tellurian bodies and the finer one of uranian bodies, she comes forth in spiritual nature from the head of Zeus, complete which passages are to be read in their whole context. In sacris Liberi omnibus tres sunt istæ purgationes: nam aut tæda purgantur, aut sulphure, aut aqua abluuntur, aut aëre ventilantur: quod erat in sacris Liberi. This lustration, at first conceived wholly materially, is raised to the image of the spiritual one. like the word from the mouth. Not from the thigh of the highest god is she born, like Dionysus, not διμήτωρ like him, but motherless, resting exclusively on spiritual fatherhood. A like transfiguration is shown by the female principle in the Delphic cult. Themis-Gaea, the material primal mother, first holds the oracle. Apollo himself is the mother’s son, and in Aeschylus is reminded by the Erinyes of this material origin when he rises to overthrow their ancient mother right. But he ascends to the highest stage of metaphysical-solar being, and so clothes the primal egg, maternal-material in its origin, with pure luminous nature. In egg form the Delphic omphalos appears on a vase painting in R. Rochette, mon. inédits. planche 35, which gains such particular significance precisely in that it raises beyond all doubt the true shape of the much-disputed temple stone, and explains the origin of the other formations, which now arise from the halving of the egg, now approach the pyramidal form.1) On a base of two steps stands the omphalos, represented in perfect egg form, set upright on the broader or female end. By it Orestes seeks protection against the attack of the Erinyes, whom the Delphic god, seated on the tripod and provided with the laurel branch, repels.2) According to Strabo’s report the omphalos was bound round about with fillets,3) as we see it on the other monuments named, e.g. on the vase painting in R. Rochette, plate 37. The bands show here the alternation of the black and white color, whose meaning and whose relation to the egg idea cannot, after the remarks made earlier, be doubtful. The alternation of life and death in tellurian creation, by which it is precisely preserved in eternal youth, repeats itself in the myth of the two ravens or eagles which, flying in opposite directions from the rising and the setting of the sun, meet at Delphi, and were represented on the omphalos itself. They correspond to the two ever counterflowing streams of becoming and passing away,

Thereby the omphalos itself receives the significance of the two-colored egg of our Pamphili tomb painting. The light side and the night side of nature, death and life, are contained in it. From this is explained the number five of the likewise egg-shaped black bodies that cover the surface of the omphalos on the Ruvo vase. This number Apollo, who is otherwise Hebdomagetes and joined with the seven, bears on his still less pure, Dionysian stage of nature. Read on this c. 9, from which I give here a passage that throws clear light on the relation of the two gods indicated. “The wise call the transformation into fire Apollo, on account of the aloneness (ἀ-πολύς, an etymology whose incorrectness does no harm to the idea that is to be supported by it), and Phoebus on account of purity and unspottedness. The transformation into winds, water, earth, stars, into the races of animals and plants, on the other hand, as well as the arrangement and ordering of all this, they represent under a rending asunder and dismemberment, call it Dionysus-Zagreus, Nyctelius, Isodaetes, and clothe destruction, annihilation, death, rebirth, in such fables and riddles as correspond to the transformations named. Hence one sings to Dionysus dithyrambic songs full of emotion and change, full of events and digressions, — ‘for, as Aeschylus says, the loud-resounding dithyramb must follow the communal Dionysus,’ — to Apollo, on the other hand, one sings the paean, a chaste and well-ordered Muse. The latter one represents on statues and paintings always young and unaging, the former, however, under many and manifold forms; and in general one ascribes to Apollo equality, order, and unmixed gravity, to Bacchus, on the other hand, all sorts of jest, wantonness, frenzy, and inequality, and invokes him as Evius, who stirs the women to frenzy, or as Dionysus glorified by frenzied honors.”

Hellas, but of the whole οἰκουμένη, the omphalos was in this sense to be the navel of the earth. From Themis-Gaea the egg passes with the oracle to Apollo, and ascends to the same height of significance to which the male god of light presses through. With Apollo himself it is more and more removed from the material nature of which it was originally the expression. In the image of the primal mother Earth, Orestes finds his protection, although he himself had violated the law of the earth, like Alcmaeon, whose foot Gaea could no longer endure upon herself. In union with Apollo the egg takes on Apollonian nature and significance. It becomes the representative of the paternal principle that rests in the sun, and the expression of that highest lustration by which Apollo purifies the soul of the dross of bodily existence and leads it back to the quiet clarity of his own highest luminous nature. In this transfiguration the Delphic omphalos-egg appears on the Ruvo vase painting. All the components of the painting emphasize quite deliberately its relation to initiation. The highest Apollonian development of the Bacchus idea emerges with particular significance in the representation of the matricide who grasps the omphalos, taken under protection by the god of the laurel against the punishment of the Erinyes.

To this egg, raised to Apollonian solar nature, the Indian-Egyptian myth of the phoenix attaches itself as an elucidation. In this the egg has wholly laid aside its materially female nature, and put on the male nature of solar light. Of myrrh the bird forms an egg, as large as it is able to carry. Then it hollows it out, lays its father’s corpse inside, and fills the opening again with myrrh. The weight is not made heavier by the burden laid in. This egg it now carries to Egypt, lays it down at Heliopolis on the altar of the sun, and gives it over to the flames.1) In all these traits, as in the bird’s adornment of colors, its crown of light, which it bears on coins, its connection with the Apollonian male palm, the male principle of light is not to be mistaken. The incorporeality of light is brought out still more by the contrast of the burden of myrrh. Weightless is the light of the sun, and wholly immaterial, corporeal on the other hand and heavy is that which it generates, myrrh as a product of the sun. Motherless, from

the father alone, the phoenix has come forth.1) The egg is not its birthplace, but rather the shroud of death which, consumed by fire, returns to the light to which the father belongs. The egg thus appears here not as the foundation of bodily birth, in which significance both the Indian and the Egyptian mythology knew it, hence also not as a representation of the material maternal womb; it is rather destined to be consumed by fire and itself united with the primal principle of all light. Material and perishable is what the maternal-tellurian egg brings forth out of itself, immaterial and partaking of immortality what proceeds from the myrrh egg. With matter the mother shares the property of heaviness, with light the father that of weightlessness. The material egg leads the life born from it to death, the sun egg conversely death to life. There white is changed into black, here black into white. Thereby the idea of rebirth from death links itself with the phoenix egg, and it is shown how near the Christian conception of the phoenix myth, as a prototype of the doctrine of the resurrection of the flesh, lay to the pagan idea itself.2) The interpreters of the Egyptian-Indian legend hitherto have confined themselves to emphasizing its astronomical-chronological relation to the idea of a great world year, and of time returning eternally, in fixed periods, to self-rejuvenation. Now if this is entirely incontestable on the express testimony of the ancients, it nevertheless shows only a particular development of the general solar fundamental idea that dominates the phoenix myth. On its connection with the conceptions of the ancients concerning the primal egg, on the other hand, it throws no light. This question has never yet been answered, and yet it was so obvious to raise it. From the female primal egg all creation has proceeded; it is ascribed to the great material nature mothers, it belongs to all the lunar women; from the two halves of the egg heaven and earth, from its content has
