everything that lives and moves in the light come into being. The egg appears in each of these connections as material. As a representation of the maternal natural principle it stands at the head of the development of the material world. In the phoenix myth, on the other hand, we see it in a wholly different nature: not female but male, not tellurian and not lunar but solar, not material but incorporeal, not as beginning but as end, not entering into the change and movement of the world of becoming, but removed from it, and through fire given back to the primal source of pure light and to the harmony of the Apollonian world of being, into which the deified bird ascends amid the sound of the death songs that it sings to itself. The egg appears here in its highest elevation. But this is at the same time its dissolution. In union with the solar potency it loses its egg nature. The consummation is at the same time a passage into a new form. The transformation into fire the mystics call, according to Plutarch’s passage communicated above, Apollo, on account of aloneness, whereby fire is conceived as simplicis auraï ignis.1) Consumed by fire on the altar of Helios, the myrrh egg lets the incorporeal force of fatherhood enclosed in it, purified of every burden of matter, ascend to heaven and return to the primal seat of the purest light. In the sun egg of Helios the Aphroditean-material primal egg attains its consummation. If the primal egg falls from the moon to the earth, the sun egg returns as pure flame to the sun. If the primal egg enters downward into the lower world of becoming and passing away, the sun egg, after the great generation year is completed, takes the upward direction, in order, leaving behind every material covering, to exchange the boundaries of the lunar world of becoming for the eternity of the solar world of being. In connection with matter, which moves between two poles, the egg becomes a representation of time; for Chronos is the necessary form of all becoming, of all material development; he is creation itself in motion. In this sense Heracles-Chronos, whom the Orphics call Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, carries the material world egg, which here too is traced back to the πατρικὴ δύναμις; he is winged, like all movement of the world of becoming, hastening swiftly along, like all life in time.2) With becoming its form, time, also ceases. Above the lunar region of transience and of material origination there is no time any more. There is no matter, hence also no origination and no

passing away, hence no time. The Chronos egg can therefore find no admission there. Into the solar world the force enters, divested of the egg’s covering. Laid aside is the tellurian materiality of the maternal egg, consumed the myrrh ball of the phoenix; freed of every material nature, as pure fire the paternal principle returns to the realm of light, completed time to the timeless world of solar being. Thus, progressing from below upward, the egg has by stages divested itself of its corporeality, and has found its dissolution at last in the highest principle of light. With the successive development of what is created, the creative principle itself too has arrived at an ever purer representation. At last every materiality appears overcome, the female egg nature wholly laid aside. The light ascends from the chrysalis of matter, and presents the divine force, the νοῦς, the νοητόν of the creating potency, in full purity. What was first comes last to representation and to human consciousness. There takes place what Aristotle states in On the Parts of Animals 2, 1 thus: “What follows in becoming is first by nature, and what is last in origination is first. — — Accordingly, in the order of time matter and origination must be first, but in the order of concept the essence and form of each thing.” — What is materially first is no longer the principial; as in the second Orphic cosmogony, purely intellectual ἀρχαί take precedence over the materially comprehensible.

9.

The lunar stage of the Dionysian nature, which led us to the solar- Apollonian and to the correct appreciation of the mystery idea contained in the burning oil lamp, presents yet another side that stands in the most intimate relation to the world of the tombs. The same combination of becoming and passing away, of the light side and the shadow side of life, of the creative and the destructive principle, which dominates the lowest stage of pure tellurism, and which alone is able to secure eternal rejuvenation for material creation, the same recurs on the lunar stage. Indeed, the more decisively the idea of generation joins itself with the moon and its necessarily hermaphroditic nature, the more clearly must the negative, destructive side of nature, the thought of death, have emerged in it. Every natural force necessarily encloses both potencies, and indeed necessarily in the same degree of development. Only where full equilibrium prevails between the two, and the two streams of origination and passing away, flowing against each other, meet with equal force, can life preserve its eternal freshness and youthfulness. Isis perceives that she must set the captive Typhon free again, and thereby

[PDF 126]

— 112 —

summon again the struggle with the evil principle itself. Typhon’s destructive activity is as indispensable to visible creation as the creative activity of Horus. Only what the former consumes can the latter replace and rejuvenate by new generation; only so, too, can Isis attain ever new fulfillment of her maternal destiny. In the release of Typhon the great mother reveals her lunar nature. The myth has indicated this by adorning her head, in punishment for that deed, with an ox-scalp, which Mercury, on the counsel of the angered Horus, sets upon the mother in place of the crown that she wore.1) In this adornment she appears as the horned Io, who receives her fecundation from the sun, and, illumined by its light, rules the nocturnal heaven. By the same connection of thought all the Dionysian lunar women, too, are representatives of the negative side of nature, mistresses of death no less than of life, and, as tomb goddesses, reveal the maternity of their material nature no less than this happens through their significance of bestowing life and prosperity. In Ariadne’s connection with the labyrinth, in the veneration of Aphrodite as Venus Libitina,2) in the swift-striking shafts of Artemis, in the relation of Demeter and Kore to Aidoneus, the darker tomb side of the maternal lunar nature comes clearly forth, and therefore the images of the great tomb mothers often appear, as e.g. on a beautiful terracotta relief from Tarsus in the Louvre, combined with the sign of the moon. The same combination of life and death shows itself also in individual attributes. I single out especially the dog. We have already come to know the dog above as a representation of matter that is ever anew fecundated, conceiving within itself, κύων and κύειν, and have mentioned the temple image of the κυνοειδὴς γυνή pursued by a man of phallic formation. In this significance it enters also into the closest connection with the moon. It is Diana’s animal, consecrated to her service and inwardly akin to her nature.3) It is the idea of generation that it shares with the nature mother; in this significance it appears connected with Aphrodite and Isis,4) and in this significance, according to Nonnus’s account,5) it ever accompanies Dionysus on his nocturnal

It is therefore itself called marriage, and is ascribed to Achilles-Lunus, who on Crete bears from it the name Pemptus,1) as well as to Athena-Luna. In these five days fortune and misfortune, death and life are joined. For according to Heraclitus the world is just like a lyre or a bow, where the strings are now drawn tight, now loosened, and Euripides says:

“From good, evil cannot be separated;

In due measure both are ever mixed.”2) a belief that made the ancients most deeply convinced of the necessity of the constant clouding of earthly fortune by the addition of a misfortune. Thus the moon becomes the embodiment of the evil, annihilating natural principle. It, which grounds all life, promotes growth, lends assistance to every work of love, seeks to partake of constant fecundation, the same bears death also within itself, joins itself with the concept of female sterility, itself becomes an expression of the thought of the tomb, and is conceived as orbandi potestas.3) In this dark nature it appears as the terrible Gorgon, whose sight suffices to give death, whose face the lunar woman Athena too bears on her aegis surrounded by serpents, and which with the same significance is placed in manifold ways on war equipment, as the bronze greaves of the Karlsruhe Museum show. Gorgo, the Cretan, takes joy in the death of Asander. The terrible Medusa too is a nature mother giving life and fertility, from whose bleeding trunk Pegasus, the generating steed, and Chrysaor, the lord of the golden harvest, as the Campana vase discussed by Em. Braun on Winckelmann’s Day of 1855 represents him, spring forth. In its night significance the moon appears as the man-slaying Amazon, and this thought of death too makes the Amazons peculiarly suited to admission into tombs and to the guarding of tombs. They bring out the darker, sterile, and bereaving side of female nature. They resemble in this Medusa, whose beauty Perseus recognizes only in death, as Achilles that of Penthesilea;4) for of the triple union

of sisters only Medusa, the youngest, is mortal. Only One eye, only One tooth have the Graeae-Gorgons, who are also listed in the singular,1) just so the Amazons only One descent, the maternal, after which alone they are named.2) Persephone is called Mounogeneia, the only-begotten.3) In all these phenomena the same idea expresses itself. Material creation knows only one origin, the maternal. The children are all unilateres, not διφυεῖς, as, according to Athenaeus and Justin, the Athenians were only since Cecrops. They have only a mother, no father. This system rules also on the lunar stage, on which woman has so much the upper hand over man that the invocation of Luna joins of itself with gynecocracy, and Plutarch, de facie in orbe lunæ, ascribes to the moon quite generally the effecting of moisture and femininity. But if the predominance of the one-sidedly maternal nature is proper to the life side and the light side of creation, it stands in still closer relation to the night side and the death side. Here matter emerges completely in its exclusive dominion. To the matter from which it sprang the soulless corpse returns. The same maternal womb that bore it into the light takes it back again into its darkness. If already in generation the activity of the father is one that loses itself in the darkness of matter, withdrawn from sight, the father therefore never natura certus et verus, but only fictione iuris pro vero habitus: so in death too this his cooperation falls away. Here the mother alone stands at the side of the corpse, whether it be Mother Earth or the earthly woman who takes the other’s place, and in all respects, in birth and in death, appears as true γῆ (γυνή from γῆ). Therefore the dead are called not Plutonii but Demetrians, and from Mana-Geneta, Manes; therefore in the Ocnus fable it is a θήλεια ὄνος that unravels the rope; therefore the mother follows the corpse,4) the mother stands at the pyre, women, the φιλοθρῆνοι γυναῖκες, take over the lament for the dead; therefore the Lycians, when they take part in mourning, dress in women’s clothing, on which I have compiled a good deal in my Mutterrecht. This Lycian custom is doubly noteworthy because it is joined with the Lycian gynecocracy, the χρηματίζειν ἀπὸ μητέρων, and with the Lycian winged egg mothers who take the dead into their keeping, as the monument of Xanthus represents them. The same ideas of the one-sidedly female-material nature are expressed in like manner by the Amazons, the Amazonian Gorgons, and the Gorgonian Persephone, and to all of them lunar nature is common, which here again preeminently reveals its shadow side and death side. Shall I add to all this Hecate’s threefold nature, and the double relation to life and death of the water so closely bound to the moon? For Hecate unites in her female nature the double pole of all life, the nascendi et vivendi and the moriendi potestas, both in her tellurian and in her lunar stage.1) Water, moreover, this life-generating element, which rolls the phallus of Osiris in its waves, hides Aphrodite’s egg, stamps Dionysus as Poseidon γενέσιος, and so often expresses the concept of male generative force in its name, as in Peneus, the Elean and Thessalian πέος (penis, πηλός),2) in Larisus, Larius, in Arsen, in mare, πέλαγος, θάλασσα (related to τάλος, τύλος), κῦμα (related to κύων, κύω), is on the other hand connected again with tomb and death, now as the subterranean Acheron, Anio, Eridanus,3) now as favorite place of the dead, whose tombs are erected preferably on the banks of waters. In the swamps around Babylon Alexander sees the royal tombs of the native rulers. At the Gygaean swamp lake those of the Lydian kings are erected. In the marshes of the Velabrum Acca Larentia has her tomb. On the forest stream Oceanus Lycians show Pausanias (1, 35, 6) the tomb of Geryon. Why should I heap up further examples, when the necropolis of Castel d’Asso shows the same arrangement, Strabo designates the Campus Martius on the Tiber as a place of tombs, and Plutarch, de mul. virtut., at the end, himself cites an example of how one sought, just as by the Euripus of the circus, to replace by artificial means the lack of water at tombs. monotonous lament of its waves is the Nereids’ song of mourning for the untimely death of Achilles. So sings the chorus in Aeschylus’s Prometheus:

Everywhere the same fundamental idea shows itself: life is at the same time death; Venus also Libitina; Aphrodite also the slayer of men; the moon at once source of becoming and of passing away, lovely and white in the former, hideous, terrifying, and black in the latter function; in both akin to water, in which it finds its nourishment, which it causes to well forth from the earth,1) with which, in the nocturnal dew, it refreshes the thirsting fields,2) and in which, as the ancients already knew,3) it also calls forth ebb and flood, the image of change, by its influence so mightily acting on everything tellurian. This night side expresses itself also very definitely in the outward appearance of the moon. Corresponding to its double dominion over life and death, it appears ever changing, ever leading fullness back into nothing, so that, as an ancient remarks, no garment would ever fit it. Ever it wages the struggle against darkness, as Horus against Typhon, now succumbing, now victorious. As the double color in the egg, so white and black divide in its disk. Black spots disfigure its bright surface. The same variegation is shown by the hide of the stag, which thereby confirms its kinship with Diana.4) For its relation to the lunar woman does not rest in this similarity alone. In its tree-like antlers and in its custom of shedding them5) and hiding them in the earth, it appears as an image of maternal earth, which lets the trees of the forest grow forth from her womb: a relation that is embedded even in the designation Dama. As the moon cries out for water, so the stag cries out for the spring, a property that even in Christian antiquity lends it a relation to baptisteries.1) As an accompaniment of the earth it appears on a cameo of the Museum Florentinum, which Stark in his de tellure Dea chose as the central point of his account.2) By its connection with night the moon is, moreover, the star of death. It brings sleep and repose and that stillness which is attributed to primal chaos, as to the grave that leads back to it, and to the mysteries; which makes the solemn still more solemn and the terrible still more terrible, lets the very face of the lunar disk appear as a grinning mask that threatens destruction, corresponds to the Manes and the silentia regna, and has found a moving expression in the tombs through the many representations of those scenes designated in art as still lifes. As the sun each morning awakens life and movement, and thus with its rays draws from Memnon’s column its first sound, so conversely the moon leads all things back to rest and silence.3) It is the star of ruins, by the same property also that of tombs, and is often depicted on funerary lamps, as e.g. also on a Tarsian one. At night the lemuria are celebrated, at night the funera are held.4) The moon yields to the sun, as night to day. The ancients conceive this phenomenon as a birth of light out of darkness,5) and recognize in it the daily repetition of a great act of cosmogony. Here too the female-material principle maintains its primacy in creation. It is the first, the originally given. Helios stands to Nox in the relation of a son; he is the mystery of the male solar force revealed through birth, he is the Dionysus-Enorches who breaks through from the egg to the light, the visible creation that steps into day from the dark maternal womb. Accordingly night shows an inner kinship with the dark egg. Like it, it is the female natural principle, like it the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. So it appears in the first Orphic cosmogony, which Damascius, principia pp. 380–384 Kopp, designates as the common doctrine, shrouded by a

In the cosmogony of Acusilaus Nox is joined, as the female principle, with Erebus, the male; in that of Epimenides, with Aer. Here too one recognizes the foundation of Orphic doctrine, which forms the chief content of the Bacchic mysteries, and of that gradual succession of becoming, already emphasized above, which takes as its basis an unfolding of creation and of the creator out of the formless into form, out of chaos into definite configuration, out of darkness into light, out of matter into the νοητόν, out of materiality into a being comprehensible only to the spirit, thus in everything a progress from below upward, in contrast to emanation in descending embodiment. On this female-material fundamental principle rests the reckoning of time by a twenty-four-hour period beginning at midnight, in which the male day appears enclosed by two female nights. On it rests also the lunar year, which expresses in the reckoning of time the lunar-material stage of religion. From it, too, the idea of the Roman Mater Matuta receives its explanation. She is at once the great nature mother and the goddess of the early light, at once Leucothea, the shining moon, and Ino, who seeks her death in the waves of the sea. All this by virtue of her significance as the female-material natural principle, which has its physical basis in the earth and its waters, but also in the moon, and which as such comprehends within itself life and death, light and darkness, and, as Aurora, gives birth to the day out of itself. In the abduction of Cephalus the significance of death in maternal nature emerges again. In the same moment origination and destruction unite. Minerva carries both attributes at once, the golden lamp and the cock. In the former she shows her kinship with the night and the nocturnal moon; in the latter she stands before us as Matuta, who gives birth to the early light. In both relations she is the material mother who, as Gorgon-bearer, as Amazon hostile to marriage, as barren Pempta, represents the side of night and death in the maternal nature of matter.

Thus everything unites to produce, for the lunar stage of material femininity as well, the same combination of white and black that forms the essence of the Dionysian nature. Luna bears maternal nature within herself in its twofold aspect, its beneficent and its destructive side. The mixture of fear and joy attaches itself preeminently to the moon. Precisely thereby it acquires special significance for the mysteries. For the mood that one feels at initiation is that of fear and anxiety, with joyful hope

united.1) To the wicked the heavenly star shows the terrible countenance that proclaims their punishment; the pious, on the other hand, will recognize its full beauty. The physical idea returns in spiritualized significance. The dark and the bright side of the nocturnal star become the image of the lot that awaits the souls of the departed. For after separation from the body the souls wander about in the space between earth and moon. Here the unjust and the vicious atone for their transgressions; the pious, on the other hand, after all the stains that stem from the body, the author of evil, have been effaced, will pass through and gain firm footing on the moon. Here, crowned with wreaths and like a ray of the sun, they hear the cry of lament and wailing, rising from below, of those who are being punished. But they also recognize the mixed nature of the star itself into which they have been received. The light and the heavy, the tellurian and the uranian component, hold each other in perfect balance in it. To the plain of Persephone corresponds the Elysian. The former is turned toward the earth,

Among the scholars of today there may now be many who ask mockingly, with the Cynic Diogenes (in Plut. l. c.), whether the thief Pataecion, because he had been initiated, has a better lot than Epaminondas? Others may see everything in the light of priestly fraud. To the latter we answer what Gorgias (in Plut. l. c. p. 59) said of tragedy: that it is a deception in which the deceiver is more just, and the deceived wiser, than he who does not deceive and is not deceived. To the former, however, we give this to consider, that the highest purpose of the mysteries was none other than sanctification and purification, and the strengthening of the conviction that between the state of the soul in that life and the morality demonstrated on this side there prevails a necessarily corresponding relation. Those who emulate the gods will return to them after death, but the vicious will be excluded from the community of the gods. Cicero, Tusc. 1, 30. The ancients combined with a religion material in its foundation the most earnest striving for ethical and moral sanctification, whereas the moderns leave nothing undone to subordinate their religion, purely spiritual in origin and content, once more to matter and to impure matter. For them no excuse is at hand. Timæus p. 90 a.

This conception, which for the most part follows word for word the statements of Plutarch on the face that appears in the lunar disk, c. 28–29, gives the moon, for the world of spirits, the same significance that it has for the corporeal-material world and for the cosmos in general. It is the connection of two worlds, a higher and a lower, the point of passage where the two currents, the ὁδὸς ἄνω καὶ κάτω, meet; thus it maintains the connection of the tellurian with the solar, of the corporeal with the incorporeal sphere, whose constant passage into one another constitutes the highest harmony of the cosmos, and at the same time the joyful hope of the initiate.1)

10.

We have now become so familiar with the egg, with its Bacchic relation, its relation to the world of the tombs, and with the mystery idea contained in it, that it becomes of ever greater interest to add still more new ones to the number of monuments that represent the egg symbol. What puts difficulty in the way of this endeavor, and makes great care doubly necessary, is the slight exactness that ancient art devotes to the representation of smaller objects, often of little importance for the main picture. Since the merely suggestive manner, especially in accompanying attributes, prevails over naturalistic execution, the question often arises whether what the eye, predisposed in favor of its task, is inclined to take for an egg may not perhaps be assignable to other objects, especially apples, whose erotic significance is, after all, beyond all doubt. The egg seems to me certain on the following monuments. A vase painting of the Louvre collection shows a square pillar resting on a broader base, on whose upper surface a white egg stands upright. MVTILI | MARVLII | VIX. ANN. | XVII. This monument can shed light on the egg-crowned grave stelae discovered in the Praenestine tombs, which Braun describes in the Bulletino 1855. Great kinship with it is shown by the stone monuments of the united collections at Munich, which are said to come from Salzburg. In this use the egg alternates with other equivalent symbols, with the pomegranate, with the pyramid, the palmette, but especially with the ball and the flat disk-like circular section, as these not infrequently occur on the tops of funerary pillars. On monuments of unambiguous significance the circle appears as the sign of apotheosis.1) The circle derives this symbolic use from the property of the circular line, which, like all life of the tellurian creation, returns ever again to itself and, in its progress, to its point of departure. Like the egg, therefore, it encloses both poles between which creation moves eternally to and fro, and which, like white and black, constantly pass over into one another. It thereby becomes itself a sign of the natural force that encloses life and death within itself. This significance recurs intensified in those concentric circles that are so frequent on funerary monuments. They correspond to the plurality of eggs, the three circles of Praenestine discs to the 3 eggs of our tomb painting. On this also rests the significance of the discus. The swiftness with which it flies along the course is equal to that of the two-horse team, a representation of the swiftness with which the united forces of death and of life bring about the revolution of visible creation and that eternal alternation of generations. Thereby ball, discus, and circle gain a definite relation to the physical bearers of natural force, to the tellurian water as well as to the heavenly sunlight. Likewise the

symbol has, like the force, lower and higher stages, the plurality of which it unites in itself. As a designation of the force of water the sphere appears in the hand of the nymphs;1) as solar power the invention of the discus is traced back to Perseus.2) From this is explained the combination of the discus with the lotus, which first came to light in the Praenestine tomb. It is the combination of the solar and the aquatic force, whose cooperation is required for every tellurian generation, so that Plutarch’s inquiry as to which is more useful, water or fire, does not particularly correspond to the ideas of the ancient religion. Now the round of the discus itself seems to correspond to the disk of the sun and the moon, and the ball to be a representation of the vault of earth and heaven. All these relations of the circle and of its various representations have truth and legitimacy side by side. The original relation, however, to which the others and finally the significance for the mysteries attach, is none other than that eternal return of creation upon itself that comes to view in the circular line, that resting of end and beginning in one another, which also lends the two-colored egg its significance. Thereby the circle becomes the expression of Fate, or of the highest law of nature governing all life, before which even the gods bow;3) thereby likewise the representation of immortality, which issues from the eternal rejuvenation of life by the aid of death. It makes, therefore, little difference for the idea itself whether an egg-shaped or a perfectly round body, or other figures composed of both forms, crown the funerary pillars and the metae. The artist followed the old sepulchral tradition, and, since he let himself be guided less by the content of the idea than by a feeling for harmony of form, could take refuge in the most various modifications and embellishments of the pure egg form and the perfected circular form. Thus these two symbols, like the κύματα and the many kinds of climbing plants, have finally become the basic components of an extremely rich ornamentation, which, like individual architectural pieces, such as especially the Ionic column, has passed out of the tombs into the dwellings of men. Images of profound ideas that formed the fundamental content of religion itself, and in which the whole fullness of the higher intimations connected with death and the tomb

little chests that we often see represented on vases and terracottas. The cista is attributed especially to Demeter;1) the surviving bronze vessels come for the most part from Praeneste and stand, beyond doubt, in the closest connection with the cult of the Fortuna preeminently venerated there, of Bacchic- Cerealian nature, a representation of the female-material natural principle. On a terracotta of the Vogelberg collection at Munich the cista appears on the arm of one of those earnest tomb mothers whom we may with equal right call Ceres, Aphrodite, Fortuna, Pherephatta. In connection with initiation the same little chest appears very often on vase paintings, always as an accompaniment of female beings. The meaning, therefore, cannot be doubtful. The cista is the representation of the maternal womb, of the locality in which all life is conceived and developed to birth, of the χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη γενέσεως, as Plato calls femininity in contrast to masculinity conceived as the vertical line, of the Varronian locus genitalis, in quo vitæ primordia consistunt, of the female chamber, which German usage has retained, and which many a myth, such as the one mentioned above of the Dioscuri’s penetration into the maidens’ chamber in Phormio’s house, has in part made the subject of its representation. To male force every idea of locality and spatiality is alien and opposed; in the materiality of woman, on the other hand, it is necessarily contained, woman by her nature χώρα καὶ δεξαμένη, a locus, a chamber, a spatiality,2) which only matter, not force, admits. Thus the cista corresponds perfectly to the female nature. It is the attribute, or better the representation, of maternity in its natural determination, of fecundation, of the seminis immissio in monetam, of the conception, cherishing, and sheltering of the seed and of every young life. Dark is its space, like that of the gloomy maternal womb. In it, shut off from the light, the male phallus develops its work. It is therefore also enclosed in the mystic cista, as it penetrates, invisible as generative force, the maternal matter of the earth and of the moon. When in so many myths the newborn child is shut up in a chest and entrusted with it to the sea, the idea of the sheltering maternal womb is repeated therein, whose image the ancients also recognized in the shells,3)

the nuts, the legumes, such as peas and beans, which owe their tellurian significance precisely to this property. From the chest Cypselus received his name, that is, he is named after the mother. Of illegitimate birth, he has no father, but only a mother. He is called Cypselus from the female locus genitalis, as spurius is named from the female sporium the one sown in it by an unknown sower. We now recognize, then, the inner kinship of the egg with the cista, and the relation of both to Luna and to the pair of Dioscuri born from the moon egg, who, like death and life, bring up light and darkness in the sky, one day after the other. But at the same time we recognize also the connection of the various meanings of Mundus. The opened Mundus, into which the founders of cities throw the first fruits of all produce and of all riches, is the maternal locus genitalis from which all blessing proceeds. Its opening stands in the nearest relation to the Cerealian egg and to the funerary significance of the circus games. But as the egg becomes the image of the universe, so the tellurian Mundus becomes the representation of that which the Pythagoreans first called κόσμος. As finally in the fable of Psyche Proserpina’s pyxis holds all the means of beauty required for Aphrodite’s adornment, so too the Mundus changes into the toilette and the container of everything that can give Aphroditean charm. By the same combination of concepts the cista becomes the jewel box of woman, and it is entirely understandable why most of the surviving ones held within them female toilet articles, perhaps also mixed with male ones. They may have served the living for actual use, and thus justify the name of jewel boxes. Their religious significance, however, which corresponds to the nature of the Praenestine mother, is entirely independent of the question of practical purpose.

I turn to other monuments that still leave some doubts as to the occurrence of the egg. On the Xanthian tomb, which in the British Museum, in the hall of Lycian antiquities, under the gloomy clouded sky of England proclaims the laughing splendor of Asia, the egg that forms the womb of the Harpies is beyond doubt; but less certain is it on the scenes that adorn its west and south sides. neglected. According to Fellows’s drawings the matter admits of no doubt. On the west side the egg appears twice, namely in the left hand of the female seated figure, in whom an Aphroditean earth mother is unmistakable, and likewise in that of the last figure, which closes the procession of women. The position that the cow suckling the calf occupies precisely in this picture seems not only to explain the thought of the offering of the egg, but even to require it. For the egg is, like that cow symbol so generally diffused in the ancient world, omniparentis terræ fœcundum simulacrum, and by this significance a symbol that expresses the whole Aphroditean nature in its twofold aspect. In the representation of the south side the egg enters into a similar combination with the dove, whose connection with the Aphroditean nature and with Aphrodite’s egg is already clear from the above. Such a predominance of the egg symbol cannot in the least surprise on a funerary monument of Lycia, which was devoted to gynecocracy. The predominance of maternity emerges clearly enough also in the fables of Bellerophon’s reverence before the sight of the female κτείς, of the meaning of Leda in the Lycian language, and in the myth of the Lycian frog lake of Latona-Leda, the great primal mother. All this has in a certain measure found its total expression in the egg. On the tomb especially, where maternity always emerges as alone ruling, the egg symbol is doubly justified in its twofold significance, embracing life and death equally.1)

11.

Having so far found the egg preferentially on funerary monuments, we shall now demonstrate it on monuments of other purpose as well. I begin with the one that offers the most doubt and difficulty. On various coins the Minotaur holds in his right hand a round object, which has been taken now for an apple, now for a ball. The one is a silver coin of Knossus, depicted in Pellerin, recueil, T. 3. tab. 89, 24, and Böttiger, Ideen zur Kunstmythologie 1, pl. 5, 1. On its reverse the labyrinth is represented in square form. coin belongs to Metapontum in Lucania, and has been communicated, after Magnan, Lucania Numismatica tab. 34, 3, by Böttiger on the same pl. 5, 2. The form that this coin gives the object excludes the thought of an apple, and there remains only the question whether we have before us a circle or an egg. Both assumptions would in the end yield the same idea, and agree with the total significance of the Minotaur. For the egg, several reasons seem to me to speak. First, the special prominence of the female natural principle in the Cretan religion. In Ariadne, Pasiphaëssa, Artemis, Dictynna, Britomartis it appears with the physical foundation of the tellurian and the heavenly earth, the male generative potency standing over against it preeminently still as Poseidonian force of water, conceived in a chthonian manner. As Ariadne’s labyrinth represents the inextricable passages of the maternal womb of earth, so too the Minotaur shows force on the lowest stage of the Dionysian nature, as chthonian potency of water, with the bull’s head, διὰ τὸ γόνιμον τοῦ ὕδατος, and therefore with special emphasis on the dark, destroying side of life, in which significance he recommended himself especially to the usage of the legions as a victory-bringing standard.1) On this tellurian-lunar stage of religion female materiality has the preponderance over male potency. Therefore Ariadne appears as ruler of Crete. Therefore the Cretans say even later, as Plato and Plutarch testify, not “fatherland” but “dear motherland,”2) and therefore the egg also would be quite eminently suited as a symbol of this Aphroditean-female religious principle, which encloses earth and moon, death and life. Given the close kinship that connects Crete with Lycia, the community of the symbol too cannot surprise, and when we recall the inner relation that connects the Minotaur with the bull-bodied Bacchus-Hebon, the Cretan egg of the Minotaur leads back in the end to the Bacchic one of the Dionysian-Orphic mysteries. By just this kinship with Dionysus the occurrence of the Minotaur in Magna Graecia is explained, where he enters into the closest relation with the bull-shaped Bacchus. His defeat by Theseus stands on a line with the destruction of the Amazons. Both deeds prepare the transition from a lower, more material stage of religion to a higher one, more akin to the Apollonian luminous nature; it is the progress from the stage of earth and moon to the solar region, which in Dionysus is still more phallic and directed to fecundation, in Theseus, on the other hand, ever since

I turn to a second doubtful work of sculpture, but one that is probably to be counted among the egg monuments. Winckelmann, Monumenti inediti, communicates to us at the end of the trattato preliminare the illustration of a relief in rosso antico preserved in the Capitoline Museum at Rome,1) whose content admits of no doubt. We see here the representation of a sacrifice that a newly wed woman offers to the goddess Hygieia. If the significance of the whole is thus unmistakable, yet precisely the determination of the offered object presents difficulties. In the left hand of the girl an egg-shaped object appears, which, however, according to Winckelmann’s assurance, shows a flat surface, whereby it remains undecided what share time may have had in the form now visible. Winckelmann guesses at the oblation of the Πέμματα, which, mentioned by Pausanias 7, p. 600, 10, p. 817, are explained by Pollux 1, 29 and Hesych. The egg has indeed a deeply grounded inner kinship with Hygieia’s divine nature. Even in her connection with the maternal Athena, Hygieia presents herself as a material nature mother who bestows prosperity.1) The same principle that gives life bestows also health and the adornment of bodily beauty. All this is Hygieia’s gift, and herein she shows the general maternal nature of matter developed on a particular side and in a particular direction. The egg too has gone through the same transition from the more general to the more specific significance. By its foundation the beginning of all life, the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως for the whole and for each individual thing, it now becomes the bearer and symbol of every kind of salvation, especially of bodily well-being. Lustration with the egg protects against the harmful influence of the fever-laden September, and against the enervating sirocco, which Horace 2, 6, 18 calls plumbeus. Metuique jubet septembris et austri adventum, nisi se centum lustraverit ovis, the castrated mendicant priest of the Great Mother proclaims in Juvenal 6, 518 to the superstitiously listening people. The same purpose of averting misfortune is served by that egg lustration of which Ovid A. a. 2, 329 expresses himself thus: Et veniat, quæ purget anus lectumque locumque, Præferat et tremula sulfur et ova manu. Thereby blessing is brought into the house, especially into the marriage bed. The eggs that serve for lustration are offered to Hecate, the great material mother, the mistress over life and death, at the crossroads. This ᾠὸν ἐκ καθαρσίου Lucian mentions, Dialog. mort. 1, 1. ed Bipont. 8, p. 129, on which one must read Hemsterhuys’s exposition, more collecting than explanatory, ibid. pp. 397–401. Plutarch, Symp. 7, 6 places Hecate together with the gods who avert misfortune, and sees in the δεῖπνα set out for her at the crossroads, which are called καθάρματα and Ἑκάταια, Sueton August. 80.) rests the egg to which the serpent draws near. On this summis digitis Deos colere, which emerges on so many monuments of sacral purpose, speak Lactant. 1, 20; 5, 19; Ovid. F. 2, 573. The combination with the tripod and other Apollonian attributes cannot be surprising for Hygieia any more than for Aesculapius; and Eros, who stands as a little boy at the right of the goddess, enters into connection with her as with Fortuna and other mother goddesses, as he is indeed called her father by Proclus on Plato, Timæus 3, 158. On the present monument he may moreover have a still more specific relation to love, marriage, and fertility, and thus stand close to the idea of the egg. — On a Pompeian wall painting in Zahn, second series, pl. 52, Müller, pl. 61, 782, Hygieia stands wreathed with laurel, holding a laurel branch in her left hand. The serpent entwines the whole figure in great coils, and brings its head near a patella that the goddess holds out to it on her right hand. On it lie, intended for feeding, fruits and eggs. On the bronze coin of Hierapolis in Phrygia illustrated in Wieseler 791 I do not wish to decide. Nevertheless here too I think first of all of egg feeding, which would be especially fitting for Phrygia.

a means of averting misfortune and harm from one’s house. The egg thus appears here too as a means bestowing salvation and prosperity, as a true fundamentum salutis. The superstition of the time grasped the process quite externally. It was believed that the misfortune threatening the person was now diverted into the egg, as Juvenal 6, 520 puts the purpose of another purification ceremony in the words ut quicquid subiti et magni discriminis instet, in tunicas eat. Clement of Alexandria, Strom. 7, p. 844 Potter, follows this conception in order to bring the nonsense of egg lustration fully to light. People are said to believe that the egg takes upon itself all the evils of the one purified with it; but this is already refuted, he says, by the fact that one can see how those lustration eggs, supposedly afflicted with misfortune, when hatched, bring living chicks into the world.1) Here one sees quite clearly how the purifying force of the egg itself is only an expression of its nature, which bears life and salvation within it, and hence attaches itself to the fundamental significance of the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. The same connection holds also for the other καθάρματα, torch and sulfur, which emphasize the generative element of fire, and water, which bears within it the generative force of tellurian moisture. As they give life, so they are able also to rejuvenate it, and to take from it every blemish and sickness. Therefore it is preeminently woman who performs the purification ceremonies. As Ovid speaks of an old woman who carries sulfur and eggs before her with trembling hand, so Clement, op. cit., quite generally entrusts women with the lustration, and by the same thought the ἐγχυτρίστριαι appear at Athens, of whom Plato, Minos p. 315 D speaks. Female is the natural principle that rules over life and death; a woman must therefore perform the ceremonies that are to check destruction and promote welfare. Only the primal mother Earth is able to banish misfortune, because from her proceed all blessing and all plague.2) Thus the lustration egg must appear in the hand of woman. If, therefore, a trembling old woman is preeminently chosen, this corresponds to the same conception of the maternal principle of earth that reappears in the representation of the friendly, beneficent nymph of the Numicius, Anna Perenna, who nourished the hungry people with warm loaves even during the leanest months of the year, as a busy, trembling anus, canens sæclis innumerabilibus.3) Countless centuries have turned her hair

In a trembling hand the ᾠὸν ἐκ καθαρσίου has a double significance. In connection with the anus it appears quite properly as a leading back of life to that primal ground from which, aeons ago, the development of the κόσμος and of every individual life took its departure.1)

As in the lustration significance of the egg the idea of the salus lying in it emerges, so also its application as a means of divination leads back to the same. On ᾠοσκοπία Hermagoras of Amphipolis wrote in his book περὶ σοφιστείας πρὸς τοὺς Ἀκαδημικούς, according to the report of Suidas. On Persius Sat. 5, 180: Tunc nigri lemures, ovoque pericula rupto, the scholia give the following explanation: Sacerdotes, qui explorandis periculis sacra faciebant, observare solebant, ovum igni impositum utrum in capite an in latere insudaret. Si autem ruptum effluxerat, periculum ei portendebat, pro quo factum fuerat, vel rei familiari eius. Here the egg appears as a true augurium salutis, and indeed in its twofold direction toward bodily prosperity and toward the extension of the personality in property. Periculum has accordingly here, like the egg itself, a wholly material meaning. It denotes diminution or total destruction of substance, as salus denotes not so much health as the existence of life and of goods in general. In this meaning periculum is found often, e.g. Macrob. Sat. 1, 7, p. 242 Zeune, quite generally in the usage of the ancient jurists. It is, however, the corporeal substance of earthly things that has its origin in the egg, so that the ᾠοσκοπία remains entirely faithful to the fundamental significance of the egg, which embraces prosperity and ruin alike.

A further proof of the close relation of eggs to the idea of material salus is found in a remarkable account of Pliny 29, 3, 12. That the ovum anguinum, to which the Gauls ascribe such lofty powers, had no physical existence but owes its origin to a mythological combination of egg and serpent, such as we find also among Greeks and Romans, I need not remark. But whatever may have given occasion to the assumption of such a serpent’s egg, formed from the coiled body of a serpent and covered with a mushroom-like

If we now hold this significance of the egg together with that of Hygieia, there results for both so perfect an inner agreement that the connection of the symbol with the goddess establishes itself of itself. What offering could be more agreeable to Hygieia than the egg? what could correspond more to her connection with Dionysus and Telesphorus than the egg of Bacchic initiation? what could also more clearly reveal the thoughts of the sacrificing girl herself? That she prays for fertility of her maternal womb, for prosperity for house and marriage bed, for preservation of life and health for herself, for her beloved, and perhaps also for the egg’s little chick, is clear enough. Should she perhaps go still further in her thoughts, and implore a male offspring from the goddess? Pliny 10, 55 relates what use Julia Augusta, daughter of Drusus Livius, made of the egg in her pregnancy. Julia Augusta prima sua iuventa Tiberio Cæsare ex Nerone gravida, cum parere virilem sexum admodum cuperet, hoc usa est puellari augurio ovum in sinu fovendo atque cum deponendum haberet nutrici per sinum tradendo, ne intermitteretur tepor; nec falso augurata proditur. For, as Sueton in Tiberio 14 adds in explanation: pullus insigniter cristatus exclusus est. Scribonius prophesied, etiam regnaturum quandoque, sed sine regio insigni. Here the egg is not only the image of the fruitful maternal womb: a significance in which the hen itself also occurs, as the augurium that befell Livia Augusta

This leads us to the discovery of a still further relation of the egg to Hygieia. We know what close kinship connects Hygieia with Aesculapius. She is called now his daughter,2) now his consort.3) She stands at the side of the male god as the representation of female natural potency, and is therefore called quite generally also μᾶτερ and ἄνασσα.4) In the face of this general significance the manner of the connection is of no importance, fixed by the myth at a time when the general ideas of nature, of a doubly shaped material force, were clothed in the forms of human appearance and of human family and kinship articulation, and therefore in this, as in many other cases, represented in the seemingly most irreconcilable way. Thus the primal woman too is now born of the egg, now herself in turn giving birth to the egg, now the egg itself, out of which she emerges again in duality or triplicity, double-sexed. So Aesculapius himself is now Coronis’s son, now her consort.5) Thus mother, daughter, consort, and sister are only four designations of the same femininity, subordinate to the general significance of the maternally receptive natural principle, at whose side, in equal generality, the male-active principle steps, complementing it, now as father, now as consort. That Hygieia and Aesculapius are to be thought of side by side in this relation, thus like the Tenedian double head, and were really so thought of by the ancients, is proved by their repeated union in a single cult, in which any determination of the kindred bond is lacking. In such a connection we find them at Corinth6) and at Argos,7) and the same recurs in works of art, so in the beautiful group from Palestrina in the Pio-Clementino, illustrated in Visconti 2, 3, Clarac, musée de sculptures 4, 546, n. 1141 B., so also on two reliefs in the Louvre, whose illustration and description may be found in Clarac Atlas 2, pl. 177,

text 2, pp. 312–315.1) From this connection of Hygieia with Aesculapius it follows that the egg-birth of the latter corresponds to the nature of Hygieia as well. That Aesculapius, the life-giving god who calls back from death to existence, was conceived, no differently from Dionysus-Enorches, as the son of the materially maternal primal egg as well, is shown by Lucian’s account in the Pseudomant. 12–16 of the frauds of the charlatan Alexander. For in order to secure success for his arts, this man was obliged to take as his starting point religious ideas that were familiar, and in particular related to the mystery cult. How closely he adhered to them is shown by the circumstance that he fetched out of the muddy waters of the earth, with the phiale, the egg from which the new Aesculapius was to emerge as a mighty dragon: a connection of water with the egg such as recurs in the story of the egg of the Euphrates, in the egg-bearing moon women, who stand in such close relation to swamp waters that Helen-Aphrodite herself is called after ἕλος, and in the general conceptions of the primal generative force of tellurian moisture. In the egg-born Asclepian dragon Glycon2) female materiality appears once again as the natural principle at the head of things, the male force in the relation of son as the revealed mystery, the former as egg, the latter as the egg-born dragon. Accordingly it could not contradict the ancient manner of viewing things to conceive Hygieia as well in the same way. The dragon belongs to her no less than to Aesculapius. On the numerous works of art of antiquity, of which a rich selection is to be found in Clarac, nos. 1145–1182 B, it is her constant companion, and for the most part, as on the Capitoline relief, it is represented in connection with the water bowl, whose related contents it thirstily longs for. It is therefore Hygieia herself, and sank from the independently venerated fetish to a mere attribute only with the progress of anthropomorphic formation of the gods. Hygieia and Aesculapius are accordingly originally to be thought of as a pair of serpents, the egg as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, from which they, in their duality representing the duality of the sexual potencies, have issued. It would therefore correspond perfectly to the spirit of the ancient nature religion were we to represent the said divine pair itself by the image of two dragons in connection with an egg set upright in their midst. It seems incredible that anyone could ever have been in doubt about the word ΥΓΙΑ. It is perfectly certain. Whether we take it as a designation of the goddess, or, more indefinitely, as an expression of well-being in general, it remains perfectly indisputable that the symbolic representation of the cameo must agree with the content of the inscription. The concept ΥΓΙΑ and the egg coincide. The latter expresses symbolically what the former word renders in language, and the two dragons as guardians of the egg join themselves, in perfect accord, to the divine union of Asclepius and Hygieia. The inscription of the picture on the Florentine cameo and on the cut stones of the Stosch collection throws light on the representation of a funerary monument which Fabretti, Inscriptiones domesticæ p. 28, no. 17, communicates. As its founder one A. Herennuleius Hermes is named. Fabretti describes the pictorial representation in the following words: vir libamen ex patera effundens et gemini ad utrumque latus serpentes cristati et erecti, ovum ore apprehendentes. Evangel. 1, 7 longævum animal est, nec solum senectam cum pelle deponens reiuvenescit; sed crescit etiam in adolescentiam redactum; vel ut ex concordia illa quasi maritali serpentum, coniuges improles adhuc sobolem sibi augurarentur ex ovo prodeuntem, tamquam principio et originario fonte generationis, ut illud vocat Plutarchus Quæstion. Passeri, gemmæ astriferæ ad tabulam 123, Genii symbola, t. 2, p. 159 adds: In Aegyptiorum hieroglyphicis, immo fere in omnium obeliscorum apice, observari ovum hoc, unde serpens exsiliit. Fabretti’s twofold explanation has little probability; to express on the funerary monument the wish for a long life, or to implore the blessing of children for a hitherto barren maternal womb, corresponds too little to the purpose of a funerary stone and to the usage of the ancients for us to be able to presuppose such a thought. The salus that can alone be thought of here is that higher one which lies beyond the limits of bodily existence and of tellurian being. These are the nova salutis curricula which Apuleius presents as the higher content of the mysteries. The egg, in its physical significance the inexhaustible primal source of tellurian life, becomes on that higher stage the symbol of the existence that presses through material death to a rejuvenated, higher being, in which Psyche, freed from the coarse husk of matter, like the chick breaking forth from the dark egg, rejoices in a purer existence in the realms of heavenly light. The serpents too are raised to the same significance. They, too, designate here not the natural force, conceived as material, of the generative phallus, but rather rebirth, which renews life by rejuvenating it. It is not the dragon of the dark depths, but the pair of serpents of light, the spiritus qui per universum orbem permeat,1) that holds and guards the egg of the higher rebirth. The connection of the egg with the mouths of the serpents stands in a special relation to this idea. The Egyptian world egg proceeds from the mouth of the demiurge Kneph,2) a formation of the divine breath, not generation by the phallic force of matter. Thus we see on the Fabretti tombstone the pair of serpents guarding the egg as the expression of a higher idea, such as best befits a tombstone, as the symbol of a higher salus that grasps death itself as the point of departure of a rejuvenated existence. Here too Hygieia is the

guiding fundamental idea, but this Hygieia is no longer the material one, who secures the well-being of the body and bestows fertility on the maternal womb, but a spiritualized potency leading matter itself through to a higher blessedness, in which that physical-sensual one continues and is fulfilled.1)

Through the representation of the Florentine cameo the egg sacrifice of the Capitoline relief seems to me removed from all challenge, and a secure basis of explanation is given for several other monuments as well. Gorlaeus communicates, on pl. 233, fig. 492 of his pierres antiques gravées, a gem picture that shows serpent and egg once more in connection. A male figure kneels before the altar and brings the egg near to the blazing flame, in a posture which permits us to think of the ᾠοσκοπία. A standing female figure directs her attention to the result of the divination undertaken, the relation of which to the augurium salutis is emphasized by the attribute of the serpent coiling in the girl’s left hand. On another gem picture in the same work, pl. 256, fig. 579, a young female figure hands to Aesculapius, recognizable by his serpent staff, an object in which we may recognize first of all an egg. On other monuments the feeding of a dragon seems rather to be represented. To this belong Gorlaeus pl. 43, no. 86, and the relief from the collection of the Louvre, already mentioned earlier, in Clarac, pl. 177, no. 268. Hygie ne tient ici, says the French commentator 2, 315, ni sa patère, ni son serpent; c’est à celui de son père, qu’elle présente, à ce qu’il pârait, un gâteau, et elle est en aussi bonne intelligence avec cet animal favori, qu’avec celui, qui l’accompagne ordinairement. The setting out of cakes for sacred serpents is often mentioned, for which the story in Herodotus 8, 41, Propert. 4, 8, 3– 16, and Museo Capitol. t. 4, t. 42 furnish decisive examples.2)

A vase painting in Caylus, recueil d’antiquités vol. 4, t. 40, 1, is to be joined to the egg monuments. On an altar lie three eggs; a bird, whose identification is difficult, seizes in its beak a serpent, which seems to defend them. The whole representation recalls the myth of the raven, the serpent, and the Crater, as Hygin. Poetic. astr. 2, 40; 3, 39 and Ovid Fast. 2, 243–266 relate it. The connection of the serpent with the egg is found also in the ovum anguinum of the Gauls, about which we

at Leiden. The male figure reclining on the couch holds it in his hand. Opened at the top, it serves him as a drinking cup, as water is presented to the Persian king in a golden egg.

By the great Syrtis there stands on the seashore, washed by the waves, a tomb, a column on a broad base. On this is found the following picture: in the swamp stands, comparable to Tantalus, a man, drawing water as if he wished to drink. Around his foot a serpent coils, the poisonous dipsas. Women carry water in vessels and pour it over the thirsting man. Nearby lie some ostrich eggs. An epigram, which we must imagine engraved on the base, compares the sufferings of the man with the never-quenched thirst of Tantalus, the water carriers with the eternally vain labor of the Danaids. Four other verses, which Lucian does not communicate, mentioned the eggs and told how the poor man, while he was occupied in gathering them, was bitten by the dangerous serpent.1)— The connection of egg and serpent is met with further in the second Orphic theogony, which Damascius, principia p. 581, Kopp, traces back to Hieronymus and Hellanicus. Threefold in form is the dragon. Between the head of the lion and that of the bull, in the middle, appears the divine countenance of Heracles, who is called Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, and is joined with Ananke-Adrasteia, who spreads herself through the All. From the force of the dragon-shaped Heracles an egg proceeds, and from this Protogonus Zeus, who shows wings on his shoulders, bulls’ heads in his flanks, and a serpent on his head, and assumes manifold animal shape. From the Orphic conception certain Sicilian and Cilician coin types become intelligible. The bearded double head on a coin of Camarina points to that Heracles-Chronos of the Orphic

Müll. Here an Etruscan work of art deserves mention, which seems to receive its explanation from Lucian’s account. Micali, antichi monumenti to the Storia degli antich. popoli, pl. 40, 3, p. 53, communicates the picture of a bronze candelabrum found in the tombs of Vulci, from the collection of the Prince of Canino. As its pedestal serves a nude satyr, recognizable by the formation of his ears, who with his staff presses down a huge serpent striving upward, while the raised right hand seems ready to hurl a stone. Expression and bearing of the figure show fear and horror, which find their explanation only in the appearance of that dangerous inhabitant of the swamps. This thought finds its confirmation in a small, inconspicuous attribute that the startled companion of Bacchus holds in his left hand. It is a plucked mushroom, represented with perfect distinctness. Could we not connect with this a story very similar to Lucian’s? As he gathers mushrooms the serpent appears; frightened, the satyr seeks to defend himself against it. With the staff he holds it down, with the right hand he wants to throw the stone at it. We recognize here the same fundamental idea as in the Syrtis stone. For comparison let there serve further the story in Plutarch de Is. et Os., according to which Dictys, the ward of Isis, reached for an onion and thereby lost his life in the river. The onion, which brings forth tears, is abhorred by the priests. As the image of every swift, unexpected death the serpent’s bite appears in Plin. 7, 7.

Shown in swift running, he carries the egg, which is held at half the height of the whole figure by both hands.3) In these representations the egg does not stand at the head of things. It is traced back rather to a paternal origin. The relation is thus the reverse. The dragon, which first came forth from the egg, now appears as the father of the egg. In this lies an advance from the materially maternal origin, the ἀρχή perceptible to the senses, to a higher, paternal-creative principle, to a first ἀρχή, in relation to which matter enters a subordinate position. Above matter appears the male force, no longer conceived merely as a tellurian potency of water, as in the swan of the swamps of Camarina, but raised to the highest stage, to the heavenly power of light. sun, surround the divine countenance of the light hero Heracles. Immortality is his attribute; the principle of transience and of death lies wholly on the side of the femininity assigned to him, Ananke-Adrasteia, who pervades all matter. As a power of the sun, Heracles bears the principle of time within himself. But in him it never ages; he is not Chronos, who always and necessarily belongs to the world of becoming as its temporal form; he is rather Χρόνος ἀγήρατος, the never-aging principle of time itself. From this solar nature is explained the connection of the egg-generating Heracles with Dionysus-Hebon, as it appears on the Camarinian coin. As the highest power of light, even if still conceived as material, Bacchus himself becomes Heracles-Chronos, the son of the maternal egg becomes its solar father. The same meaning belongs to the egg encircled three times by the dragon on a coin of Antoninus Heliogabalus, the representation of which Felix Lajard communicates in the recherches sur le culte de Vénus Pl. 14. H. no. 11. The original, of bronze, lies in the collection of the Bibliothèque nationale at Paris. Beside the egg stands a fruit-bearing palm. The inscription shows the Phoenician Tyre as the place of minting.1) The relation to the sun cult cannot be doubtful here. The egg is subordinated to the highest male force of light, and is itself represented as its creation. So there appeared to us above the Delphic omphalos-egg, so the myrrh egg of the Egyptian phoenix, itself represented as a generation of light, so the great egg that on a vase from Panticapaeum the Bacchante offers to the initiate riding on the sun-griffin.2) With this conception is connected the report of Porphyry in Eusebius Præp. Evang. 3, 11. According to Egyptian doctrine Kneph causes an egg to proceed from his mouth. It is the world egg; the father is the demiurge, who lets it go forth complete from his mouth, like the word, as the highest λόγος. The creative act is here conceived as νοητὴ ἀρχή, as that first unspeakable causality which the Orphic cosmogonies passed over as ἄρρητον. Passeri gives in his Atlas Farnesianus etc. p. 180 the representation of a bronze serpent which in his time was in the museo Gori. In the opened mouth rests an egg. Here the dragon appears, as Kneph does among the Egyptians, as demiurge. And that the Egyptians thought of and represented Kneph, the father of the egg, as a serpent god is definitely attested by Euseb. Pr. Ev. 1, 10. In this elevation the serpent appears at the highest stage of spiritualization. In its lowest materiality a representation of tellurian waters and of their generative force working in the dark

of motifs, all of which find their explanation and resolution in the idea of initiation. The story that Lucian has connected with it appears only as an attempt to lay a historical event at the foundation of the symbolic representation, and to transform the mystical content into the death story of the one buried. But even in this dress the religious idea is still clearly enough present. Egg and serpent lead through to life only by way of death. Only out of destruction does a higher existence bloom. Passing away as the precondition of new becoming, darkness as the passage to light, the terrors of the underworld as the ground of a more vigorous revival, through suffering and affliction to joy: this is the mystery idea that governs the fable of Psyche, which is also the innermost kernel of Lucian’s story and of the Vulcian candelabrum. The search for the egg, the plucking of the mushroom, becomes the occasion of death, the serpent brings destruction. But both prepare the fulfillment of the higher hopes of the mysteries. The harmful animal of the swamps is not only the destroyer but also the redeemer of the initiate, the egg not only the bearer of death but, through death, the giver of salvation, of the renatio ad nova salutis curricula.1) On the candelabrum this is indicated by the female figure issuing from the opened flower calyx at the upper end of the candelabrum’s shaft. A pair of serpents serves her instead of feet. Here the life-giving side of the Bacchic animal comes forth, as at the lower part of the candelabrum its life-destroying side.2) We see anew the union of the light side and the shadow side in the same force. What wounds heals at the same time; what brings death bears within itself also the force of life. From the serpent’s bite the serpent heals. So the Mosaic story represents it, of the serpent set up at Jehovah’s command.3) The dragon is to

assumption seems to me by no means certain. On these funerary implements everything down to the smallest detail has symbolic meaning and relation to the Bacchic mysteries. What meaning, then, can the stone contain? More fitting is the assumption of an egg, which Micali’s drawing brings out clearly enough. It appears here as a saving Bacchic attribute. Thereby everything gains a far more satisfying sense. Against the threatening serpent’s bite stands the saving symbol of the Bacchic mysteries. This rescues from the destruction that the plucking of the mushroom prepares. The assumption of the egg, moreover, does not exclude the idea of defense with it. So the wheel too appears on well-known funerary monuments of Etruria as a weapon of defense and at the same time in a symbolic-hieratic significance. Its consecrated force is joined with the use that the threatened man makes of it. Raoul-Rochette, mon. inéd. t. 39. The same representation is found also on a cinerary chest of the Leiden Museum.

heal the dragon’s bite. ὁ τρώσας καὶ ἰάσεται. Among the manifold applications that antiquity already made of this natural proposition, the healing lance of Achilles deserves special emphasis. It not only wounds, it also brings healing. The same force necessarily embraces both potencies. The serpent is at one and the same time ἀγαθοδαίμων and κακοδαίμων, as the water, to which it belongs in its lowest stage, is at one and the same time the origin of life and the seat of death. On a coin of the elder Faustina in Spanheim de usu et præstant. numism. 1, p. 415 it bears side by side an ear of grain and a poppy, the symbols of the life-bringing and of the death-bringing power, just as two dragons are assigned to Demeter, and the two serpents that hold the Hygieia egg are represented, by the stars set above their heads, in the nature of the Dioscuri, who bring up life and death, day and night.1) Egyptian mythology clothes not only the good but equally the evil principle in the form of a serpent. So appear Serapis, so Python, so the great serpent Ahriman, who girds and combats the realm of light. This identity of both forces, by virtue of which Marsyas first blows the double flute with a single breath, holds first of all for the domain of physical life; through the mysteries, however, it is transferred to a higher domain; here the serpent, like the egg, appears not only as the preserver of life in material creation, but as the image of the higher existence of the individual that issues from death. It is the idea of the palingenesis of the individual life that attaches itself equally to the egg and the serpent. It is this spiritualized meaning that we must recognize above all on so many funerary monuments: in the serpent of the sarcophagus of Bomarzo, now in the British Museum, in a gravestone of the Louvre that shows nothing but an upright dragon, in the bronze serpents, some of which are preserved in the museum of the Collegio romano at Rome, in the remarkable amber fragment from a tomb at Ruvo in the Pourtalès-Gorgier collection,2) in the serpent of the rock sarcophagus of Thera,3) and on many similar funerary monuments. Not the physical significance of material generation, but the mystical one resting upon it, that of the higher existence mediated through death, is what was to be expressed pictorially by the serpent symbol on the tombs of the initiates, and has also found its representation in Lucian’s account of the gravestone at the Syrtes.4)

To the egg monuments considered thus far is joined a group of three Pompeian wall paintings, all of which go back to the same type. We see the serpent once more in the closest connection with the egg. On the first of the monuments belonging here, the representation of which is also to be found in Gargiulo’s Raccolta, two mighty dragons approach an altar in powerful coils from the right and from the left, in opposite directions; on its top, surrounded by smaller fruits, lie two eggs. The head is adorned by the cock’s comb. From the opened jaws the tongue springs forth, formed as a fine line, its double curled tips touching the two eggs. The plants shooting high up indicate the luxuriantly fertile meadow ground which the serpents traverse before they halt their mighty movement all at once before the egg altar. This whole representation forms the lower part of a picture whose upper half, separated from it by a dark line, sets before the eyes the preparation for a sacrifice of a pig to be performed at a rustic altar. The same division appears on two other Pompeian wall paintings, of which one was found in the so-called casa di Castore e Poluce, the other in the casa del Labirinto. The former is reproduced in the Museo Borbonico vol. 8. t. 24, the second in the same work vol. 11. t. 38, both together in the monumenti dell’ Instituto. 1839. vol. 3, t. 6. On these two paintings a strip is set apart at the lowest place, on which the same altar with two eggs and the dragon is represented. The only difference of the last two pictures from the first consists in this, that here we find only one serpent in each, which on the one picture approaches the altar from the right, on the other from the left. I do not rate this deviation highly, and see in the singular number of the serpent not so much a conscious intention as rather merely one of those abbreviations which ancient art often permitted itself, especially in the execution of such accessories. The dual number of the eggs shows that we are to add in thought to the one dragon a second, approaching the altar from the opposite side: a supplement which presents itself to the eye of the modern, but especially of the ancient beholder, from the composition of the whole and from familiarity with other more fully executed recognized, since hardly any of the ancient animal symbols, from crude fetish worship to the highest spiritualization, has passed through so many stages of development, and appropriated so manifold interpretations, physical and mystical relations, as the serpent.

Schulz enriched the Annali of the year 1839 (vol. 11, pp. 101–127) under the title “rappresentazione della Fortuna sopra tre dipinti Pompeiani ed una carniola intagliata.” That an exact relation must obtain between the main picture and the representation of the serpents is clear enough already from the external union of the two scenes into one whole. The idea that the sight of the upper half calls forth finds necessarily its echo in the lower. This connection does in fact emerge clearly enough. We are now sufficiently familiar with the significance of the egg to recognize, in the representation of the female, veiled figure, distinguished by high majesty and the expression of commanding power, one of those great nature mothers whom the ancient religion places at the head of the material world, identifies with the fecundating moon, and sets in the closest union with a demon of male force, whom she has given birth to from herself into the light as Primigenia, as the night does the becoming day. On both scenes, however different they are in other respects, all the characteristic traits are repeated which lend such a mother goddess her unmistakable stamp. We see the goddess in connection with that paredros who is assigned, as Sosipolis, to the Tyche of Elis,2) as Jacchus to Demeter, as Cupid to the Erycinian Venus, as Plutus to Pallas Ergane and Eirene,3) as Telesphorus-Euamerion-Eros to Hygieia, as Jupiter Arcanus4) and Κτήσιος, or as Genius Jovialis to the Praenestine Fortuna, as δαίμων ἀγαθός to the Tyche of Lebadea,5) and who on works of art appears as a small, often winged figure, in the most various postures, now as an Eros flying toward her, now standing on the ground or on a column, now also sitting on the knees or on the shoulders of the primal mother.6) On

our paintings the goddess stands beside the little Eros, wrapped in a garment which on one of the pictures is covered with stars. On this one she carries in her raised right hand an olive branch,1) while the left rests on a rudder and holds a scepter staff. If on the second picture the starry garment and scepter are lacking, the Cerealian relation of the goddess is on the other hand put beyond doubt by the particulars with which the offering of the sacrifice is accompanied. It is more difficult to determine more closely her unmistakable maternal nature. For Aphrodite, Leda-Nemesis, Demeter, Hygieia, Fortuna would not only agree with both representations in respect of the general fundamental idea, but would also meet with no significant difficulties in the particulars. Most closely, perhaps, to the native Italic cult will correspond Fortuna Primigenia, who in a wholly Cerealian conception formed the center of religion at Praeneste, but was also venerated in all Latium, at Rome, at Antium, and under various names in Etruria, as a representation of the great female principle of nature, as giver of all blessing of the earth, of all wealth, as mistress over the light and shadow side of life,2) as bearer and announcer of all good and evil fortune. Like the Praenestine, so too the Pompeian Tyche appears as the material primal ground of all life, of all tellurian creation in general, at once as chthonian and heavenly earth, endowed through the olive and the nocturnal starry garment with the nature of Aphrodite-Astarte, or of the lunar woman Athena, related in the rudder to the Rhamnusian Leda-Nemesis, in the scepter as ruler over all material creation, uniting in her hand the physical ground of life and death, and so also of the Dresden Gallery, which shows us Aphrodite leaning on a small figure of Priapus. The idea of fecundation cannot be mistaken here. To a certain extent the counterpart to it is formed by the statue of the Louvre in Clarac musée de sculptures pl. 341, no. 1293. Aphrodite, leaning on a column on which Eros, robbed of his wings, sits, treads with her right foot on an embryo lying in its envelope: thus the idea of fecundation, combined with that of hostility to the begetting of offspring.

We found the egg earlier in connection with Leda-Nemesis, with Hygieia, with Demeter, with Isis, with Aphrodite-Syria. We see it here united in the same way with Fortuna-Tyche. In all these combinations it appears constantly in the same character: as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως τῶν πάντων, as the content of all material life, in general as a representation of the great female principle of nature, which has received its human form in all those primal mothers. But it is older than all anthropomorphization, and has no part in the individual developments which the common idea of material primal motherhood has taken among the single peoples of antiquity under the combined influences of national disposition, occupation, political fortunes, and the character of the land, and the result of which appears deposited in the differing individual coloring of those mother goddesses. Whether Demeter, whether Aphrodite, whether Leda-Nemesis, and Hygieia with all those lunar women to whom egg-birth is ascribed, each have developed in a different direction, and so the common fundamental idea finally appears in a plurality of different local nuances: the physical foundation on which they rest is the same in all, and only this foundation comes to representation in the mother egg.1) For this reason the egg can also appear by itself alone, and without the accompaniment of a personally formed mother goddess. So we find it in the Orphic-Bacchic doctrine. So it is represented on the Pamphili tomb painting, so on the Fabretti stone. If, then, for the Pompeian wall paintings the connection of the upper and lower halves is established in relation
