From the same idea that makes the circus a place of freedom there has proceeded the prohibition which closes many sanctuaries to slaves and takes them under protection, even by force, against their entering. “With us at Chaeronea it is the custom,” writes Plutarch, Quæst. rom. 13, “that the ædituus of the temple of Leucothea comes to the door with a whip and proclaims that no male slave and no female slave, no Aetolian man and no Aetolian woman, shall enter it.” At Rome, too, the temple of Matuta is closed to female slaves. Only a single one do the Roman women take in with them, and they give her blows on the cheek, evidently in order to indicate thereby, as Plutarch adds in explanation, that entrance is denied her. Matuta- Leucothea shares with the deities named earlier the same material maternal nature. In her honor the Matralia are celebrated. Melicertes Palaemon stands at her side, in the nature of a fecundating Eros-Plutus, as a phallic daimon. What is born from Matuta’s womb partakes of the freedom of material life. By entering her sanctuary the slave, too, would become free. To keep him from doing so is the purpose of the violence that is exercised at Chaeronea as at Rome. To the Megalensia magnæ matris slaves have no access, as appears from Cicero, de haruspic. responsis 11. 12. The material-female foundation of the religion of Dionysus develops in the same way into the significance of freedom and equality on earth. Indeed, here the concepts of material life and of freedom coincide so exactly that one word designates both. The different meanings of liber are in fact only a single one. Belonging to a root that in a great number of formations always retains the basic meaning of water, and specifically of the moving, flowing stream that resounds clearly in its course, Liber designates the content of the materially generative force of water, hence the bast of trees, which owes its origin to that force, likewise the children who, sprung from natural force, also continue it,5) and finally the condition of freedom, as it necessarily belongs to material force and to all its births. Of the many relations that offer themselves here in abundance, I wish to point only to the name of the country Libya, which stands in connection with the Ammonian spring god, to λίβερνα, εἶδος πλοίου, to Λίβερνος, the name of the chasm of the earth into which Curtius plunged, to λείβηθρον ὀχετὸς ὑδραγωγικός, to the expression λείβεται and καταλείβεται τοῖς δακρύοις, to the Thracian Λείβηθρα of Orpheus and the Λειβηθρίδες, as nymphs and Muses are called,3) and finally to lichor, and to recall Plato’s connection of the Μοῦσαι λίγειαι with the γένος μουσικὸν τὸ Λιγύων.4) I am convinced that lignum, λίμνη, limus go back to the same stem. This is especially the case with Λικνίτης, a designation of Dionysus himself. The ancients explain the name from the fact that the god at his birth is said to have been laid in the λίκνον, a basket plaited of willows, which served the child as a cradle. Servius, in his scholion on Georg. 1, 166: Arbuteæ crates, et mystica vannus Jacchi, calls the basket a cribrum, and traces that tradition back to the cribrum of the mother Isis, in which she laid down the torn limbs of her consort. From this the original cultic significance of the λίκνον results with certainty. It is, like Vesta’s sieve, like the cask of the Danaids, the earth itself, which takes into itself the generating moisture, and precisely for that reason is conceived as a perforated vessel, now as dolium, now as cribrum, now as vannus. Thus from the perforated willow basket there comes to be the cradle of the god, then the mystic receptacle that holds the mystery of natural generation, on monuments mostly in the form of a serpent, and finally the fruit receptacle, or the winnowing shovel of the farmer that separates grain and chaff.5) In all these turns the λίκνον has an unmistakable relation to the phallic, fruit-generating nature of Dionysus. In its original significance, however, it shows us the god as the fecundating force of water, which

In the designation of Bacchus as Liber pater his generative force resting in the water is thus first of all expressed. Masculinity, however, enters into the relation of son to femininity, as the male Eros, as Enorches comes forth from the egg, as Dionysus himself is conceived as the son of Beroë or of Ino, and as διμήτωρ.1) That is why he is now also called simply the son. This is the meaning of Liber formed in the singular. In Hyginus f. 9 we read: Niobe procreavit liberos septem, totidemque filias. According to the original meaning only the sons, not also the daughters, are liberi, because only they bear the generative force of water within them. Hence Liber the son, as in Quintilian Declam. 11: Liberi ac parentis non alius mihi videtur affectus. If to Liber the designation pater is added, as to Adonis the equivalent Papas, the reason for this lies in the fact that in the son male generation as such is represented, so that the son in fact stands there as the father of all visible creation. As the preeminently material god he now becomes also the bearer of that freedom which distinguishes the life of purely material creation, and yields only to positive human legislation, to the institutions of the life of the state. Hence the word Liber receives the meaning free. Hence Marsyas’s image appears as the sign of the liberæ civitates.2) Hence he is worshiped in Boeotia under the name Eleutherios.3) That is why the cult of Dionysus has also exercised so unmistakable an influence on the democratic development of the ancient world, which raised the lower and neglected

classes so greatly, gave to women in particular a significance that stood in such contradiction to the civil institutions, and allied itself so closely with the tyranny of a Pisistratus1) and a Caesar,2) grounded on the freedom and equality of the whole mass of the people. The life of the state and of politics brings distinctions of station, restriction, and complete abolition of freedom. Over against this the Dionysian religion contains a reduction of existence to the domain of pure materiality and of merely bodily existence, which is the same for all members of the great human society, free and equal by its nature. When the civil standpoint of the state everywhere erects barriers, separates peoples and individuals, and develops the principle of individuality to the most consummate egoism, Dionysus on the contrary leads everything back to union, everything to peace and to the φιλία of primordial life. In his mysteries slaves and free persons have an equal share, and before the god of material pleasure all those barriers fall which the life of the state with time raises to ever greater height. The consciousness of unitary descent from one matter wins the victory over positive differences, and at the same time the material development, and the love of enjoyment and splendor that rests on it, which the Dionysian religion favored so especially, prospers to the highest cultivation. In all these tendencies Dionysus confirms his significance as Lyæus. As, in the role of generative Liber, he awakens the life sleeping in matter and frees it from the bonds that hold it captive, like the chick from the egg, so he also abolishes all differences, puts an end to enmity even among the animals, and leads back into creation that peace, that joy, that universal equality which appeared to the ancients as the original golden age, and which found its expression, its temporary return, in the festal practices of the Saturnalia, of the Dionysian Χόες, and of so many Sacaean festivals, as a recollection of prepolitical, purely material existence. In wine and its influence on man this very side of the Dionysian nature seemed to reveal itself most clearly. When it promotes friendly union, awakens sexual life, puts an end to enmities, abolishes distinctions, and breaks cares, one might recognize in all this the expression of the force of Dionysus, refer the names Liber and Lyæus to this as well, and explain them from the effects of wine.

But if one went further, left the domain of material life in order to celebrate the god who brings freedom as a redeemer from the bondage of passion and of the flesh, one climbed to a height of spiritualization and idealization similar to that on which the mystica vannus Jacchi was conceived as the image of the purgatio animæ through the mysteries, the egg as an assurance of a higher spiritual rebirth, and the Bacchic-Orphic doctrine in general as a melioris spei initium. With that, however, one had overstepped the outermost limits of the religion of Dionysus, and in the midst of the moral decay to which that religion necessarily had to lead, had pointed to Him who was called, by the word of the spirit, to break the dominion of matter and to transfigure the freedom of material life into a higher, divine one.

16.

We have shown so far in what manner law attaches itself to the female-material principle of nature, and have demonstrated this connection first of all for the lowest stage of tellurian life, the purely Aphroditean. The same is confirmed, however, for the higher Cerealian-Demetrian stage as well. Indeed, on this stage it acquires an incomparably higher significance. For that jus naturale which connects men with the animal world is destined to be overcome and to yield to a higher law. The material-Aphroditean standpoint forms the point of departure of a development that is to lead ever farther away from it, to advance toward an ever higher spirituality, and to raise man ever more above that material community with the animal world. That is the law of all human development. It underlies also the development of religion, and gives it a progress that unfolds from below upward, from tellurism to the solar world of light of being, from the formless to form. Indeed, it is clear that this very development of religion also conditions and bears that of law. For religious thought necessarily governs all sides of human life, shapes everything according to its content, and can be designated not only as the most powerful but outright as the sole factor of civilization. What the end of this development will be, no one can determine. But of what kind its beginning and point of departure were is beyond doubt. Men have, to be sure, and quite recently again, treated that jus naturale, into whose nature we opened an insight above, as a mere abstraction and philosophical theory, denied it all historical truth, and so sought to come to the aid of the honor of humanity. But that the things which are treated as a mere abstraction

[PDF 215]

— 201 —

were real conditions and experiences of the human race, the definite and constantly wholly concordant tradition of the peoples leaves not the slightest doubt. Unregulated sexual union, absence of all property, of every special right of any kind whatever, community of women, of children, and as a necessary consequence of this also of all goods, together with this a perfect freedom of all creatures without form or articulation, and as the sole bond among them Aphroditean pleasure, all this is as certain1) as the prepolitical condition, and that wandering life which ends only with death, and apart from the grave knows no fixed point, no native place.2) Indeed, for the first spread and the rapid growth of our race, conditions of this kind, however deep and however degrading they may now appear, were without doubt indispensable. Religion and law received a higher form through the transition to agriculture. The purely Aphroditean principle yields to the Cerealian. With this there enters, in place of community, the exclusive right of an individual, in place of hetaerism marriage, in place of swamp generation and Aphroditean self-sufficient vegetation the laborata Ceres. Carpus and Calamus enter into combat with each other. Nonnus gives the myth surely in the form in which ancient tradition handed it down.3) Drawn by the magic of the golden fruits, Atalanta turns aside from her course, and sacrifices victory and freedom to the enticing possession. The Schœneia virgo, daughter of the rush man, renounces her proud unboundedness and yields to her new lot.4) Among men a culture develops toward which the gods of the pure life of nature behave in a hostile manner. Silvanus threatens destruction to the woman in childbed. Broom, pestle, and ax, tria signa culturæ, protect her against the adversary of all higher human existence.5) The daughters of Pandareus are snatched away by the Harpies

would they stand to battle; cities and fixed dwellings they otherwise had none. The tombs are in this nomadic life the only fixed thing. Before death, eternal wandering. So it was written on Trivulzio’s tomb: qui numquam quievit quiescit. Of the Memphites Diodor 1, 51 says that they bestowed little care on their houses, very great on the tombs. at the moment when Aphrodite ascends to heaven to beg of Zeus for them the τέλος θαλεροῖο γάμοιο, the crown of female upbringing.1) For marriage, and the Cerealian mystery into which it introduces, is hateful to the primal powers of matter. These, although egg-mothers like Demeter, and like the Cerealian powers containing the life-giving force no less than the annihilating one, fall back, over against the new life, into the position of sinister powers hostile to conjugal consecration. Thus the human race steps out of the community of the rest of material creation. A mighty elevation takes place, which at first disturbs the harmony of earthly life. The jus naturale is abandoned in order to come to validity again in ennobled form. In agriculture maternity receives a new significance, a higher development. In place of wild swamp generation, which in eternal self-embrace eternally rejuvenates matter, which brings forth only reeds and rushes or the λιμναῖα κρηνῶν τέκνα, and shoots up uselessly without the contrivance of man, there now steps the deed of the plowman, who opens the maternal womb of the earth with the plow, entrusts the seed to the furrow, and reaps nourishing fruit, the food of Demeter,

“When the merry reapers cut asunder the limbs of Ceres.” The earth has now become wife and mother, and man, who guides the plow and strews the seed, husband and father. The relation of marriage binds the man with female matter, and there is given also for the pairing of the sexes with one another the model of an intimate, lasting, and exclusive community. The earth and mortal woman stand on one line, and γάμος is derived from γᾶ just as γύια, the plowshare, and γυνή, Gaia herself. The male plowshare opens the womb of the earth as of woman; this double deed is at bottom only one, and, toward the earth as toward woman, no longer a passing hetaeric sexual mingling but conjugal union. Not on the satisfaction of sensual pleasure, but on the production of golden fruits is the man’s deed directed. Liberorum quærendorum causa, not ἡδονῆς ἕνεκα, do the sexes unite. Only in this elevation does woman find her repose. In lasting union with Eros, Psyche attains that happiness which she sought in vain to hold fast in unregulated hetaeric mating and in low swamp coupling. We see femininity raised from pure tellurism to the lunar stage of existence, and given over to the man for

lasting exclusive possession, like Luna to Sol-Lunus. The children now have, besides the mother, also a father; they are genuine children, like the descendants of the Idaean Dactyls, the Eteo-Cretans. They are διφυεῖς, as the Athenians have been since Cecrops. To this stage of life a new law corresponds. The Aphroditean jus naturale yields to the Cerealian. But the new legal condition, too, attaches itself wholly to the female principle of nature. It retains, even on the new stage, the materially maternal character. Demeter becomes θεσμοφόρος, Ceres legifera, as the pure jus naturale attaches itself to Aphrodite. Indeed, Demetrian law, too, is a true jus naturale, but one that rests on earth-generation regulated by agriculture and not left to itself, on the laborata Ceres, not on the creatio ultronea of Aphrodite. On this stage the conjugal principle of exclusiveness prevails over hetaeric universality. The earth, and after its image mortal woman, gives herself to the man as exclusive property. She is no longer mother in unrestricted universality; she now has this quality in relation to a determinate man, whose seed she receives, for whom she develops the birth, to whom at last she presents the fruits. She is no longer Penia, who goes after ever new men, delights in every fecundation and without cease partakes of it, no longer that daughter who bends without will before the male scepter. She shuns, rather, everything male, succumbs to violence and to rape, and preserves the mystery character of unprofaned matronhood.1) Precisely thereby she becomes the bearer of a higher law, which extends to all relations of life, and may be designated as conjugal mother right. It has been asserted that the θεσμοί of Demeter refer exclusively to the conjugal union of human beings. There is this much truth in it, that marriage in fact forms the center of all Demetrian law. But marriage itself must not be restricted to human beings. It embraces also the man’s relation to the tellurian sown field. It has the double direction toward agriculture and toward sexual union, comprising in one concept, in one mystery, in one law, property and family. Indeed, the relation to woman is subordinated to that to the field, family law to that of agriculture. In the Menexenus, p. 298, is set forth

Verrium Flaccum juris pontificii peritissimum dicere solitum refert Varro, quia feriis tergere veteres fossas liceret, novas facere jus non esset, ideo magis viduis quam virginibus idoneas esse ferias ad nubendum. Here again nature has taken law into her lap. The comparison of the female sporium with a fossa serving the purposes of agriculture here too has more than the significance of a mere image. Both are rather regarded as inwardly of the same meaning. The cultic significance of the fossa emerges from the deed of the Cumaean Malakos,3) and likewise from the tale of the charlatan Alexander’s Asclepius egg. rests the pontifical decision of Verrius Flaccus, in which the law of agriculture decides questions of marriage. In the mysteries, moreover, both relations of Cerealian law were conceived wholly as a unity, marriage itself represented as an agrarian relation. The two Eleusinian deities are at once and without distinction a representation of tellurian and of human marriage. The priestess of Demeter shuts herself up with the newly married in the bridal chamber, and impresses on them the θεσμός of the earth mother as the highest law of marriage.1) Thereby every γάμος itself becomes a Cerealian mystery, each one a τέλος θαλεροῖο γάμοιο. Conjugal fidelity is sworn by the Eleusinian goddesses.2) To Ceres legifera Dido sacrifices at her wedding,3) as girls also implore Demeter for a husband.4) All these phenomena are emanations of the same fundamental idea: woman imitates the earth, the γάμος agriculture. In both lies the same mystery. The Demetrian θεσμοί embrace agrarian law as well as conjugal law, indeed they subordinate the latter to the former. If one wishes to designate them as conjugal ordinances, one must give this expression the widest scope, enclosing the whole of agricultural life.

Demeter Θεσμοφόρος shows us, then, law again as an emanation of the female principle of nature. If we saw it above linked with Aphroditean nature mothers, it here confronts us as an attribute and emanation of Cerealian maternity. The fundamental idea remains the same; only the stage of culture is different, there the lower, hetaerically conceived, here the higher, conjugal maternity. The female matter that harbors, tends, and develops the seed, and sends the fruit upward, is also the source of the law that regulates the relations of economic life. Therefore Ceres is called legifera in a quite general sense. All law that the cultural stage of agriculture brings with it proceeds from the Cerealian mother. How deeply rooted this conception was is shown by the fact that the temple of Ceres served as an archive of laws.5) It can therefore by no means Augustine, C. be treated as a philosophical abstraction, if the ancients not only make manifold use of the designation legifera, but also emphasize ownership of land quite especially as a component of Cerealian law.1) For the same connection recurs in many features, now more openly present, now more hidden. In Servius, Aen. 4, 58, Calvus writes: leges sanctas invenit, et cara jugavit corpora connubiis et magnas condidit urbes. I lay particular weight on the expression sanctæ leges. The connection of the sanctum with tellurism, and the idea of the ἀκίνητον lying in it, have already been set forth above. Through both relations sanctitas enters into a more intimate union with the nature of Demeter and her legislation. The laws themselves partake of the goddess’s inviolable being. They are sanctæ like her. The whole of Cerealian law bears the character of religious ordinances, over whose observance the great primal mother herself keeps watch.2) It is therefore in the proper sense θεσμός, an ordinance of divine law, ἐκ θεῶν δοθείς, as Aeschylus, Eumen. 392, adds in explanation. It is not only jus but fas, a pronouncement (from fari) of the primal mother herself, and hence, like the fatum, like the λόγος—for so Lactantius and Tertullian explain the λόγος at the opening of the Gospel of John—eternally unalterable. This character is borne by all those laws kept in the sanctuary of Ceres. They are held to be unalterable and not to be annulled. From the religious protection follows the inviolability of civil institutions. If for the patrician commonwealth that protection lies in obtaining the divine approval through the auguries, as I have shown in my work on the foundations of Roman constitutional law, then for the plebeian community it rests in its relation to the material primal mother Ceres, who at Athens stands in the closest connection with the popular assemblies, to whom at Rome the plebs preeminently belongs, and whose nature has found its expression both in the principle of the old constitutional law: ut quod primum populus jusserit, id ratum esset, and in the provision: actus legitimi nec diem nec conditionem recipiunt. Under the protection of Ceres the community sits in assembly. To the higher consecration that the patriciate possesses, it opposes the inviolability of the material nourishing mother, to the male principle of the former the female principle of the latter. To her temple it entrusts the community treasury, the laws, and the senatus consulta, which are here safe against falsification.3) With

custom and ordinance there is joined the founding of fixed dwelling places. Ceres is the founder of cities. So Calvus calls her. As she is the mother of customs and laws, so she is also the mother of fixed seats, and through the union of all these qualities a true Ἀστυνόμη. In her relation to the founding of cities, too, she shows herself true to that character of the sanctum and ἀκίνητον which forms her innermost nature. The walls founded with the use of Cerealian rites stand under the protection of the goddess, from whose womb they ascend into the light like the plants. On account of this relation the walls in Nonnus 41, 360. 370 become the bearers of the great law of fate that Aphrodite learns from Harmonia. She shows her the ἀγλαὰ θέσφατα τοίχου. On the walls the great fatum of the world is written down. They proclaim the law of matter in which they themselves are grounded. Here the same connection of fixed buildings with law is present which is also found again in Ceres. The custom of writing laws down on walls, which African discoveries confirm to us, has thus its deeper ground in ancient religious ideas. On the temple wall of Apollo Ptous at Lake Copais stood, according to Plutarch in the Gryllus, the words “the beautiful Achilles,” and in Lucian, in the Dialogues of the Courtesans, the shipowner Hermotimus writes his declaration of love to a beautiful courtesan on the wall by the city gate. Here, too, Cerealian ideas come to light. To what protection could such expressions of affection be better entrusted than to that of the goddess quæ cara corpora connubiis jungit, and whose being is formed by immovable firmness and unalterable fidelity? In Apuleius we find the speaking tower, which knows all the secrets of the underworld and betrays them to Psyche. It is the announcer of the great Cerealian secrets, like Harmonia’s wall. In a similar relation to Ceres stands Terminus. Issuing from the earth, as the son from the maternal womb, he reveals the male force, is therefore called male, and on the well-known Etruscan mirror is represented with Juventas in phallic form. But, resting in the mother’s womb, he partakes of her sanctitas, and is therefore called preeminently sanctus.1) The ἀκίνητον is what distinguishes him. Thereby he becomes the guardian of the Cerealian laws and is propitiated with the porca lactens. In him all parts of the Cerealian nature come to representation. He is the revelation of the mystery that the mother bears locked within her. He fecundates the field, separates and protects landed property, and defends the immovability that forms the foundation of Cerealian life even against the gods of a newer, more political order

of things. With the funerary stelae he shares the same nature. Immovable like the terminus, the funerary pillar proclaims Demeter’s mystery. It is at the same time a representation of the male force pervading it, a λίθος ἔμψυχος, a guardian of her Cerealian law, often also at the same time the terminus that divides lands, and as πυραμίς is itself called by a Cerealian name.1) — The aediles stand forth as priests of Ceres. Their very diverse attributa can all be explained from this character. They stand to the yield of the earth, to the community of the people, to the market, to the buildings, to the administration of justice, in the same relation as the goddess to whom they belong. Their whole sphere of business is of Cerealian nature. But they have their name from the buildings, which here, as in the mural crown, appear in their whole importance for the agricultural life that leads to fixed settlement.2)

Having found, then, in Ceres and Demeter, as in Aphrodite, law as an emanation and attribute of the material maternal principle, and having thus demonstrated, for two different stages of life and of culture, that intimate connection of the materiality that bestows wealth and distributes wealth in the concept of one and the same maternity, it now still deserves emphasis that also in the expression jus Quiritium law again enters preeminently into relation with the materially female side of life. From their maternal Sabine descent the Romans are called Quirites, and all private law is treated as Quiritary law. Ex jure Quiritium hunc agrum meum esse aio, says the claimant; ex jure Romanorum would emphasize the paternal side. Roman is the name of the gens Romulea in its political significance, as a political whole, and therefore in its direction outward. Quirites they are according to their material nature. In the expression Populus Romanus Quirites or Quiritium both sides of life enter into connection.

The same Romans are, in their whole extent, Populus Romanus, and in their whole extent Quirites: the former as state, the latter as people; the former according to the male-political, the latter according to the maternal-material side; the former as bearer of the state’s imperium, the latter in their bodily existence. Law belongs to this latter side of existence; it is the emanation of the female natural principle, and therefore, from Juno Quiris, Quiritary. For this very reason it extends also to the plebeians, the πλῆθος, to whom the formula ex jure Quiritium belongs just as fully as to the patrician; for on the materially female side the plebeians are in no way distinguished from the Quirites; they share with them the maternal origin, which stands out predominantly in the relation to Ceres, to Anna Perenna, to the Veientine Juno; whereas the patricians raise the male-solar paternal principle above it, set themselves up alone as those qui patrem ciere possunt, and relegate the lunar sign of material, bodily birth, the symbol of natural generation, to their shoes, as it reveals itself in the shoe of Rhodopis-Nitocris, in that of the Delphic Charila, in that of Tanaquil-Fortuna, in the crepida of Perseus and of Jason. The whole stock of the Opicans, to which the plebeians preeminently belonged, bears, like the Quirites, a name that has maternal descent for its foundation. They are named after the great mother Ops-Tellus, who is placed alongside Bona Dea. The temple of Ops- Diana is raised by Servius Tullius to be the central point of the Latin confederation.1) For all these peoples have in common the maternal-material origin. From this side they enter into community with Rome, while the political side of the imperium remains closed to them. — A further relation of law to the materially female natural principle emerges in the connection of the praetor with Bona Dea. In this a particular relation of that goddess, whom the Greeks simply designate as γυναικεία θεός, to the welfare of the state is revealed. But this is conceived here not according to its political-male side, but according to the materially female. Bona Dea is the maternal natural principle that gives to all material life its origination and its nourishment, that bestows all prosperity and all wealth, and promotes every bodily well-being. She belongs, then, to the Quiritary or Cerealian side of life; she is herself conceived as the Junonis potentia, identified with Ops and Ceres, worshiped as Murcia, equipped as Salus-Medea with the nature of Hygieia, and represented under the name of Maia as magna mater. She appears, then, as the materially maternal foundation of the welfare of the state, the praetor and consul in connection with her as the representatives of this material side of the existence of the people. To this relation to Bona Dea their administration of justice is tied. The ordering of the life of property, which constitutes the content of law, rests as natural law in the same goddess who forms the ultimate material foundation of all those goods. To recognize this law, to pronounce it, is the praetor’s calling. Bona Dea as Fauna-Fatua proclaims it to him; he himself is her organ, her viva vox, the enactment itself an Edictum. This female-tellurian origin of law makes it possible for the praetor to turn his attention more to the substantive æquum than to the formal strictum jus, and to lead the civil law of the patrician state back to the jus naturale of the æquum et bonum, and to that Justitia, identified with the left hand, which excludes all dolus, all calliditas and astutia, and sees the highest Elegantia juris in the highest maternal æquitas. Law itself is a material law; it inheres, therefore, in woman. Bona Dea is θεσμοφόρος like the Eleusinian Demeter; law itself is always a female mystery, like the origination of all material life. The secret service of Orphic nature that the women alone celebrate in the praetor’s house for the good mother embraces law also. According to the scholion on Theocritus 4, 25, the women and maidens on the Eleusinian ἡμέρᾳ τῆς τελετῆς carry the holy books of laws in procession to Eleusis. All law is the enactment of Demeter or of Bona Dea, whose material law is laid down in it. For this reason both deities bear the scepter, and indeed in the left, preserving female hand, both also the scroll, which in its enclosure conceals the highest law of matter, fate in its widest extent. Thus appears

1) Macrob. Sat. 1, 12. p. 269. Plutarch, Cæsar 9.

[PDF 225]

— 211 —

the law of Bona Dea as a mysterious law resting in matter itself, given with matter and as old as it. It is for the praetor, as for the aedile, only to investigate this substantive law, to listen to its revelations, to pronounce them, to choose them as the standard of his own decisions, and to subordinate the political viewpoint as well as that of purely individual conception to the one given in the matter itself. His law becomes a scripta ratio; it contains the revelation of the ratio naturalis lying in the natura rerum. Of the initiates of the mysteries it is not so much spiritual self-activity as rather passive receptivity that is demanded. They have only to receive, and stand before the mystery as listeners. Τοὺς τετελεσμένους οὐ μαθεῖν τι δεῖ ἀλλὰ παθεῖν.1) The praetor takes up a like position toward the material primal mother. He is not the source of law, but only the proclaimer of a natural law that the female natural principle bears within itself. His house is the temple of Bona Dea, as Cadmus on the citadel at Thebes dwells in the house of Harmonia. But on the day of the May festival everything male must avoid the presence of the goddess. Only the women celebrate the nocturnal orgies, which, to use Nonnus’s expression, may be designated as ὄργια θεσμῶν. Woman, like Bona Dea, is the bearer of the material mystery, the content of the Cerealian natural law, man its revelation and proclaimer. He is the secret that has stepped into the light, who learns the primal fate from the mother, as Prometheus learns it from Themis, not from Zeus, from whom it remains hidden. The same views recur in the ideas of the ancients on the origination of speech. It is a law inborn in the maternal matter of the earth. Bona Dea is also Fatua, every Lara a Lala, who bears within herself the power of speech. Only through contact with the earth does the child receive its speech.2) But it attains to revelation among men only through the force that steps into the light, unveiled, in man. The phallic Hermes is the creator and shaper of speech, who as Thoth also records the laws hitherto hidden, and so communicates them to the human race. The names of things themselves are no arbitrary invention, any more than law. They lie mute, as mystery, in the things themselves, are inborn in matter, and as old as matter. It is man’s task to recognize them and to read them out of the thing itself. Moses calls him the greatest who created things, and after

sacris adjungi dicunt, quia vox nascenti homini terræ contactu datur. Scimus autem Mercurium vocis et sermonis potentem.

2) Macrob. Sat. 1, 12. Mercurium ideo illi (Maiæ, sicut et Magna mater in sacris vocatur) in

him the one who recognized and shaped their names, and Eusebius, in the Præparatio Evangelica 11, 6, has developed this primal idea of mankind further, and has shown it also to be a Platonic doctrine. The same idea is taken into account by Lucretius, de nat. rer. 5, 1040, when, in a highly noteworthy discussion of the origin of speech, not brought out by Grimm in his Geschichte der Sprache, he sets up the proposition: aliquem tum nomina distribuisse rebus, et inde homines didicisse vocabula prima, Desipere est, and, instead of a single individual, assigns to the whole race the task, Pro vario sensu varias res voce notare. This self-speaking of things has a last echo in the custom of letting the funerary monuments, like the column of Isis, speak in the first person like living beings. From Plato’s Phaedrus p. 264 the inscription is known that is said to have been made for Midas the Phrygian. It has all the higher significance here because, according to Macrob. Sat. 1, 12, Bona Dea herself was identified with the mother of Midas.

“Maiden of bronze am I, and I lie on the tomb of Midas.

As long as water still flows and tall-stemmed trees still bloom,

Ever abiding here at the much-bewept monument,

That the traveler too may know where Midas lies buried.” “Of bronze” the maiden here calls herself, she who preserves the memory of Midas. The significance of bronze in the ancient nature religion and its relation to maternal tellurism thereby receive a new confirmation. It stands in a special connection with the Cerealian cult. The æneæ falces are mentioned by Virgil, Aen. 4, 513. From a bronze sickle Drepanum has its name. In the founding of cities the Etruscans made use of a bronze plow, as Carminius reports from the Tagetica sacra.1) Hence the Cerealian enactments were engraved on bronze tablets, and a wholly Cerealian nature mother was called Cupra, Aphrodite Cypria, two designations that are without doubt connected with the German Kupfer. Hence bronze also acquires a special relation to death. According to the ancient view of religion, the hypogea are lined with bronze, like Danaë’s subterranean bridal chamber and the temple of Athena Chalcioecus. Pieces of æs rude are found in great number in the tombs, most recently again in the often-mentioned Praenestine ones of the casa Barberini. Omnino autem ad rem divinam pleraque ænea adhiberi solita, multa indicio sunt; et in his maxime sacris, quibus delinire aliquos, aut devovere, aut denique exigere morbos volebant. To this attaches the bronze maiden of Midas.

If here the bronze is introduced as speaking, this connects with the sanctity of the bronze tone, which for the ancients counts as a revelation of the natural law sleeping in matter. The χαλκὸς ἠχοῦν of the Corcyraean votive figure at Dodona, the æra crepitantia of the Curetes, to whose clangor the child Zeus steps into the light, the sound of the Tyrrhenian tuba, of the Isiac sistrum, of the Salian shields, every tone that a vessel of bronze gives forth, proclaims as mute speech the latent mystery of matter, as the bronze maiden at Midas’s tomb pronounces it in words, as the bronze tablets of law also set it forth. In bronze, then, all sides of the maternal natural principle, conceived above all as Cerealian, come to representation: we see in it matter in its life-giving and equally in its life-reclaiming potency; we see it, moreover, proclaiming the law that pervades it. Bronze is what Ceres herself is, at once wealth and the law that orders and guards its distribution on earth. For this reason æs et libra have acquired so high a significance in commercial life that all nexum rests on it, and all legal force depends on it. The scale, too, must be of bronze, and be touched with the piece of bronze. When it rings under the blow, everything that the parties say to it acquires the significance of a Cerealian enactment, of a lex, the violation of which would amount to a violation of the material nature mother herself and of her will, made known in the sound of bronze. The ænea libra shows us the nature mother as giver, as just distributor, and thereby also as director and mediator of all traffic in goods. Upon this, if I may say so, material significance of the scale is built the higher one, in which it designates abstract justice and becomes the attribute of justitia. In the scale, then, we see the same connection of the concepts of law and justice with the material natural principle that confronted us in the primal mothers, in Ceres, Syria, and Aphrodite herself.

Bona Dea, whose connection with law we have so far elucidated, gives me occasion for two further remarks. Following the lead of Macrobius 1, 12, we have placed her together with Juno. Now Juno appears under an epithet that especially stresses that nature of female matter which proclaims its own law. In all the reports we possess about Juno Moneta, this goddess confronts us always in the same nature, as a power that admonishes, that proclaims to men the law of matter. But this quality must not be conceived in abstract incorporeality. Moneta bears within herself, like Fatua, the whole materiality of motherhood, which makes itself known not only in admonitions and revelations but generally in the bestowal of every material well-being. She therefore stands to the welfare of the state in a

[PDF 228]

— 214 —

relation similar to that of Bona Dea. The concept of law and of its administration connects with Moneta as well. For the building of her temple the Senate assigns the area where the house of M. Manlius Capitolinus had stood. If he had aspired to the overthrow of freedom, and thereby violated the materially female principle of law, then the deity who counts as the content of this very law is to receive her dwelling on the same site. The temple itself had been vowed by F. Camillus in the Aurunican war.1) Why precisely to Moneta? I think, because she was to grant victory to the just war. Thus she appears altogether in the nature of a Victoria, who stands by the wronged and favors his undertaking.2) By Suidas Moneta is straightaway identified with the justitia in bellis. She punishes injuria, harms him who curtails others, and by the imposition of punishment gives her displeasure to be known. Thereby she admonishes continually to justice, to the observance of her maternal law. The name Moneta, then, proceeds itself from her quality as bearer of the highest maternal justice. For this reason Apollo too is called Moneta, because by pestilence he avenges injustice and summons to atonement. Now the relation of Moneta to the minting of coins receives its true explanation and deeper significance. Not because the coin recalls some event — for this significance of the stamp is not an original one — nor because the stamp contains a guarantee of the entirely correct value — for this could be achieved just as perfectly by weighing —, but because minted money was introduced at first as the equivalent of the fines to be paid from of old in cattle and sheep, and consequently the atonement for a wrong committed, the compensation for harm inflicted, the restitution of a loss, was its nearest purpose, therefore the mint was placed in the sanctuary of Juno Moneta, and the minted money, as well as the die and the mint, were lent the name of the goddess. In all these manifestations, then, Juno Moneta preserves her character as the highest justitia, in which she receives her seat on the citadel itself, in a sense as guardian of the state. We have again the same connection of the female-material natural principle with justice that we have by now found so often. Only here maternity is conceived not so much as mere bearer of the highest law as rather as a power that pursues, and rises up itself for the atonement of wrong, in the nature of a Nemesis-Erinys restoring the disturbed order of nature.

2) Lucan. 1, 380.

A second remark is furnished me by the conception of Bona Dea as Murtia. Gellius N. A. 5, 6 reports that the lesser triumph, the so-called ovatio, was dedicated to Murtia, and that the corona ovalis worn by the victor consisted of myrtle foliage.1) Here we see the celebration of victory, and hence victory itself, brought into connection with the female natural principle and the material side of the state. This finds its confirmation in the sacrifice of a sheep that gave the ovatio its name.2) Precisely on account of its religious linkage with Murtia we may call this lesser triumph the plebeian one, and thereby distinguish it from the great or patrician one, in which the victor, as sun god and equipped with all the attributes of this highest paternal power of light, drives up to the Capitoline temple. Murtia preserves here too her character, so intimately akin to the jus naturale. This is shown by the individual cases in which the ovatio is to be applied. Ovandi autem, writes Gellius 5, 6, ac non triumphandi causa est, quum aut bella non rite indicta, neque cum justo hoste gesta sunt; aut hostium nomen humile et non idoneum est, ut servorum piratarumque3) aut, deditione repente facta, impulverea, ut dici solet, incruentaque victoria obvenit. cui facilitati aptam esse Veneris frondem crediderunt, quod non Martius, sed quasi Venerius quidam triumphus esset. With this Festus v. ovalis corona agrees. The provisions of positive law are repugnant to the female natural principle. It unites with the natural side of material life, and therefore comes to the fore whenever the war, for want of observance of the positive fecial law or because of other similar defects, cannot lay claim to the character of a justum et legitimum bellum. In such a case only the order of the plebeians and the equestrian order belonging to it take part in the victory celebration, whereas the whole state attends the ox sacrifice of the triumph. Plebeiandom stands, precisely on account of its purely material character, in closer connection with the female natural principle; the patriciate has a higher character. It possesses the higher solar initiation, and unites with the paternal principle of heavenly light, by virtue of which the imperium of the state rests in it. Bona Dea-Murtia bears, according to Festus, also the name Damia, her priestess is called Damiatrix, her sacrifice Damium. Here we see her as Tellus. For Damia has, as we remarked above, the meaning of the fruitful earth. Damia and Auxesia are joined at Troezen like Demeter and Kore,

As Damia, Bona Dea appears once more in her closer connection with the plebeian element of the state. She is the mother of the δῆμος, which plebeiandom precisely forms.

17.

The connection of law with the female natural principle continues in remarkable phenomena that receive their proper light only through linkage with the general standpoint set up. With the generally prevailing ideas about the degradation of the female sex in antiquity, certain undoubted reports of its participation in the office of judge stand in the sharpest contrast. In Elis it is a collegium matronarum that settles, as the highest judicial authority, the dispute of the Eleans with the Pisans. In the alliance that Hannibal concludes with certain Gallic tribes there stood the provision that, in the event of a dispute over its interpretation, the supreme decision should be laid before a college of Gallic matrons. In the quarrel of the Boeotian Cadmeans with the Dodonaean oracle the priestesses of the latter demand that as many women as men be called into the judicial body. At Athens, in the quarrel of Neptunus and Minerva, women too sit in judgment alongside the men, and Aristophanes’ Ecclesiazusae and Thesmophoriazusae appear as a parody of older conditions actually experienced. From a woman the Germans obtain the decision even in questions of the nature of international law, phenomena that I have subjected to closer consideration in my Mutterrecht. If we recognized above this female natural principle as the bearer of the law inborn in matter, so we see here the matrons entrusted with the administration of justice, and administering law itself. They take over the office of the tellurian primal mother, as they continue her physical vocation through birth, and fulfill it in her place. There can be no doubt that this supreme matronal administration of justice forms a chief component of that gynecocracy which transfers the religious idea of the material-female natural principle into the life of the state, and seems to have constituted the primal state of human society. We find it among the Lycians, in Crete, among the Carian-Lelegian and the Libyan tribes, and, as among German peoples, so also among the Cantabrians. As the mortal image of the great nature mother the matron enjoys special esteem and a sacred character, which passes to her from the latter. Inviolability distinguishes her. She steps between the combatant parties and at once all deeds of arms cease. So we find her in the Balearic Islands, and whoever compares the

[PDF 231]

— 217 —

account preserved by Diodorus on this subject with Livy’s narrative of the intervention of the Sabine women between the ranks of the fighting Romans and Sabines finds so perfect an agreement of the two phenomena that his belief in the correctness of this tradition too receives a new support. The high position of the Sabine women has also left an echo in that narrative of Plutarch’s, Qu. rom. 82, according to which the provision was contained in their alliance with the Romans that no Roman should compel his wife to the labor of cooking or grinding. This must have appeared to those peoples as an impairment of the high position that the matron occupied in house and state. The more alien such customs were to later times, the more authentic is their transmission. Whether this was decided in a treaty or not: as a trait of the old life the report is beyond doubt. It corresponds perfectly to those conditions that founded gynecocracy and found their highest expression in the office of judge held by women. When the Roman matrons were to be deprived of the right of the currus, Themis- Carmenta protected them. The myth preserved about this in Plutarch Qu. r. 53 shows us the matron once more as the image of the primal mother, sharing in her initiation, specially guarded by her. Every violation of womanhood Mother Earth avenges. In this exclusive connection of the female-material primal principle with the mortal mother rests the special relation that links the Erinyes, these tellurian primal mothers, with the vengeance of the injured woman. Heedless of the higher Apollonian father right that brings atonement, they demand the blood of Orestes, which belongs to them according to that ancient right and law of the maternal earth, which reveals itself with equal decisiveness also in Alcmaeon’s banishment to a newly born island of mud. From the connection with the female-material primal principle the mother derives that special sanctity that surrounds her. She is the birth-giving matter that encloses within itself the mystery of things, that bears the natural law within itself, from whom man must inquire it, as Zeus from Themis, who proclaims it in oracles, unveils it in judgments, who by her appearing commands a halt to every hostile encounter of men, who everywhere appears as the principle of union, of peace, of rest, and precisely thereby, in the midst of the wild strife of warlike primal tribes, stands forth as the beneficent principle of order, as the true center of the first civilization, as the power that holds together, reconciles, and orders. As against war the mother is peace, as against combat reconciliation, as against the roving life of man the domestic settlement, as against the decision of arms the peaceful decision of law, as against the

[PDF 232]

— 218 —

winning by combat, preservation; as against violence, harmony. For this reason all property also belongs to woman. As all wealth corresponds to matter, so all possessions belong to material woman. As Hermes lays the filled purse in the lap of Fortuna, so man brings to the mother, as property, everything that his arm wins. In the system of gynecocracy all law of inheritance rests on this. Only the daughters inherit, not the sons. Only upon the daughters rests the duty of maintenance, not upon the sons. Dominion passes by inheritance to the sisters’ children, as even the Roman women in the temple of Matuta still pray for the welfare and blessing of their sisters’ children. Man has sword and bow, and the arm for acquisition. Whether he gains this in the hunt and in distant war, whether he gains it like the sooty Ψολόεις in the smithy, like the Ozolian Locrians as herdsmen, like the Egyptians at the loom: what he acquires falls into the mother’s lap, passes by inheritance from her to the daughters alone, matter to matter, the acquiring force to the sons, to whom the woman brings the property. Here too law shows itself bound up with woman, not only in that it bears the same within itself, not only in that as arbitress she proclaims and administers it, but also in that it ties its object, the material goods, to her person and propagates it only in the female line. So the material jus naturale brings it with it, and the same reveals itself in the exclusive regard for maternal descent, according to which the children bear the name of the mother, as among the Lycians; the nobility of birth is measured only by the female ancestors, as among the Locrians; the same in the admission of marriage between the nearest relatives, between brother and sister, mother and child; the same in the right of the maiden to dispose of her own hand, to choose the husband of her own accord, indeed, as among the Cantabrians, also to give her brothers in marriage. The material-female standpoint dominates this whole law. Motherhood is not only the bearer of the principle of law, it also determines its content, and stands in exclusive connection with the goods, the object of legal life. Precisely thereby woman becomes the scepter-bearing queen, the bearer of the potentia that confronts the political imperium as the epitome of material power. Thereby the mother becomes the Creusa of her lineage, therefore the sole source of nobility, therefore, as an immortal, joined to a mortal man, therefore in the Naupactia and Eoiai the guiding thread of all heroic genealogy. In Plato there is found the remark that the seed is very often transformed into the nature of the mother by the soil to which it is entrusted, but never does the land pass over into the nature of the seed, and this agrees with the account of Aeschylus and Euripides, in which they carry through the mother’s closer connection with the

[PDF 233]

— 219 —

child, entirely. In this physical truth lies the foundation of that whole mother right whose individual aspects we have briefly indicated. Gynecocracy thus presents itself as jus naturale in the proper sense, as law of material creation. It is no positive institution, but a natura ductum, developed natura duce, nulla ratione, nullaque doctrina.1) It rests on the view that, as the æs receives its impress from the die, so man’s seed receives its stamp from woman’s moneta.2) It is the Jus terræ, which in Roman law too is opposed to the jus seminis. He who sows a foreign field does not gain the fruits; they fall to the owner of the ground: jure terræ non jure seminis. The same holds of building on foreign ground and soil. The same of the fecundation of a slave woman, the same of illegitimate mating, where the spurio editus, the sown spurius, follows the maternal earth. The principle of Aphroditean-hetaeric life is carried over into the conjugal relation. Cerealian law does, to be sure, give the child also a father, makes it a διφυής, a legitimate offspring. But in this relation of exclusiveness the maternal matter has the upper hand over the paternal incorporeal force, as at the lunar stage of religion Luna has over Lunus, who recedes behind her. Over against this female jus naturale Rome founds her family and her state on the higher immaterial law of fatherhood. It wrests itself free from the material natural law that attaches itself to the female natural principle, and founds its family, and as the consistent extension of it its state, on the basis of the paternal imperium, which, apart from the Gallograeci of Asia, no other people has developed and maintained in so decided a manner. With this law Rome enters into history. For this very reason she is from the day of her foundation more a state than a people, from the first day dominated by the grip of the imperium, and holding to it always until the completion of her world-historical task. The material-female natural principle forms no unified state, only peoples and natural wholes, no political bodies. It produces only external union, no concentration. It communicates its own nature to the peoples it rules; gives them the tendency toward the development of material life, which the Hellenic tribes carry through to the farthest limit of idealization, the Asiatic and Egyptian to the most sunken materialism; promotes the development of the arts and sciences, which, like navigation, astronomy, poetry, and all erotic

1) Cic. off. 3, 17. Cic. Tusc. Disp. 1, 13.

2) Macrob. Somn. Scip. 1, 12. p. 269.

[PDF 234]

— 220 —

refinement of life, attach themselves preeminently to the Aphroditean- Dionysian cult; is, in uncorrupted times, a mighty lever of valor, which finds in the encouraging love of woman its highest spur and the greatest reward of chivalry; carries also a very vigorous element of political conservatism within itself, so that gynecocratic peoples in particular are praised and extolled as εὔνομοι: but with all these qualities, in part excellent, it nevertheless remains always in matter, and entangled in a development of material, natural life that is now more refined, now more material: whereas the Roman principle, in the paternal imperium on which family, state, and world dominion are founded, raises to the throne a political idea of wholly incorporeal nature, and subordinates to it the female-material side of the existence of the people. Thereby its private law too acquires more and more spiritual content. Whoever follows its progress will recognize the elevation from the material-maternal character to the immateriality of the paternal principle in all its parts, in the development of adoption, in the doctrine of inheritance, in the fiction of a personality reaching beyond death, holding the property together, as it were animating matter, in the ever-advancing legal shaping of merely factual relations, and in a great number of particulars. In the political idea of the imperium lies that higher spiritual content which Rome possesses beyond all the peoples of the ancient world. When this faded more and more toward the end of the Republic, that inclination to the material-female side of life emerged with unbridled force. Now those Asiatic-Egyptian cults in which the maternal natural principle predominates found so rapid an entry and so powerful a diffusion. Now Rome had to live through the spectacle to which she had never been accustomed, feminam præsidere signis romanis. What a contrast to the earlier time, which excluded women even from representation in court, which promoted subjection through the guardianship of the sex and through the restriction of their right of inheritance, to which it counted as an ill-omened event when once a woman had appeared speaking in the Forum, and which allowed woman so little connection with the state that even the taxation of woman’s property counted as a sacrilege. Whoever does not conceive the patria potestas and the patrem ciere of the patricians in contrast to the material mother right and the wholly material formation of the other peoples will never be able to appreciate their whole significance; nor will it come to his consciousness what special difficulties the spread of the Christian doctrine was bound to meet precisely in the Roman idea of the state.

18.

A whole class of monuments on which the egg occupies a significant place has remained excluded from our account so far. I mean the representations of the circus games, which form the content of many sarcophagus reliefs. A complete enumeration of them would be pointless. It suffices to single out a number of the most important. One finds them assembled in Visconti, Museo Pio-Clementino vol. 5. tab. 36–43 and on the tavole d’aggiunta to the 11th volume of the Annali dell’ Instituto di correspondenza archeologica. Guattani, notizie sulle antichità di Roma per l’anno 1785. Ottobre tav. 3. On a high scaffold, supported now by four, now by two columns, egg-shaped bodies appear, set up now in the number seven, now in the numbers five and ten. Another structure, entirely corresponding, carries an equal number of dolphins. The nature of these objects can be subject to no doubt, because eggs as well as dolphins are not seldom singled out among the appurtenances of the circus in written testimonies. To win a secure foundation for what follows, the pronouncements of the ancients are first to be assembled. Cassius Dio 49, 43 names the eggs and dolphins together: κἂν τῷ ἱπποδρόμῳ σφαλλομένους τοὺς ἀνθρώπους περὶ τῶν διαύλων ἀριθμὸν ὁρῶν, τούς τε δελφῖνας καὶ τὰ ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα κατεστήσατο ὅπως δι᾽ αὐτῶν αἱ περίοδοι περιδρόμων ἀναδεικνύωνται. Agrippa, to whom this account refers, seems to have made some new, expedient arrangement with regard to the dolphins and the eggs and their setting up in the circus. For the use of eggs at the circus games does not derive from him. Already for the year 578 of the city it is attested by Livy 41, 32. (Censores Q. Fulvius Flaccus et A. Postumius Albinus locaverunt) et carceres in circo et ova ad notas curriculis numerandis et — —. The remaining part of the passage is so corrupt that a tolerable restoration of it has so far been attempted in vain. Here too there is no talk of the introduction of a new usage. Only the structural restoration of the individual parts of the circus, among them also the eggs, is ordered by the censors. The ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα seem accordingly to have been made of wood or of baked clay1) and to have been of considerable size. Particular attention is deserved by Varro R. R. 1, 2. In that conversation which he says he held in the temple of Tellus at the feriæ Sementinæ with C. Fundanius and other friends, C. Licinius Stolo says the following: Nam non modo ovum illud sublatum

1) Sueton. Claud. 21.

[PDF 236]

— 222 —

est, quod ludis Circensibus novissimi curriculi finem facit quadrigis, sed ne illud quidem tum vidimus, quod in Cereali pompa solet esse primum.1) These words show with certainty that at each circuit of the chariot teams one of the eggs was taken down from the scaffold on which they were set up, so that with the completion of the seventh circuit the last one vanished. Sublatum cannot without strain be explained otherwise. When Visconti puts forward the opinion that it was not so much that an egg was removed each time, but, conversely, that one was set up, several reasons can be urged for this. First, the representation on individual monuments in which the presentation of the victor’s wreath and the full number of eggs appear side by side. Moreover, however, the following words of Cassiodorus, Var. 3, 51: Nec illud putetur irritum, quod metarum circuitus ovorum erectionibus exprimatur quando actus ipse multis superstitionibus gravis, ovi exemplo, geniturum se aliqua2) profitetur. Et ideo datur intelligi, volitantes atque inconstantissimos inde mores nasci, quos avium moribus aptaverunt. Yet several objections can be raised against the probative force of these representations. The artist must have been free to indicate the sum of the circuits by affixing the full number of eggs, without seeing himself hindered by the completion of the contest, which of course presupposes the bestowal of the victor’s crown. Cassiodorus’s words, however, are not entirely certain. Instead of the decisive erectionibus, Salmasius, Plinianæ exercit. ad Solinum p. 640, reads, after old manuscripts, exceptionibus, and proposes to emend this to exemptionibus, while others give preference to ereptionibus. At any rate, the passage falls short of full probative force in that it speaks not of the successive erection or removal, but in general of the significance of the erected eggs and the relations tied to them. Accordingly there is no reason to depart from the removal of the egg after the completion of each individual circuit, assumed already by earlier writers, like Bulenger and Salmasius, and by later ones, like Raoul-Rochette and Friedländer.3) — To the eggs of the circus, finally, the following passage of Juvenal, Sat. 6, 589–591, is to be referred.

Plebeium in Circo positum est et in aggere fatum.

Quæ nullis4) longum ostendit cervicibus aurum

Consulit ante phalas, delphinorumque columnas,

An saga vendenti nubat, caupone relicto.

While the rich turn for divination to the Phrygian augur or to Indian Brahmans, and buy their oracles with money, the plebeian woman, whose neck no costly jewelry covers, goes to the circus, and there inquires of the eggs and dolphins the voice of fate concerning her future husband. Phale designates the ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα of Dio Cassius. If only eggs can be associated with the dolphins, then also everything that the ancients remark about Falæ proves a fundamental meaning that finds its full application in the ovoid form of those Demiurgemata. According to Nonnus 2, 114, Fala is turris lignea, according to Servius Aen. 9, 705 simply turris. Festus: Falæ dictæ ab altitudine, a falando, quod apud Etruscos significat cælum. Among the Greeks we find φάλαι, which Hesychius explains as ὄρη, σκοπιαί. Thus we arrive, for fala, at the meaning of a rounded elevation, at the top, of a body projecting above the surface of the earth, and this it is that enables the word also to designate those ὠοειδῆ δημιουργήματα. Unmistakable is its kinship with palus, stake, φαλλός, and the divus pater Falacer. The stake that rises out of the earth, the conical stone formed like an omphalos, is the image and expression of the generative natural force that penetrates the matter of the earth. In φαλλός both relations lie united: the external one of elevation, according to which the phallic Dionysus is called ὀρθός,1) and the internal one of the generative force, which finds its expression in that image. Falacer is accordingly a god of the generative natural force represented in phallus form, which is confirmed by his association with Pomona.2) A perfectly corresponding parallel is furnished by Τύλος; for in this word too the meanings of a bulging elevation, and of the male generative force represented by it, are united, concerning which I refer to a special section of my Mutterrecht. Accordingly I do not doubt that by his falæ Juvenal understood the scaffolds crowned with the seven egg-shaped rounded bodies, as we see them represented on the sarcophagi mentioned. Eggs and dolphins are to the poor plebeian woman the fate that she consults about

her marriage, while the rich women buy by large payment the favorable pronouncement of a foreign charlatan. That precisely the eggs and the dolphins, the animals of the generative Neptunus, are used for such a divination is explained by itself in the light of what was remarked earlier. As ἀρχὴ γενέσεως the egg stands in the closest relation to marriage and generation. Among the superstitiones that Cassiodorus mentions, the practice of the women of the lower people alluded to by Juvenal may also be included. The ovi exemplo geniturum se avem shows that the original significance of the egg lived on still in popular tradition. It appears in the circus also as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, and can for this very reason be brought into so close a connection with the egg of the Cerealian pompa. It is in the circus too a representation of the female natural principle, and older than the bird-birth that breaks forth from it, winged and swiftly flying onward, like the quadriga from the carceres, in unconquerable desire of becoming. This is the idea that Cassiodorus recognizes in the connection of the egg with the circuit of the chariots. The race itself, he says — for this is what is to be understood by actus — gives us to know that from each of the erected eggs a lightly winged bird-birth will emerge. The swiftly flying four-horse team appears here as the image of egg-birth. As the bird breaks through the shell of the egg and, freed from its enclosure, tries the force of its wings, so the four-horse team storms forth, impatiently and with winged course, from the carceres that enclose and restrain it, and thereby gives us to know what relation the erected and removed egg has to the race itself. If in this connection the original significance of the egg and its relation to the circus games have been preserved with remarkable purity, then, on the other hand, the relation of the swift flight of the quadriga, compared to the bird, to fickleness of customs is a continuation and development of the fundamental idea which does not belong to it at all, and had its occasion in the conditions of the later time. The effect of the circus games, that is Cassiodorus’s idea, consists in this, that they make the customs of the people like those of birds. Volitantes atque inconstantissimi inde mores nascuntur. In the words that follow, instead of avium maribus, avium moribus is to be read. The whole connection of this passage, so little understood hitherto, is now clear. Cassiodorus says in the context the following: the erection of the eggs, whose successive removal corresponds to the individual circuits, is as little without meaning as everything else that the circus and its games offer us. Manifold superstition attaches itself to the relation of the egg to the race. In my opinion the birth of a bird is indicated to us by the egg, and the

[PDF 239]

— 225 —

circuit of the four-horse team is itself the image of this event. But at the same time we are also taught what influence the circus games exert on customs. The life of the people becomes like that of birds, fickle and inconstant, like that of the restless and unresting winged inhabitants of the air. In this sense too, from the eggs of the circus, insofar as they direct the games and announce their actual undertaking, a race of birds is born, namely the fickle and inconstant people itself that looks on at them.

From the testimonies considered so far the following propositions result. The eggs stand in an inner connection with the circus games. Their setting up had, to be sure, also an external purpose, namely to remove every doubt about the number of completed circuits, and to give both the competitors themselves and the spectators certainty about it at every moment. To attain this purpose it was also indispensable to have ovoid bodies, artificially made and of considerable size, set up on a high scaffold instead of the all too small natural eggs. But this external purpose by no means exhausts the relation of the egg to the circus and its games. This could just as well have been achieved by some other objects. If eggs in particular were chosen, and from of old, the ground of such a choice rests in the religious significance of the egg itself. To each circuit of the meta corresponds an egg. At each circuit one of them is removed. This inner relation of the egg to the racing was not entirely obscured even in later times. In many a superstitious practice of the people, particularly of its lower, plebeian classes, the old consciousness lived on, and so far as we see from Cassiodorus, from Juvenal, and from Varro, it was always the thought of the maternal, Cerealian primal principle of tellurian creation, of marriage and birth, of the female ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, that found its expression, now purer, now more unclear and obscured, in such popular views.

It is now our task to bring fully into the light the original idea that governs the connection of the eggs with the circus games. Earlier remarks have long since led him who followed my exposition to the right path. I recall here in particular what has been remarked about the Dioscuri and the Elean Molionidae. Both pairs of brothers have sprung from the mother egg. Both are distinguished by the unattainable swiftness with which they fly along on horse and chariot. As mighty racers and charioteers they come forth from the maternal primal egg. If in this the seed of all things lay enclosed in the deepest rest, now from the opened shell the visible creation emerges, and in this everything is

15

[PDF 240]

— 226 —

restless, eternal motion. The life of tellurian generation endures no standstill. In it everything comes to be and passes away. It was of this that Heraclitus, according to Aristotle, Metaphysics 4, 5, 26, used the image of the river, saying that one cannot step twice into the same river, to which Cratylus replied with censure that one cannot do so even once. Of this too the physicists asserted that, because of the eternal flux of the world of the senses, nothing at all could be said about it, and that existence in general must rather be denied it. Between two poles material life moves. Its realm is not that of being but of becoming and passing away, of the eternal alternation of two colors, the white of life and the black of death.1) Only through the equal mixture of the two is the continuance of the material world secured. Without death no rejuvenation is possible, and in the eternal labor of nature the destroying force is no less indispensable to the preservation of ever-young life than the creative and generative one. Indeed, at no moment can the positive force subsist without the negative. Only what the latter dissolves can the former restore. Death is therefore not the opposite but the helper of life, just as the negative pole of magnetism forms not the opposite of the positive but rather its necessary complement, without which the latter too would at once vanish, and life would have to yield to nothingness.2) Two forces, then, govern tellurian creation and by their cooperation assure the progress of things. Together they were born. As twin brothers they go forth from the same egg. At equal pace they run side by side. A two-horse team they have mounted; it is their doubled effort, directed to the same goal, that assures them invincible speed. Actor’s sons, the Molionidae, owe the victory of their team precisely to this united effort. Swift as an arrow it flies along. Swift as an arrow, too, is the course of the tellurian world of appearance. The rapidity with which the two united forces sweep creation onward has found its expression in the speed of the chariot that the Molionidae drive. In the progress of the motion the team always returns again to its point of departure, like the circular line, whose completion is lost in the

It lay at the confluence of two streams, of which the one contained deadly water, the other healing water.

beginning. If one of the forces drives straight ahead, the other turns aside and leads back again. The completion of every existence is a return to its beginning, and in every distance from the point of departure there lies at the same time a renewed approach to it. Two directions are bound together in a manner just as inexplicable as the two forces themselves to which they correspond. The result of their combined force is the circular course in which all tellurian life eternally moves. The image of this circular course is the circuits of the chariots, which with the utmost speed fly around the metae in order to return to the point of departure, and then to traverse the same space anew. By this two things are now made clear: first, the connection of the egg with the chariot racing of the circus; second, the correspondence that connects the completion of each single circuit with the removal of one egg at a time. If the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως lies enclosed in the egg, the two-horse team shows the motion of the creation that has stepped into the light from the womb of matter. With each return to the point of departure the circuit of one existence is completed, and a new one is about to begin. Come into being, grown, vanished is the offspring of one egg; a new one takes the place of the one removed, and so in the unforeseeable series of the generations there follows always one after another, always the brood of one egg after that of the other, and always with that unattainable speed which is presented to us in the myth of the Molionidae as the result of the union of two forces, of two twin brothers uniting their effort. Now it is clear what we indicated above: how close Cassiodorus’s thought, actus ipse, ovi exemplo, geniturum se avem profitetur, is to the original and true significance of the circus egg. The team bursting forth from the carceres is rightly represented as an egg-birth. As the chick from the egg, so the team hastens winged out of the prison that until now set bounds to its lust for becoming. What was hidden becomes visible; what was motionless passes now into restless haste. With the first moment of existence begins that unrest which forms so decided a contrast to the stillness and immobility that formerly reigned in the egg. So Pegasus, the winged horse, breaks forth neighing from the Gorgon’s bleeding trunk; so the black horse of the Phigalians from the womb of Ceres,1) so the wild Scythius, whom the scholiast to Pindar, P. 4, 246 calls Σκύφιος, from the depths of the earth, like the water of the spring, which from its source onward, never resting, never pausing, rolls wave upon wave in hurrying haste.2) Not meaningless
