2) Serv. Georg. 1, 12; 3, 122.

[PDF 242]

— 228 —

in fact is the erection of the eggs in the circus. Nec illud putetur irritum, quod metarum circuitus ovorum erectionibus exprimatur. The idea of generation from maternal primal matter, the birth of a chick that comes into the light only to succumb very soon to the law of matter, governs the circus egg no less than the one that is carried at the head of the Cerealian pompa. The people watching the games recognizes in the swift flight of the teams, and in the corresponding disappearance of the upraised eggs, the spectacle that all tellurian life presents, the law that governs its own existence; and when it awards the palm of victory to the one who surpasses the others in speed, it confesses thereby that the highest glory of a people and of every individual man consists not in the longest duration of existence, not in the longest possible prolongation of it, but in the mightiest unfolding of force, which is always accompanied by the swiftest consuming. Into his description of the Roman circus Tertullian de spectac. 8 has taken the remark: ova honori Castorum attribuunt. We see from this that our juxtaposition of the circus games and their eggs with the Dioscuri and with the mother egg, from which the mounted, swift-footed twins, the brother-kings of creation, to whom the horse is consecrated, issued, was fully justified. Though the relation of the circus egg to that of Leda-Nemesis may seem no less arbitrary than the similar relation of that egg which hung from the roof, bound in fillets, in the Laconian temple of the Leucippides, yet the whole fullness of the idea that lies in the circus egg is nevertheless thereby quite rightly brought out. The alternation of life and death, the night that takes the day into itself in order to give birth to it again, rejuvenated, out of itself, the speed that irresistibly sweeps on the stream of life as soon as it has once emerged into the light from the mother egg: all this is the physical fundamental idea of the Leda egg and its twin birth, all this too the content of the circus games and their eggs.

19.

The circle of thought in which these conceptions move governs also all the other parts of the circus, all the sanctuaries, cults, and institutions connected with it. Natural force in its threefold, tellurian, lunar, solar sequence of stages, in its twofold, female-passive, male-active potentiation, in its twofold expression as vivifying and as destroying power, found in the Roman circus a representation so perfect and so manifold that it could count as a true pantheon and be designated by the Church Fathers

[PDF 243]

— 229 —

to the believers of their time preeminently as an unclean place of the pagan world of demons, to be carefully avoided.1) If the female natural principle has received in Murtia, in Cybele, in the mother triad Seia Segetia Tutilina, in Pollentia, Libera, Ceres an expression embracing both the Aphroditean and the Cerealian stage of material life,2) the male generative potency, which awakens life and fecundates, is to be recognized as tellurian force of water in Consus-Neptunus, but as heavenly power of light, on the other hand, in the obelisks and in many other details to which we shall return later. The connection of the tellurian and the solar stage of natural force is a phenomenon that demands particular attention. It can no longer cause us difficulties. For have we not seen those two degrees of the force of natural generation united in one and the same divine figure? Achilles, Dionysus, and many other gods we recognized as bearers of the tellurian power of water and at the same time as lords of the heavenly light, and the apparent incompatibility of water and fire we found disputed by the ancients themselves as an assertion not admissible in the domain of mythology.3) The male-generative force rests on more than one factor. Its physical foundation is the heavenly light no less than the moisture of the depths. From their united action on the female matter of the earth all tellurian fertility proceeds. Yet on the different stages of religious development now the chthonian, now the uranian power, now the water, now the light, now the Neptunian, now the solar element will come to the fore. To a more material, and therefore deeper, conception, water counts, to a less material, and therefore purer, way of viewing, the immaterial, weightless sunlight counts as the seat and bearer of the fecundating force. Murcia, a primal mother conceived as Aphroditean, had her cult. The luxuriant meadowland bore the stone of the gods, the Metæ Murciæ, and the neighboring Aventine itself the name Murcus. As a chthonian demon Consus stood at the mother’s side, as Eros stands beside Aphrodite, whom she addresses in Virgil as mea magna potentia. He is her Virbius, her Adonis, her Euamerion, her Sosipolis, the beloved and fecundator without whom Murcia can do nothing; he dwells with her in the depths, rests in her womb, apud metas sub terra delitescit. This place Tarquin chose for the erection of his circus, and there can hardly be any doubt that it was precisely the veneration, native to that valley, of Murcia and her πάρεδρος Consus that determined the choice. The stage of religion to which this cult, and the games now entering into connection with it, belong, can be subject to no doubt. It is the tellurian-Neptunian, which conceives the force itself as chthonian power of water. The horse and chariot races held in its honor are, in agreement with this conception of the force itself, celebrated preferably in luxuriant moist meadowlands, on the banks of brooks and rivers. The proximity of that element which was regarded as the seat of the force, as the bearer of the generative Lar of the earth, had itself to appear as the presence of the deity, and when now on the bank the swift horses flew by, as Pindar emphasizes of the Elean games in the first Olympian Ode, one could see in the turning of the wheels, in the hurrying stride of the foaming racers an image of the water itself, which in the midst of an immovable nature alone enjoys the privilege of unstoppable haste. The connection of the circus games with water, with rivers, swamps, moist grassy lowlands emerges everywhere, and especially at Rome. At Anagnia there is a circus maritimus. Liv. 9, 42. Concilium populorum omnium habentibus Anagninis in Circo, quem maritimum vocant. But Anagnia is an inland town in the land of the Hernici; the designation of its circus as maritimus is therefore not geographical but sacral. It contains the acknowledgment that the circus games are dedicated to the generative element of water, whether it appear as Neptunus, as Consus, or as Mars. It is possible that a small body of water that lay nearby, or was purposely led thither for the purpose, was given the name mare. This would have fully accorded with ancient practice. So we find in Plutarch de virtt. mull. in fine an example in which a tomb was brought into connection with water by an artificial conduit, because it was customary to erect for the dead their resting place on the bank of the life-generating element. So too in Lydia, according to Pausanias 1, p. 87, a little stream bore the name Oceanus, and its connection with the tomb of Geryon shows that one actually saw in it the image of the great Ocean. How much attention must be paid to the form given to the festival cakes is shown by many reports, among others Plutarch de Is. et Osiride. The wheel belongs among the most significant symbols of antiquity, and therefore already among the ancients, as Clement reports in the Protrepticus, occasioned special treatments. Whoever collects the particulars will find that it, like the majority of symbols, has first of all a physical meaning, and embraces in this all sides of natural force, the chthonian-Poseidonian and the heavenly-solar, hence both that of swift passing away and that of becoming, but that one then advanced from the physical to the abstract, figurative meaning, as it emerges especially in the wheel of Nemesis. The Heroon itself formed a part of the Athenian hippodrome, which accordingly bore the name Enechelidon. The chariot race thus took place in the neighborhood of a body of water, and was held in honor of the generative Consus-Echelus who rules in the swamp. The name itself is without doubt connected with ἕλος, as Ἴλος with ἰλύς. So too Euripides in the Hippolytus, 207–210, 213, joins lake and racecourse, and places both under the protection of Artemis. On the seashore Hippolytus drives his team of horses along, when Poseidon’s bull brought him destruction. For this reason Euripides, lines 1072–1074, has the chorus sing that henceforth the Amazon’s son will no longer guide the Enetian racers, no longer hold, on the lake, with the swift horse the circuit of the racecourses. In the beautiful description of the Greek camp that is found in the Iphigenia Aulidensis, Achilles is depicted as he, the fleet racer, on the sandy seashore leaves the four-horse team behind in the run. Lines 204–212. Indeed, in the Ἀχιλέως δρόμοι the river beds themselves appear as racecourses, as indeed the name and conception of Achilles demonstrate the complete identity of the course of the world and the motion of water. Now we shall also appreciate the whole weight of the remark of the scholiast on Pindar’s ἄριστον μὲν ὕδωρ, when he emphasizes that the poet’s thought runs thus: as water occupies the first place among the elements, so too the Olympian agon, consecrated to the water of the Alpheus, has greater dignity than all the other contests of the Hellenes.

A very remarkable example of the retention of the Neptunian relation, even for such circus games as were celebrated at a distance from water, is furnished by the ludi capitolini, as they appear on two glass images communicated by Buonarroti, osservazioni sopra alcuni frammenti di vasi antichi di vetro, ornati di figure, trovati nei Cimiteri di Roma, Firenze 1716, plates 30, 31. On both the victors of the Capitolina are represented with all the attributes of a river god. I wish to describe here in more detail the picture of plate 30. With the upper body half bared the victor reclines, with his right hand grasping a bundle of reeds, in his left the cornucopia. The left arm rests on an overturned vase from which a rich stream of water wells forth. At the victor’s side, with her left arm embracing the man’s shoulder, sits a female figure, whose significance we shall discuss afterward. Beside her, closing the picture, there appears, overtopped by tall reed stalks, a boy’s figure, who

In the hands of the second of the genii one sees an open garland of flowers, which likewise is being offered to the victor. The third, finally, carries in his arms a bundle of rods, which seem to me to have much less the appearance of palm branches than of swamp stalks. Around the upper curve of the picture one reads the acclamation: — — RIS VIVAS VALEAS VINCAS. — RIS evidently forms only the final syllable of the name, whose beginning has become illegible. games. This one is thereby traced back to Pelops. From this the female figure is explained who, on our glass pictures, is depicted at the side of the Capitoline victor, lovingly embracing him. To take her merely generally as the victor’s consort, and to explain her embrace as an expression of joy over the prize carried off, would by no means exhaust the idea. Rather we have here to recognize Hippodamia, won by Pelops in the race with Oenomaus, and thereby released from her father’s hands and restored to her higher female destiny. A youthful consort must stand at the victor’s side, if the model of the Olympian agon is to be completely recognized in the Capitoline games and their prize vessel.1) Thereby the games themselves appear as the foundation of the first higher culture, grounded in agriculture and marriage, and it gains heightened significance when the Capitolina are traced back to the founder of the Roman state and of marriage with the Sabine daughters, as the Olympia are to the union of Pelops with the daughter of Oenomaus. The Achaean Pelops for his part leads back again to Asia, especially to Lydia; for Pelops is called a Lydian.2) Now, that the chariot races were known to the Lydians is attested by a very remarkable proof preserved in the myth of the meeting of Gyges and Lixus.3) From the Lydian emigrants, moreover, the ancients derive the naturalization of the circus games in Etruria,4) and from there an Etruscan prince brought them to the Romans. Thus an immediate connection between Rome and Asia is established, and the tracing back of the Capitoline games to the Lydian Pelops and his victory in the plain of the Alpheus, the swampy Elean lowland, is explained also by the historical connection of the lands and peoples.

In view of these occurrences the Neptunian relation of the Roman circus and of the games celebrated in it no longer appears as an isolated phenomenon, but rather as an expression of that general idea which assigns to the generative force its seat in the tellurian waters. To this element point the dolphins, whose connection with the eggs now

In the circus the god of the generative waters appears not in anthropomorphic form but in the shape of a fish, as indeed the cult practices and cult representations of the circus have remained faithful preeminently to an earlier, more ancient, more original stage of religion. With the dolphins Cassiodor 3, 51 connects the mention of the Euripus. Euripus maris vitrei reddit imaginem, unde illic delphini equorei aquas interfluunt. By Euripus is here understood not an actual water channel but rather the intermetium, the spina, which extended between the two metae in the middle of the circus and divided it lengthwise into two halves. One must conceive it as an agger held by two side walls, on whose height were set up the many objects required for the celebration of the sacred games, and the images of the gods, among them especially Cybele, præses Euripi, and the tres aræ.1) If now this earthen dam is nevertheless conceived as an image of the sea, and brought into connection with the dolphins, those inhabitants of the waters, well disposed to man and distinguished by the greatest speed, there lies in this again an idea corresponding to the original maritime nature of the circuses. In elaboration of the same thought the Euripus of the circus was compared with that Euripus which separates Euboea from the mainland of Boeotia. The sevenfold ebb and flow that drives the water of the strait up and down seemed to correspond to the sevenfold circuit of the teams, to the seven eggs and seven dolphins, and to express perfectly the thought of the waves of existence flowing eternally back into themselves. According to Suidas in Σεβήρῳ the Byzantine hippodrome moreover contained a lavacrum Zeuxippi, which Ismenius and Manasses also praise as an especially beautiful work. Its connection with the Draconteum and with a seated Athena justify the comparison of this Zeuxippus with Erichthonius, the serpent-footed demon of the tellurian waters, to whom the four-horse team is traced back in a very significant manner.1) Through all these particulars the essential connection of the circus games with the tellurian waters receives ever new confirmation.2) Indeed, their relation to the fertility of the land and to the blessing of the harvest remained, down to the latest times, in the consciousness of the pagan world. It is very remarkable that ideas of tellurian fertility were also connected with the colors that the contestants wore, and that one especially observed in the choice of the horses, and that relations to the causæ elementorum were found. Not only did one relate the colors themselves to the seasons and to those elements which become important precisely for the yield of the crops; one saw also in the victory of the individual colors the omens of the coming blessing of the harvest or of impending infertility. Especially noteworthy is a saying of Joannes Antiochensis, which one finds with several similar ones in Salmasius p. 634: ἐβάλλοντο κλῆροι, καὶ ὃς ἔλαχεν ὑπὲρ τῆς γῆς ἀγωνίσασθαι ἐφόρει χλοανόν, ὃς δὲ ὑπὲρ τῆς θαλάσσης κυανόν. ἐπετίθει δὲ Οἰνόμαος ἔπαθλον τὴν ἑαυτοῦ θυγατέρα, καὶ ὁ νικηθεὶς ὑπὸ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν θεωμένων ἀνῃρεῖτο. Εἶχον οὖν σημεῖον οἱ τότε, καὶ εἰ μὲν τὸ χλοανὸν ἐνίκα τῆς γῆς εὐφορίαν ἤλπιζον καὶ οὕτως ἐγίνετο. εἰ δὲ τὸ κυανόν, τῆς θαλάττης εὔπλοιαν, καὶ ηὔχοντο οἱ μὲν γεωργοὶ τὸ χλοανὸν νικᾶν, οἱ δὲ ναύτιλοι τὸ κυανόν. Even if the individual presuppositions, combinations, and meanings of the colors, about which one finds much in Tertullian de spect. 9 and Isidor Orig. 18, 41, appear wholly arbitrary and without justified foundation, nevertheless the idea of a general connection of the circus games with the fertility of the earth, and the belief in it, so deeply rooted and bound up with passionate outbursts that Cassiodor also describes,

If we sum up these discussions, they yield a result that agrees perfectly with the significance of the eggs developed above. If these appeared to us as the ἀρχὴ γενέσεως, destined to let all things of visible creation issue from their dark womb in a never-ending succession of generations, then the deities of the circus that surround them, and the games that accompany them, are a representation of the great forces whose action on the maternal matter of the earth completes the work of fecundation and of the eternal rejuvenation of all things. In this direction of the circus games toward the generative, life-giving force, the opposite direction toward the destroying and annihilating potency is necessarily included. Thereby the races become true funeral rites, and this their somber side comes to the fore the more, the more, in the conception of the force itself, Neptunian tellurism had retained its significance. In Consus, in Summanus, in the Canicidium, in the Dii magni, valentes, potentes,2) the relation to death emerges very definitely. But quite generally too the funerary significance of the ancient festal games is emphasized, so by Tertullian de spectac. 6: Nam et a primordio bifariam ludi censebantur, sacri et funebres, id est Diis nationum et mortuis. Sed de idolatria nil differt apud nos, sub quo nomine et titulo, dum ad eosdem spiritus perveniat, quibus renuntiamus, licet mortuis licet Diis suis faciant. Proinde mortuis suis ut Diis faciant. So too by Cyprianus de spectac. p. 3. ed. Joannes Cistert. Quis ludus sine sacrificio? quod certamen non consecratum mortuo? For all the great national games of the Greeks this latter saying has its full correctness. At the funeral rites of Azan one saw the horse races first in Arcadia.3) Archemorus is celebrated at Nemea, Melicertes-Palaemon through the Isthmian games. The Olympian games are linked to the funeral rites of Oenomaus, on which one finds the testimonies collected in Argoli on Panvinius, de ludis circensib. p. 4, or, as by Ausonius in the Eclogues,4) conceived as the funeral games of Pelops. Now if such an individual connection is lacking for the Roman

Pythia placanda Delphi statuere draconi.

circus games, the general funerary significance emerges especially in the laying bare of the subterranean altar of Consus, in the cult of Summanus and its wheel-shaped, Plutonian bread cakes, as well as in the Canicidium. Therein the admission of the circus races and of other games among the tomb representations, as it recurs in so manifold a form on the walls of Cornetan hypogea, in the aforementioned sarcophagus reliefs, and on Etruscan cinerary urns, finds its justification and explanation. Whatever sculptural representations of the circus games have come down to us derives wholly from the world of the tombs. The scenes in which the highest expression of force of fullest life, the highest enjoyment of existence, speaks itself out have taken on, in the place of death, a prevailing funerary significance. If eggs and dolphins form a prominent component of tomb ornamentation, their transference to the circus games seems incompatible with it. And yet these two applications are only two expressions of the same fundamental meaning. When I saw in the Vatican for the first time the sarcophagi adorned with circus reliefs, and put to an archaeologist who accompanied me, now deceased, the question in what relation, then, these representations stood to tomb and death, he was very embarrassed, and made the open confession that the interpretation of art had taken little pains to clarify this point, but rather directed all its effort to the explanation of the particulars, to recognizing the carceres, the column of the sun, the meta, the parabatæ, the many sanctuaries and symbols, and considered its task solved as soon as the agreement of the surviving testimonies with the representation on the monuments had been demonstrated. Should archaeological curiosity, however, extend still further, and beyond the limits of what is represented put to the mute monuments the question of their relation to the world of the tombs, and so to speak demand an accounting of their use for funerary purposes, one could think, to be sure, of all sorts of relations. Might not those interred in such sarcophagi perhaps themselves have been distinguished charioteers, or even have met their death in the circus games? Might not perhaps the thought suffice that the circus games were indeed the mightiest passion of the Romans, that they had often led to factions and bloody strife, and that for this very reason the wish had arisen to retain after death a memory of the joys so often enjoyed during life? And if one wished to go still further, life itself offered indeed the most beautiful comparison with such contests, with their exertions, their expectations, their deceived hopes. Might not the falling desultores, the shattered bigæ,

16

— 242 —

the overturned vessels recall the fortunes of human existence, which founds the victory of one on the ruin of many, which always leads only a few to the goal, which hurls quite a few into the abyss early on, one at the very beginning of the contest, another at the moment when the palm of victory seemed secured to him? I confess that among all the explanations proposed this last allegorical interpretation appealed to me most by its inner truth. Now, however, even it appears to me very secondary. “To decide larger, general questions one must, to avail myself of a wise saying uttered by Plutarch, take one’s standpoint higher.” As sarcophagus pictures the circus games have no other significance than the games actually celebrated; and these refer to material force, first of all to natural generation, conceived wholly in tellurian terms, which includes in itself all the factors that cooperate in the creation of the earth, and embraces life and death, matter and force, and which forms the content of the idea of deity itself. In this significance the games themselves have a predominantly funerary character; in this they take their place beside the great national games of the Hellenes, which through their connection with famous dead appear as true funeral rites. In this they recall those numerous funeral games of which myth makes mention, and which are so often represented on Etruscan cinerary chests. All the games have the character of funeral rites, those celebrated in the circus, in the Terentum of the Tiber, on the shore of the Mincio, no less than the Olympian ones in memory of Pelops, the Nemean around the tombstone of Archemorus, the Isthmian in honor of Palaemon, the Lydian around the monument of Lixus. The meta is always a tombstone and as such the monument of a tellurian Dameon, a λίθος ἔμψυχος, who as Taraxippus frightens the horses, as meta sudans proclaims his relation to the generative moisture of the depths. On this general religious significance rests the admission of the games into the world of the tombs, whether they adorn, as at Corneto, the walls as painting, or, as on our sarcophagi, the funeral chests themselves as reliefs. In the funeral rite, however, the whole of natural force is glorified in its twofold potency, bringing life and death. Death appears bound up with life, and even as its ground. Therefore the symbols of life are so frequent in the tombs; therefore the phallic Priapus on the inscription of the Campana columbarium calls himself at once mortis et vitai locus. Therefore the circus games, too, are a representation of the united force of both, and of the eternal cycle of tellurian creation brought forth by their union. That is the fundamental idea to which our sarcophagus representations attach; that the idea which the world of the tombs disclosed to them. And upon this a higher one is erected, that of deification, of apotheosis. Augustus’s admission

[PDF 257]

— 243 —

among the immortals is to be proclaimed by the games on the shore of the Mincio. The highest idea of the circus reliefs is therefore this: that the dead man has now passed over into the company of the gods and put on the garment of immortality, of which further discussion is to follow at the close of this treatise. Measured against this relation, all those personal explanations drawn from the rank or favorite occupation, the manner of death of the one interred, appear as petty expedients of an archaeology little familiar with the fundamental ideas of the ancient view of life, and no better than many similar attempts that undertake to explain mystery scenes, such as those of the Cumaean tomb, or symbolic accessories, such as the dice,1) hands, shoes, and much else of the kind, from personal circumstances of the buried. Allegorical interpretation is, to be sure, by no means foreign to ancient times,2) and has also been practiced in many ways by the profoundest minds. Indeed, it seems, when faith and understanding of the oldest religious way of thinking vanished, to have overgrown everything, and to have contributed much to securing continuance for the traditional tomb representations. The foundation of the mortuary symbolism it nevertheless by no means forms, and may never be chosen as the starting point of interpretation.

20.

What we have reproached in the preceding remarks as an essential defect of the archaeological interpretation of ancient tomb monuments applies to the whole literature that the last centuries have produced on the games of the ancients, in particular on the circus games. It strives far less for an understanding of the idea than for the development of an erudition often astonishing, which, however, precisely through the massiveness of the accumulated material makes the complete lack of guiding fundamental ideas only the more palpably

It is enough if the significance of the egg and its connection with the nature of the circus games and with the individual circus sanctuaries and cults has been brought to clarity. In closer connection with this stand the numerical relations that govern the circus and its games. To these a special consideration shall now be devoted. It is all the more justified because it gives us occasion to assign to the number of the eggs, three, on our Pamphili tomb painting its proper relation to the idea of the Bacchic cult, and finally to bring to consciousness in its whole fullness the higher content of the mysteries, the destiny of man to press through death to a higher existence.

The seven-stringed lyre, formerly known to the Greeks as well, had fallen out of use in Hellas. Rome, then as now still ever faithful to what has been handed down in religious practices, retained it. Dionysius does not fail to emphasize this adherence to old usages especially in the case of the circus games. The nakedness of the athletes, the use of a third horse joined freely to the yoked pair, the race of the parabatae, all these practices, likewise known to the Hellenes but abandoned by them, continued unchanged in Rome, like the use of the seven-stringed lyre; from which it follows that the Romans did not first take all these things from the Hellenes, but rather retained them even after they had fallen out of practice among the latter.1)

The three odd numbers named (3, 5, 7) must necessarily stand in an inner relation to the significance of the circus and its games developed by us above. The idea that governs them can be no other than precisely that from which the circus games themselves sprang. And this agreement is in fact a complete one. If in the circular course of the teams we have recognized a representation of the fundamental law of all tellurian generation, its motion produced by two cooperating forces, and the continuance lying in this motion itself, then in the first three odd numbers the same property of visible creation makes itself known once more. All three belong to the world of appearance, to the world of becoming and passing away, like the egg and what proceeds from the egg. In all of them we find the idea of motion, not that of rest, such as dwells in the Monas. If the one belongs to the solar world, to which all composition and divisibility remain alien, to the divinity in which absolute simplicity dwells, to which only rest, eternally unchangeable essence, and timeless being pertain, then the three odd numbers, by contrast, designate the entry of the Monas into the change of the sublunary world, in which everything is subject to eternal becoming, eternal motion, eternal cycle between two opposed and yet connected

1) Sylb. p. 456.

[PDF 261]

— 247 —

poles. It is the world of matter that the three, the five, the seven represent, but not the world of resting, dead matter, but of matter awakened to life through fecundation and thereby given over to constant motion. If, accordingly, the numbers named have a common domain to which they belong, that of the world of appearance, and a common property that they express, namely that of motion and of the life that appears only in this form, yet each of them develops the general idea in its own particular way, each in a different tendency. Force takes shape as the triad through its own nature, directed toward generation; as the five through the necessity of the union of both sexual potencies; as the seven through its dependence on the law of the cosmos. As Trias and as Pempas the generative natural force, the source of motion in the world of becoming, appears following only its own inborn drive, the inclination toward the sexual act that constitutes its being, obedient to it alone, directed only toward its realization; as Heptas, on the other hand, it subjects the untamed drive of nature to an ordering, regulating law that is of higher origin than itself. If it appears in the Trias in the highest fullness of force and in the perfect development of its content, in the Pempas, on the other hand, as the indissoluble union of the two potencies required for every generation, then in the Heptas its previously unregulated sway is subordinated to the harmony and the moderating influence of uranian orchestics. It is no longer left to itself and to its own wild drive, but has entered upon the course of the great cosmic order. Applied to Dionysus, the three shows us the lord of all physical life in the perfection of his generative force, the five in his union with Libera, the seven as χορηγὸς ἄστρων and ἀστροχίτων, as leader and king of the great round dance that maintains the movements of the heavenly bodies in never-disturbed harmony.1) The principle of generation and of the eternal motion introduced by it into the realm of matter

It thereby itself becomes the designation of the ἀρχὴ καὶ γένεσις or ἀρχὴ τῆς γενέσεως, and is suited for that very reason quite especially to the representation of the phallic force of an Osiris-Dionysus and to connection with the egg, which is itself designated as ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. If in the Monas the divine force appears as the principle of the world of being, the Trias shows it as the origin of the world of becoming. It is the ἀρχὴ καὶ δύναμις as γόνιμον; it is the material primal force in its direction toward generation. For this reason the Osiris-phallus is necessarily threefold, for this reason Dionysus, too, is threefold, for this reason the whole world of the material gods is in general triplex, that of the female no less than that of the male.2) At the head of things there always stands a threefold ἀρχή, whether

that place is assigned to the female receptive or to the male-active potency. The idea of multiplication through generation leads into the infinite and, strictly speaking, is subject to no limit that could be expressed by any number. Its being consists, indeed, in the infinity of progress, in a never-exhausted multiplication. If now the three is chosen preeminently before every other number to designate such infinity, the ancients base this significance on a particular property of it, and indeed on that which is emphasized by Aristotle right at the beginning of his four books on the structure of the heavens: “Of magnitude, that which extends in one direction is a line; that which extends in two directions, a plane; and that which extends in three, a body,1) and besides these there is no other magnitude, because the ‘three’ is as much as ‘all,’ and ‘thrice’ as much as ‘on all sides.’ For, as the Pythagoreans also say, the All and the Whole are bounded by the three, since in end and middle and beginning lies the number of the All, and end, middle, and beginning make three. In taking from nature, then, its laws, as it were, we apply that number also in the sacred observances relating to the gods.2)

We distribute, moreover, even the linguistic designations in just this way. For ‘two’ we also call ‘both,’ and ‘two men’ also ‘both men.’ But ‘all’ we do not call them; only with three do we pronounce this word for the first time. In these designations, as has been said, we have only followed nature, because nature itself leads to it.” In this passage Aristotle agrees completely with Plutarch as regards the significance of the three. The three, both say, has, besides the limited, purely arithmetical significance, also a second significance, in which it leaves behind every limitation, every number, and passes over into the sense of ‘All,’ ‘Everything,’ ‘Perfect.’ So it appears in the τρισμάκαρες, which means not thrice-blessed, but all-blessed, perfectly blessed. In this, however, Aristotle becomes more instructive than Plutarch, in that he traces the second significance of the three back to nature and a general natural law, thus presenting it not as an improper significance, but rather as an independent, material significance grounded ἐν φύσει. In what this procedure of nature consists, the Stagirite tells us clearly. The three creates the body, which indeed extends in three directions, and besides line, plane, body there is no other configuration. For this reason the three is perfection, the All and Everything. The Pythagoreans arrive at the same result from another side. For they say that to the All belongs the union of end, middle, beginning, and this yields in turn the number three. Accordingly the three appears as a somatic number, which nature itself has made it. In this significance it designates the All, Everything, perfection; in it the number itself becomes perfect, the first odd number the first completed number. In the same significance it unfolds into the triangle, and indeed into that most perfect of all triangles under whose form the Egyptians and the Pythagoreans conceive the nature of the universe, in which the lowest side contains 4 parts, the side standing at right angles to it 3, and the side opposite the right angle 5, and in which, according to the Pythagorean theorem, the squares of the first two taken together have as much area as the square of the last alone.1) In the same significance the triangle appears on that image of the phallic Poseidon whose It is noteworthy that the ter beatus is here placed together precisely with the triplex telete and the expression felix, faustum, salutare.

nature, which as the abiding element in motion towers over the material world and its constant revolution. This property belongs preeminently to the heavenly powers of light, which are enthroned high above the change of tellurian matter, where it does not reach. In this sense the three is so preeminently ascribed to Apollo and Dionysus. In this sense the former is also called Hecatos,1) a designation meant to emphasize the remoteness in place, the summum. In this sense the Flamen Dialis is not to climb beyond the third rung of the ladder; he would otherwise raise himself above the height of the god of light. Now the application of the three in the Bacchic mysteries appears in its higher spiritual significance. It proclaims to the initiate the participation allotted to him in the eternal power of the Lord, to whom he has given himself through initiation. The number three of the eggs especially bears this meaning in itself. It shows the mysteries as the means of pressing through to divinity. The initiate will be raised through death to the completion of the Trias. Thus the number three is the number of salvation, of σωτηρία, as it makes itself known especially also in the proverb: the third helps. It is therefore called the number of the upper, the Olympian gods, while the two belongs to the chthonian powers.2) It passes itself into the significance of light, becomes like light the paternal number, and is called pater.3) Female materiality recedes entirely into the background. Thus the Trias in its highest development designates the perfected paternal luminous nature, the eternal force of creating, in which Dionysus and Apollo appear as the saviors and healers of the human race, as conquerors of tellurism and its transience. In this significance the three is the mystery number, in this significance the triquetra, as it also appears on funerary vessels, e.g. on a bowl of the Vienna Cabinet, is a sign of Bacchic initiation.

The idea of generation and of the motion called forth by it in the material world returns in the five. But here it takes a different direction than with the three. If the Trias shows the ἀρχή as multiplication through generation, then in the Pempas there lies the striving toward connection and mixture. Both odd numbers represent matter to us in its drive toward perfection and self-completion. But they do so from two different sides: the three from the side of perfect unfolding through the All, the five from that of the connection of what is separated, of the fusion of two sexual opposites. The motion of the Trias is thus a multiplicative one, in which the basic number always remains the same; that of the Pempas an additive one, whose nature Aristotle, Metaph. 14, 6, 3, designates as mixture. The former proceeds from the unity of force, the latter from its scission.1) The former develops what is unitary, the latter leads what is separated back to unity. The former is thus itself still a unitary number, the great one, indivisible, and in each of its parts the whole Trias; the latter, by contrast, is a composite number, arisen from the combination of two different magnitudes, which are to be distinguished in it even after the union. The three has no parts, but the five does. The perfection of the two numbers is thus of a wholly different nature: that of the three an outward corporeal representation of the inner perfection contained potentially in force; that of the five one that presupposes the separation that has entered into force, and now represents this as overcome and vanquished. Accordingly the Trias stands nearer to the immaterial Monas in the same relation in which the line departs less from the nature of the point than the plane or the body. With the one the three is akin in that it grasps force, like that, in its inner unity and perfection, distinguishes no sexes in it, and in general does not inquire into its constituents. In the five, on the other hand, the double sexual potentiation of force itself is presupposed, and the starting point is not the Monas but the Duas, not unity and concord but duality and discord. For this very reason the five is a far more material number than the three. Somatic they are indeed both, for both show us force entered into matter and moving matter; but the progress from the unity of force to duality rests on the consideration of the sexual

1) Macrob. Som. Scip. 1, 6, p. 32: ratione scissionis.

[PDF 270]

difference, as the organisms of animal creation show it,1) while the unity of force belongs not to physical corporeality but to a presupposed Monas. The five therefore leads us deeper into the world of appearance than the three. It shows us not only the motion of eternal becoming that prevails in it, of the constant multiplication of the same ἀρχή; it descends yet a stage further into the realm of the world of becoming, and recognizes in force itself a composition of two materially distinct potencies, the male and the female, and consequently also a second law of motion, namely that which strives to overcome that discord and always to unite again what is separated. Thus it comes about that the five is now not only conceived as marriage, but is itself also called φύσις. For it shows us force as it presents itself physically in the world of appearance, namely separated into two corporeal forms, not as it can be conceived before corporeal configuration, without entry into matter. This perfection of the corporeal world of generation the three is unable to represent. In the Trias we see force only multiplying itself, but not splitting itself into bodies of different sexual formation; in the five, on the other hand, this scission is presupposed and canceled through reunion.

The concept of material sexual union emerges in all the accounts of the ancients as the distinguishing mark of the Pempas. Some things on this have already been adduced earlier. In Plutarch’s work de Ei apud Delphos Eustrophus, to whom the development of the mathematical significance of the E is put in the mouth, adds to his manifold instructive remarks on the Pempas c. 8 also the following: “because the five arises from the first male and the first female number, the Pythagoreans, on account of the similarity, called it marriage.” Isis et Osiris 56: “The five is partly like the father, partly like the mother, because it consists of three and two.2)” The same lies in the report cited above from Plato’s Laws, that at wedding celebrations five guests are to be invited, no more, no fewer. The same in the five wax candles of the Cerealian aediles, while the praetors carry only three,3) and in the Quincuncialis ordo in Plin. 17, 78.

Therefore children who have father and mother in common stand in the relation of the five. So Joseph and Benjamin, the sons of Jacob by Rachel. In recognition of this significance it says in Moses 1, 43, 34: “and Joseph had dishes of honor brought from himself to them (his brothers), and the dish of honor of Benjamin was greater than the dishes of honor of them all, fivefold. And they drank, and became drunk with him.” For Jacob’s ten other sons were by three other mothers, Leah, Bilhah, Zilpah (1, 35, 23–25). According to Moses 1, 45, 21 the same Benjamin receives five festal garments. The significance of sexual union lies also at the basis of the five days of the Sacaean festivals,1) of the five classes of the Roman people, which appears in them united like man and wife, of the Censura quinquennalis,2) in particular also of the number five of the Idaean Dactyls, to whom Achilles belongs as Pemptus, and, through the mediation of Hercules Idaeus, of the five-year period of the Olympic games.3) On the monument of Alyattes on the shore of the Gygaean swamp lake, which the Lydian hetaerae had for the most part erected, stood five phallic cones. As many pyramids were shown by the Porsenna tomb at Clusium, and the same number by the still preserved tomb by the road near Albano.4) With the birth of Minerva the Argive-Faliscan Quinquatria are connected.5) They are the festival of the consecration of the trumpets, whose significance for generation and fecundation we have already emphasized above,6) also a matrons’ festival celebrated in spring, of a Saturnalian-natural character.7) Five is therefore preeminently consecrated to the moon, for in the moon the double formation of nature appears in indissoluble hermaphroditic union. The 35, as the highest development of 2 and 3, underlies the number of the Roman tribes, which as the highest limit could not be exceeded, and those 35 children of Rhegium in Pausanias. Like the number of the five classes, it has a purely material significance, comprehending in itself the two potencies of the Roman commonwealth, and thus attaches itself confirmingly to the developed idea of the Pempas. — Once more the basic significance of marriage returns in the following conception: Plutarch Is. et Os. 56: “The Egyptians have in all likelihood imagined the nature of the universe chiefly under the image of the most beautiful of all triangles. So Plato too seems to have made use of this symbol in his books on the State, where he sketches the picture of the married state. This triangle consists of three such sides, where the lowest contains four parts, the one standing at right angles on it three, and the one lying opposite the right angle five, and where the squares of the first two taken together have exactly as much area as the square of the last alone. (4² + 3² = 5².) Here one must imagine the side standing perpendicularly on the base line as the man, the base line itself as the woman, and the one lying between the ends of those two as the child begotten by the two.”1) Here, then, the five appears once more as marriage, namely as the child representing the union of father and mother, in whom the materially separated sexual potencies return ever again to original unity; and from this is explained why the Elean matrons, who otherwise appear in the number sixteen, celebrate their games in every fifth year and weave the splendid Junonian garment in every fifth year.2)

From the basic significance of the five it follows now that this second odd number is preeminently a numerus naturalis and justifies the designation φύσις to a special degree. The union of the two sexes for generation belongs exclusively to physical-animal life, to the domain of purely material existence. For that very reason it becomes, in the number of the fingers, a sign of natural justice; for that very reason it can be attributed to the likewise material censorship, to the transactions of the mancipatio, to the Cerealian aediles in the five cerei, never to the civil praetorship.3) For that very reason it assumes a preeminently

From the material significance of generation there now emerges that significance, appearing in many applications, of the limitation of the material world by the five. If the generating force consists of five parts, which now present themselves as five elements, then what is generated itself cannot possibly exceed the number five. This significance of the five is especially emphasized by the ancients. Most noteworthy on this are the expositions in Plutarch de defectu oraculorum c. 35–37, de Ei apud Delphos c. 7– 16, and in Macrob. Somn. Scip. 1, 6. p. 31. 32 Zeune, Philo, de mundi opificio § 20. For this very reason the number of the elements, too, must be limited to four, so that the fifth place, that of the soul, which is to set the dead body in motion, may remain open. “For the five has as many advantages over the four as the animal has over the lifeless body.”1) Now by the fact that the five limits infinity, it acquires a preeminent kinship with the idea of form, of articulation, and of the harmony lying therein. Infinity is by its nature formless and unregulated. The imparting of form always contains a limitation, and conversely every limitation necessarily contains articulation and form. This may also be put thus: through clothing in a definite number the formlessness of the infinite is overcome. The ancients say to the same effect: the odd number overcomes the even to which it is added. The view on which this rests is set forth with great clarity, precisely for the five, by Plutarch in his work on the decline of the oracles, c. 35: “But now I ask you to consider attentively with me this circumstance also, that of the two highest principles, I mean the one and the indefinite two, the latter is the primal matter of all shapelessness and disorder, and is therefore called infinity;2) the former, however, by its nature defines and limits the empty, groundless, and indeterminate element of infinity, gives it a shape, and brings it about that it can at least in some measure bear and accept the designation proper to sensible things. These principles become visible first in number, or, to speak more properly, multitude is not a number at all unless, like the form to matter, it is added to the indefinite infinity and now more, now less is separated from it. Only then, determined by the one, does every multitude become a number; but if one takes the

one away, the indefinite two confounds everything again and abolishes relation, measure, and limits altogether. Since, then, form is not a destruction of matter but rather imparts shape and order to every subject, both principles must necessarily be present in number, from which the first difference or inequality arises. For the indefinite principle brings forth the even number, the better one, however, the odd. The two is the first even number, and the three the first odd. From these two arises the five, which by its composition is common to both, but with regard to its force is odd. Since the sensible and the corporeal, on account of their composition, are divided into several parts by the might of difference, their number could be neither the first even nor the first odd, but had to be a third, composed of these, so that it might receive its origin from both principles, from the one that generates the even as well as from the one that generates the odd. For it was not possible for the one to be separated from the other, since both have the nature and force of a principle. As soon as both were united with each other, the better principle retained the upper hand over the indefiniteness that divides the corporeal, set limits to it, and, since matter was once divided between the two, placed unity in the middle, to prevent the All from being split into two parts. Thus the multitude of the worlds arose through the difference and inequality of the indefinite; but the force of that which is ever the same and determinate made this multitude odd. The odd, now, is of such a kind that it does not let nature extend further than is good and useful. For were the one pure and unmixed, there would be no division at all in matter; but since the one has been mixed with the dividing force of the two, matter has thereby received division and cutting apart, yet it had to stop there, because the even number was overpowered by the odd.” However one may judge this deduction, the proposition that is to be established by it is clear, and older than the halting explanation. The five imposes limitation on the infinite, form on the formless, articulation on the unarticulated; it checks the unbounded extension of the material world and sets limits to it. It is the five that, by the union of the odd with the even, prevents the division of the All into two halves. It shows us, then, matter in its tendency toward the bringing together of the severed and the opposed, in its inclination toward shaping, delimitation, and a harmonious regulation ever remaining the same. By this very fact it proves itself the most perfect expression of material creation. For it shows us now

[PDF 280]

— 266 —

matter in all its essential properties: in the need for sexual union and for the abolition again of the scission that has set in between man and woman; likewise in its limitation and finitude, in its inseparability from form and articulated shape, and finally in its harmony and conformity to law, which pervades all parts of creation, the heavenly and the tellurian, the divine and the human, the psychic and the corporeal, and in that motion which constitutes the content of life preserves forever the same regularity. By this the whole fullness of the idea may be measured that is contained in the designation of the five as φύσις. The world of material generation has found its fullest expression in the Pempas. The motion and its eternally identical conformity to law, the full naturalness of becoming and passing away, that is the five conceived wholly somatically, and precisely this significance Aristotle attaches to the expression φύσις in the Metaphysics 5, 4, cf. 9, 8. As to this becoming, sublunary world there belongs the constant running back into itself, the eternal return to the point of departure, so the ancients do not fail to bring out this side of the five as well. De Ei apud Delphos 8. “The five is called φύσις inasmuch as, by multiplication with itself, it as it were returns into itself. Just as nature, after receiving and softening the seed grain of wheat, gradually brings forth manifold forms and shapes, whereby she completes the work and at last presents the wheat, so that at the end of the whole business she gives back the beginning, so too the five and the six (2 + 3; 2 × 3), multiplied by themselves, are wont to preserve and reproduce themselves, whereas all other numbers, when they are multiplied, are changed by increase into other numbers. For 6 × 6 is 36, and 5 × 5 is 25. Yet in the six this happens only once, and in a single way, that it makes a square of itself; in the five, on the contrary, it can happen continually in multiplication, and especially in addition with itself, whereby it also produces the ten alternately, so that in this it is like the being that governs the world. — In the same way the conjunction of the five with itself is wont to produce nothing imperfect or alien, but has its determinate alterations, because it produces either itself or the ten, i.e. either something proper to it or something perfect.” On this especially Jo. Lydus de mensib. p. 23 Schow.

But there remains yet another relation of the designation φύσις that deserves particular emphasis. The five belongs to the animal world. It therefore pertains to man only according to his animal part. In other words: as Pempas man appears on the side which

[PDF 281]

— 267 —

he has in common with the animal, not on that which raises him above the animal kingdom. The five is therefore the lunar or psychic stage, which stands midway between the somatic-tellurian stage and the solar stage of the νοῦς. For this reason the creation of the animals begins on the fifth day. The animals have the five senses, which belong to the psychic and not to the spiritual, in common with man, and the designation of this stage of life by the five is expressly emphasized by Philo § 20. As Pemptus, Achilles is not solar but lunar, as he lives psychically united with Helen on the lunar island of Leuke, hence the man of the senses, not the spiritual man. Marriage is five not according to its spiritual but according to its animal conception, as natural sexual union, such as the animals also practice, whose differing sexual formation they share with man. Hence the extramarital mating of the Sacaea, too, is a five, no less than the connubium; indeed the latter is the five only according to its natural side. When the Pempas is therefore designated as φύσις, what is purely human is not included in this, and only the lunar-psychic, which unites all that is animal, is emphasized.

If we now place side by side once more the first two odd numbers, whose relation to the movement of life in the material world we have so far explained, there results a phenomenon that deserves particular emphasis. For we now see the three pass from the sexlessness in which it appeared as Trias into the significance of the male-generative, active natural potency. As part of the five, the three is male; as independent Trias, sexless. This advance in the determination of sex is connected with the fact that the first development of force, which leads to the three, does not undertake an investigation of the components of generation. Only as a result of a second development, which leads to the five, is the sexual formation of the three more precisely fixed; an advance with which a similar one in the cult stones corresponds. For these too originally have no indication of sexuality, and receive a recognizable phallic form only in the progress of religious development. So too the three. Originally sexless, the Trias finds equal application to male and female deities; indeed, insofar as the female-material principle is originally set at the head of things, it appears at first as the basic number of the mother goddesses. But now the relation to the male force is assigned to it just as definitely, and this significance is explained by the contrast with the female two. Eustrophus is very definite on this point. Since all numbers are divided into even and odd, the one, with regard to its force, is common to both. Hence, in addition, it also makes the odd

[PDF 282]

— 268 —

to the even, and the even to the odd, and the two is regarded as the beginning of the even number, the three, however, as that of the odd. By the mingling of both with one another the five is generated, and this one holds in honor with every right, because it arises first from the first numbers, and it is called marriage, on account of the likeness of the even number to woman, of the odd to man.1) For when numbers are divided into equal parts, the even stands wholly apart, and leaves behind in itself, as it were, a space and principle capable of conception; in the division of the odd number, however, something always remains over between the two halves, and to that extent a generative force pertains to it sooner than to the other number; it also retains, when it is mingled with the other, the preeminence always, without ever losing it. For from the two no union ever produces an even number, but always an odd.” This, and what Plutarch has Eustrophus further advance to establish the masculinity of the three and the femininity of the two, may be left aside. The difference of sex between the two forms of number is itself independent of the worth or worthlessness of the explanation. It reveals itself in the Roman custom of giving girls their name on the eighth day, boys on the ninth, likewise in the relation of the odd number to the Olympian gods, of the even to the chthonian, who in this take on the nature of Mother Earth, and in the custom of giving boys three names, girls only two.2) In the Duas the first scission of unity comes forth. It is the principle of separation, of enmity, of discord. It therefore appears now as the representation of the two opposed poles of force, the creative and the annihilating, the dark and the bright side of nature, now again as the expression of sexual scission, and in consequence of this as the image of woman, who stands at the head of visible things just as the two opens the series of numbers. As the expression of scission the two becomes the evil number, which, if left to itself, would bring about a falling apart of the one, or of the unitary All. It is not creative but dissolving, as it also opens the foundation of the wholly divisible numbers. Over against it the three appears as the restoration of unity, accomplished by the Monas, which, joining itself to the two,

brings about indivisibility. In the three the Duas returns to materially developed unity, as the child unites the natures of father and mother and overcomes their separation. Thus the three, over against the two, becomes the good, creative number. It is therefore assigned to the Olympian gods, as the two to the chthonian. It is the Osirian, Bacchic principle over against the Typhonian, which appears in the fable of Ocnus given a female form. Connected with this is the fact that the even number corresponds to the principle of rest, the odd three to that of motion. It is the generative potency to which all κίνησις of the visible world goes back, while the female receptive matter is mirrored in its properties, that of locality, of space, and hence of material rest. For this very reason only the odd numbers are numbers of motion, the even conversely numbers of rest, as the four represents both the dead body and the perfected source of the material All reposing in itself. Thus the two is opposed to the three, the four to the five, the cube to the circle. When the four appears dedicated to the phallic Mercury, the eight to the generating Neptune and to Poseidon’s son Theseus, these two male gods are in such a nature of number still conceived as dominated by matter and as themselves in the motionlessness of tellurism: a conception that receives perfect confirmation from the cube of the picture of Poseidon mentioned above. On the resting cube the triangle that represents the generative and moving force of the phallus is depicted, like the Bacchic triquetra in motion. From this contrast of the even and the odd number the exclusive connection of the latter with the circus games first becomes clear in its whole significance. For since here the motion of the phenomenal world, as it proceeds from the fecundation of matter, is to be represented, it is precisely the generative and moving odd that must predominate in the circus games.

22.

With the first two odd numbers, three and five, the seven is connected. Before we subject it to a closer consideration and seek to establish its significance, it is necessary to preface a remark on the age of its adoption into the circus games. In Dio Cassius 37, 18 there is found, namely, an account that might easily give occasion for doubt. On the occasion of the Jewish custom of hallowing the seventh day, and of the advantage which Pompey drew from it in the siege of Jerusalem, the historian expresses himself as follows: τὸ δὲ δὴ ἐς τοὺς ἀστέρας τοὺς ἑπτά, τοὺς

[PDF 284]

— 270 —

πλανήτας ὠνομασμένους, τὰς ἡμέρας ἀνακεῖσθαι, κατέστη μὲν ὑπ᾽ Αἰγυπτίων, πάρεστι δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ πάντας ἀνθρώπους, οὐ πάλαι ποτέ, ὡς λόγῳ εἰπεῖν, ἀρξάμενον. οἱ γοῦν ἀρχαῖοι Ἕλληνες οὐδαμῇ αὐτὸ (ὅσα γε ἐμὲ εἰδέναι) ἠπίσταντο· ἀλλ᾽ ἐπειδὴ καὶ πάνυ νῦν τοῖς τε ἄλλοις ἅπασι καὶ αὐτοῖς τοῖς Ῥωμαίοις ἐπιχωριάζει, καὶ ἤδη καὶ τοῦτο σφίσι πάτριον τρόπον τινά ἐστι, βραχύ τι περὶ αὐτοῦ διαλεχθῆναι βούλομαι, πῶς τε καὶ τίνα τρόπον οὕτω τέτακται. Here the spread of the Hebdomades over Greece and Rome is placed in a very recent time and traced back to Egypt. Now the passage of Cassiodor 3, 51, communicated earlier, reports that the seven laps of the circus were introduced ad similitudinem hebdomadis reciprocæ, from which the conclusion seems to follow that the application of the number seven to the circus games, their eggs and dolphins, is not original but of later origin. But this conclusion is refuted at once by the fact that Varro in Gellius already emphasizes the septem curricula solemnia; that, further, the seven-stringed lyre of the circensian pompa is named an ancient sacral usage customary in all ceremonies and is traced back to the seven-stringed Orphic lyre itself; that Venus promises septem savia suavia to him who would bring back to her Psyche, the runaway slave, to the metæ murciæ; and that, finally, the number seven appears at Rome, in many applications, as an ancient holy number: in the seven hills, the festival of the Septimontium, the seven pignora imperii, the septemviri epulonum, the sevenfold renewal of the plebeian games, the seven times three tribes, the seven times three shields of Mummius, the observance of the seventh day in the planting of the vine; whence it follows that the sevenfold number of the laps, too, is original and stands wholly independent of the adoption of the Hebdomades as a number of days. What Dio Cassius alone designates as a custom previously unknown in the Occident and come only shortly before his time into general diffusion is the distribution of the seven planets over seven days and the designation of the latter by the names of the former. If this usage is traced by him to Egypt,1) where the number seven holds so high a position,2) Joannes Lydus, on the other hand, goes

If, then, no probative force can be conceded to the account of Dio Cassius for a late introduction of the number seven into the circus games, and no connection at all can be assumed between the designation of days by the names of the heavenly bodies and the sanctity of the number seven in general, then on the other hand Cassiodorus’s expression septem metis certamen omne peragitur ad similitudinem hebdomadis reciprocæ is likewise unable to raise a serious difficulty. By this Hebdomas the number of seven days is not to be understood, and Cassiodorus is by no means to be interpreted as though the seven laps had been introduced after the model of the custom, spread from Egypt, of dividing the week into seven days. Rather the whole context of the passage shows that the Hebdomas or number seven can refer only to the seven planets and the spheres corresponding to them. For Cassiodorus undertakes to demonstrate for the individual parts of the circus games a decidedly uranian-sidereal significance. The seasons, the twelve signs of the heavens, the moon, the sun, the morning star and the first light, the three zones, the rising and the setting receive their determination and representation, and in such surroundings the Hebdomas, too, can Stellung in der Weltgeschichte 5, 198 f. 336; 6, 4 f., Mainardus, Studien über den Zusammenhang der ägyptischen und griechischen Religion, p. 37, 38. have no other relation than the planetary one indicated. In the added word reciproca the nature of the planetary orbits and the corresponding property of the circuits of the circus are emphasized. Both the former and the latter always return to their point of departure, like the waves of the Euripus, which the flood drives forward and the ebb draws back again. So reciprocus stands in Plinius 2, 97: æstus amnis reciproci; 9, 57: amnis reciprocus; Varro L. L. 6, 5: tela reciproca, i.e. such arrows as fly back as they were shot off.

After these preliminary remarks we pass to the discussion of the number seven and its significance itself. Its sanctity is acknowledged by the most diverse authors and is often emphasized in the most emphatic manner. “The seven consecrated to Apollo,” remarks Ammonius in Plutarch on the inscription Ei in the temple at Delphi, “would require more than a day to enumerate all its forces.” No less admiration for it is displayed by Varro in Gellius, Noct. Atticæ 3, 10. In connection with the Mosaic story of creation Philo, in the work on the creation of the world, discusses at length all the distinctions of the Hebdomas, and introduces his account with the words, § 30: τὴν δὲ ἑβδομάδος φύσιν οὐκ οἶδ᾽ εἴ τις ἱκανῶς ἀνυμνῆσαι δύναιτο, παντὸς οὖσαν λόγου κρείττονα. It is to him the holiest of all numbers, and by an etymology current elsewhere as well is traced back to σέβομαι. With the same reverence it is treated by Macrobius, Somn. Scipionis 1, 6. p. 37–46 ed. Zeune, Sat. 2, 4, Censorin Dies nat. 14, Joannes Lydus de mensib. c. 9. p. 25–30 Schow, Lactant. 7, 14, Serv. Ecl. 8, 75, Theod. Prisc. 4, 3, med., Augustin C. For since it did not escape them that Greeks and Romans too paid manifold homage to the number seven, they recognized therein a homage rendered to the divinity of the Mosaic law by the whole rest of the world; indeed, to make the agreement still greater than it really was, even forgery of ancient Greek texts seems not to have been disdained. finitely much else, belongs to the Semitic tribes of the East, and goes back to the primeval times of Asiatic culture and observation of the heavens. This first diffusion over the lands of the ancient world, although perfectly certain, cannot come into consideration here, because it recedes into times of which no report has reached us; it belongs to a general phenomenon, before which men for so long deliberately closed their eyes, namely that Asiatic civilization has become the foundation of all ancient culture. This original diffusion from Asia has no connection with the assumption of a transmission from the Orient to the peoples of Greece and Italy that took place only in historical times. If I maintain the former, I deny the latter, without thereby denying that the scientific treatment and investigation of the number seven by the Greeks and Romans was first called forth by their later acquaintance with the Orient. The use of the number seven is older than its scientific contemplation. — A most remarkable application of the number seven is found in Eustath on Dionys. Pereg. V. 76. If, then, we are compelled to oppose the Jewish authors cited and their accounts called forth by national-religious interest, it must on the other hand be conceded that their statements about the general diffusion

sumption of conscious forgery. Nevertheless I openly confess that precisely this result, from another side, again presents me with the greatest difficulties. How could such forgeries remain unnoticed? Homer, Hesiod, Linus, Callimachus were authors whom at Alexandria men not only read but, for the most part, probably learned by heart; and how do scholars like Clement and Eusebius stand in relation to such a deception? One of two things: either they appear as ignoramuses or as accomplices. Two qualities that both fit the character of their writings poorly. Forgeries were indeed very common in the ancient world, and one has reason to wonder that the present predominantly negative tendency of mind has not yet undertaken a compilation of the numerous testimonies which the works of the ancients offer for literary deceit; but upon Eusebius and Clement such suspicion is cast nowhere. When Varro declares that one should assert nothing with absolute certainty, this principle seems to me, at least in the face of doubts, to have full justification. It is impossible to untie a knot if one does not know how it was tied. This Aristotelian saying holds above all of the question before us, which is still surrounded by so much mysterious obscurity.

of the sacral character of the number seven are in perfect agreement with what has already been adduced of Greek and Roman custom. The sanctity of the number seven is the same among all the peoples of antiquity. In this there is no difference between Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, Jews, Indians. Where they differ from one another is only in the significance that they attached to the Hebdomas in their cult practices. The transfer to the number of days, and the hallowing of every seventh day connected with it, as well as the naming of the days after the planets, is not original with the Romans and Greeks, but a custom that penetrated from outside only late.1) But even this was not without all foothold. On the contrary, among the Hellenes too an application of the seven to the seventh day appears, and indeed one that, like all the Jewish festivals, is brought into connection with the revolution of the moon. The seventh day of the month is consecrated to Apollo, as the eighth to Poseidon.2) The testimonies of the ancients are perfectly definite on this. In Plutarch’s Table Talk 8, 1 Florus says that on Plato’s birthday one must not pass over in silence Carneades, one of the most worthy heads of the Academy. Both, he says, were born at a festival of Apollo: the former at the Thargelia in Athens, the latter during the Carneian festival at Cyrene.3) “The one as well as the other,” he adds, “is celebrated on the seventh day, and you prophets and priests call the god himself, because he was born on this very day, Hebdomagetes (as Valckenaer de Aristobulo 37, p. 115 emends the usual Ἑβδομαγένην). By all these testimonies the sanctity of the number seven and its connection with Apollo, as well as with the seventh day of every month, is raised above all challenge, and at the same time demonstrated in its originality.

23.

Now we have cleared the way to penetrate into a correct understanding of the significance that distinguishes the number seven. If the three showed itself as ἀρχὴ καὶ γένεσις, the five as φύσις and γάμος, so the seven is τελεσφόρος, and this according to the Greek conception as well as the Jewish. Six birth pangs Latona has to endure until in the seventh Apollo can step into the light. Seven times the swans circle the island singing, and before they begin the eighth circuit, the god has come into appearance. With him the work of the mother stands completed. The lord of creation, the great hero of light, crowns the realm which he enters, and even before the seventh day reaches its close, all is perfect. Six days the preparation lasts, the seventh

It is the seventh day on which God completes his work which he has made, and on which he rests from all his work which he made creating. (Moses, Genes. 2, 1, on which passage see Bunsen in the first half of the first volume of his Bibelwerk; the leaf bears no page number.)1) For this reason the seventh day is called by Philo ὁ τοῦ κόσμου γενέσιος or γενέθλιος, καθ᾽ ἣν τὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἔργον τέλειον ἐκ τελείων μερῶν ἀναφανέν.2) Likewise τελεσφόρος, i.e. bringing to maturity and completion. Καλεῖται δὲ ἡ ἑβδομὰς ὑπὸ τῶν κυρίως τοῖς εἰωθόσιν ὀνόμασι χρωμένων καὶ τελεσφόρος, ἐπειδὴ ταύτῃ τελεσφορεῖται τὰ σύμπαντα.3) Philo de septenario: Ἑβδομὰς δ᾽ ἀμιγέστατος, καὶ φῶς (εἰ χρὴ τἀληθὲς εἰπεῖν) ἑξάδος. ἃ γὰρ ἐγέννησεν ἑξάς, ταῦθ᾽ ἑβδομὰς τελεσφορηθέντα ἐπεδείξατο.4) That which is perfected comes into being last. It is there not at the beginning but at the end. Therefore Apollo and creation in their perfected glory cannot come to birth on the first day, but only on the seventh. The development is the same as in the bodily birth of man, in which likewise the seventh month appears as τελεσφόρος. It always proceeds from below upward, from the imperfect to the perfect. In this sense the gods have their birthday festivals, as the Quinquatria have been cited as Minerva’s natale, and as, beside the Ἀπόλλωνος καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος γοναί, others are mentioned: Ἀφροδίτης γοναί, Ζηνὸς γοναί, Ἀθηνᾶς γοναί, Πανὸς γοναί.5) The ancients place the dedication of temples on a line with birth. They are the birthday festival of the god who rules in them. The work itself must come first; the dedicatio is the γενήσιος τοῦ θεοῦ, and as such belongs to the Fasti.6) According to this conception the elapsing of the seventh day is not required. Since the work belongs to the first six, which alone are generative, it suffices, in order to fulfill the destination of the seventh, if it merely dawns, and thus shows the completion, τὸ φῶς τῆς ἑξάδος. Apollo’s birth is complete before the seventh sun sets, before the seventh circuit ends, the seventh song dies away. Moses assigns the completing and the resting to the same day. If, further, the seventh day is decisive in all illnesses and is therefore called κριτικός or κρίσιμος; if the halcyonic brooding days are seven; if in the cycle of seven larger or smaller periods of time all growth, all bodily change, even female purification and death from hunger, attains a definite completion: then here too we see the Hebdomas again as τελεσφόρος, so that the six, as in the Mosaic story of creation, creates and leads toward ripeness what the seven then presents completed in all its parts. The applications emphasized are all the more instructive for the number seven of the circus laps, since they bring the idea of completion into connection with that of motion and of material growth, and belong wholly to the domain of material becoming and passing away. We see from this that the seven, which differs so essentially from the three and the five, nevertheless agrees with these first two odd numbers in this, that, like them, it belongs to the realm of the creation that appears, advancing in eternal motion and eternal growth, and therefore, like them, is a somatic number, existing in things, not outside them.

But here we have arrived at the point where the Hebdomas separates from the Trias and the Pemptas and assumes a nature to which those cannot rise. The seven, within whose limits all things of the tellurian world move and undergo all the changes prescribed to them, is of uranian origin; its first and most prominent manifestation

is an astronomical one. In the sevenfold number of the planets and in the seven spheres in which they complete their course, the motion of the tellurian creation, which follows the same law and measure, is prefigured. From heaven the harmony of the seven has descended into the things of a deeper, more material region. From above it governs the tellurian world, whose motion is guided and harmoniously developed by that of the uranian. “It is impossible that any motion should exist that does not agree with the motion of some star.” “The revolution of the planets brings forth all phenomena.” These utterances of Aristotle (in the Metaphysics 12, 8, 9. 15) contain a primal thought of humanity that wholly governs the mode of contemplation of the ancient world.1) In its highest uranian revelation the seven is now less material than in the tellurian, and indeed less so in the same proportion in which the stars are purer than earthly beings and stand closer to the perfect immateriality of God than the earth does. True, the stars too still belong to the sensually perceptible world, but they have a greater kinship with eternal substance than the tellurian has, to which the world of sensuality surrounding us belongs.2) They are themselves divine bodies, and the science that occupies itself with them is the one best suited to lead the spirit to the unmoved source of all motion, to the Aristotelian primal circle. Between this purely intellectual being and full materiality the stars stand in the middle. More material than the former, less material than the latter, they partake of the nature of both, act by virtue of their materiality upon matter, and indeed with the greater force the nearer their spheres approach the earth, but at the same time, by virtue of their immateriality, lead upward to the highest source of light.3) In the double nature of the stars the number seven too shares, in consequence of its astronomical origin. Without stripping off materiality, it nevertheless penetrates to its farthest boundary, and so mediates the transition from the sensual into the supersensible

Among the seven spheres, in whose orbits the seven planets move, that of the sun stands out as ruling.
