24.

Turning again, enriched by the insight into the higher nature of the number seven, to the circus games, we find that these now for the first time gain their full and highest significance. Governed by the Hebdomas, they assume all those higher relations that rest in the sacred number. The motion of visible creation, which is represented in the swift flight of the teams, appears borne and regulated by the harmonious motion of the stars, the law that governs the tellurian world as an effluence of a higher divine order of things. The earthly becomes a likeness of the heavenly; the spirit, led on from the eternal destruction that governs the former, is carried to the contemplation of a world in which the eternity of the cycle is accompanied by no destruction, whose motion points to a mover, whose harmony and beauty point to a highest source of perfected form. Overcome appears the dark violence of the powers that rule in the depths of the earth. Victorious and ruling, the gods of heavenly light come forth. In their praise the games are celebrated. Everything takes on a uranian relation. In everything the phenomena of the heavenly cosmos are recognized. Cassiodor 3, 51 calls the games of the circus an expression of the star cult,3) and when he assigns to each single act of them a definite relation to the heavenly bodies and their course, he lends expression in this only to the general popular belief. In the seven circuits one recognizes the

image of the revolution of the seven heavenly spheres, whose harmony is repeated in the seven-stringed lyre of the circus pompa and in its tones. The four-horse team is brought into connection with the nature of the sun by virtue of the perfected incorporeality of the tetractys, as already in the triumph of Camillus, while the two-horse team is assigned to the maternal lunar nature, which is related to the disunion of matter. The solar rises above the lunar, so that even the team of mules, as it was originally in use according to the testimony of Festus, has everywhere disappeared, except at the Consualia. For mules stand in a close relation to the moon. Between the ass and the horse, the animal of unregulated material force, and the noble winged steed guided by Athena, the mule occupies an intermediate position, just as the moon, which unites a higher and a lower nature in itself, stands between sun and earth, and the sterility of both seems to have offered a further point of comparison.1) Now, however, natural force is raised to its highest stage. The paternal principle of the sun stands there ruling, and whereas on the tellurian stage Consus appeared in a subordinate position as the πάρεδρος of Murcia, female materiality in the moon now recedes into the background before the greater power of the sun. — If the general solar significance of the number seven is thus to be recognized in the seven circuits, the seven eggs, the seven dolphins, and the seven-stringed lyre, then that side of its nature in which it appears as τελεσφόρος becomes especially important. In this quality it gives the circus games a quite special consecration, the correct conception of which is of the highest importance. We have come to know the solemnity of the great races as funeral games, and have recognized in them the idea of a cult offered to the highest lord of life. Now this double relation to death and life receives its closer determination. As τελεσφόρος, the number seven that rules in the circus shows tellurian life as the time of birth of a higher existence. The completion that it brings lies in the passage to a higher sidereal existence. As, according to Varro in Plutarch Qu. rom. 11,2) the Roman who turns around at his father’s grave connects with this the thought of the elevation of the dead to divinity

so too the completion of the seven circuits expresses the passage of earthly existence to a higher sidereal existence. The life of the body itself takes on the meaning of a time of birth, death that of an act of birth which lets a new being of divine nature come forth. As after six birth pangs Apollo steps into the light in the seventh circuit of the swans, so the sevenfold circling shows that the seven ages of man are themselves only the birth pangs of a divine being. When the seventh circuit begins, the dead man has come into being as Hebdomagetes in the realm of light.1) Thus it is not the sad lot of death of everything that has become that governs the circus games as their final thought; rather, above it there rises, consoling, the certainty of an immortality prepared by it. The words of a fragment of Euripides find their place here: “Who knows, remarks the poet, whether life is not what is called dying, and living death? Unhappy are the living, but nothing torments the dead; their woe has departed.” The same holds for the egg. It is not the downward-going birth into material life, but the upward-leading one, from the material into an immaterial existence, that is recognized as the highest idea in its setting up and its removal. If at birth the genius leads the soul of man into the change of matter and into all its deceit, then death, through the annihilation of the coarse garment, conducts it back to the stars and raises it to a uranian existence in which, united with the heavenly lord of the pure stars, it shares in the glory of the prince of light.2) The hope of such an elevation to sidereal life is expressed in many ways by the initiates on their epitaphs, of which we have already adduced several examples earlier. “I am joined to the heavenly host, for the god was my guide,” we read on that epitaph of the fisherman of Marseilles.3) The same thought is shown by the circus sarcophagi, which we therefore without hesitation

in general, the manifold emphasis on the world of the stars in the tombs, the use of the white color in initiation and in mourning: everything proclaims the thought of a birth of light mediated through the death of the body, in contrast to which tellurian life appears as the time of birth completed according to the law of the number seven. The material primal egg is now, in a higher sense, ἀρχὴ γενέσεως. It shows the birth of man no longer only in its limitation to the narrow bounds of corporeal existence, but as the ground of an eternal existence that develops out of the tellurian, and hence the motion in the stream of the appearing sensual creation as preparation for a participation, removed from the motion of becoming and passing away, in the eternity of the realm of light, whose kingship rests in Apollo and Dionysus.1) In accord with this, uranian significance is ascribed to the egg itself. It stems from heaven, to which it leads its births back. Egg-bearing are the moon women. From heaven falls that egg into the Euphrates which gives the Syrian Aphrodite her origin. In the egg-birth and the egg caps of the Dioscuri the same connection of the stars with the egg emerges, which has often found artistic representation. On the Pompeian paintings we see the starry garment of the female nature mother combined with the representation of the egg on the lower half of the painting. In imitation of this uranian origin we found the egg also in temples, hanging down from the tholus and, like the stars, floating freely in the airy space. Thus it itself partakes of the pure nature of the stars and lies, like them, on the boundary of two worlds, the material one of the earth, the immaterial one of light. Precisely thereby it is able in one act to bestow two births, the tellurian and the sidereal; thereby too it receives its purifying, lustrating force. Thereby it is suited to be the center of the mysteries,2) thereby for connection with

Returning, enriched with these views, to the Pamphili tomb painting, we find that the colors too in which it is executed gain sense and meaning. Blue, red, and yellow are the only ones of which the artist made use.2) The colors named have, all of them, a solar significance. Light and color stand in an inner connection, so that the latter can be called an embodiment of the former. From this it follows,

shows itself in the seven days which the souls spend in the Platonic meadow (Plato Republic 10, 616), in the sevenfold immersion of the head in the lustrating spring in Apuleius, probably also in the seven-day duration of the festival of Demeter in Pausan. 7, 27. 3 and in the septem fabæ in Ovid. F. 2, 574.

The Karlsruhe Museum possesses several of them. To think of a jest is forbidden by the gravity of the tomb. If one wishes to recognize a satirical conception, this may well not contradict the ancient cast of mind. It always lets parody follow at the heels of earnestness. In the description of the great festival games with which Rome celebrated the victory over the Latins, Dionysius Halicarn. 7, p. 352 brings out very definitely the combination of satire with earnestness as a peculiarity of the ancient conception, and in the Laws Plato declares that earnestness without the corresponding jest is incomplete and unintelligible. Just for that reason parodies of the mysteries, such as those in Aristophanes’s Birds and their cosmogony, were not so offensive to the ancients as they might seem to us. Thus satire itself receives a serious character, and this one cannot deny to the said bird-men either. They too have a Bacchic relation to the mysteries. — With the picture of the bird breaking forth from the egg may be compared the flying up of the eagle, as it was represented at Olympia, and to which the simultaneous sinking of the dolphin corresponds. Its symbolic application, moreover, seems to agree admirably with the purely symbolic significance of the Pamphili painting. Among the colors predominantly ascribed to the sun the red takes the first place. In the work on the tenets of the philosophers 3, 5 Plutarch remarks that among the colors of the rainbow the red always takes the first place, and that it comes from the bright and brilliant ray of the sun falling on the raindrops and being refracted in them. In the triumph of Camillus, Livius 5, 23 emphasizes at one and the same time the team of the sun and the complexion of the victor painted with red ocher. From Plutarch Qu. rom. 98 there emerges the custom of the Romans of painting the Capitoline image of Jupiter red. The same color is attested especially for Dionysus. With red ocher the wooden carved image of him at Phelloë in Achaia was painted, and likewise the one at Phigalia in Arcadia.1) According to Macrob. The color of the flammeum is rendered by Plinius 21, 8, 22 and Lucan 3, 361 as luteus color, but this is said of sulphur (Ovid. met. 5, 351), of egg yolk, of the saffron yellow of the early light. If we put together these statements of the ancients about the three colors named, which were applied on the Pamphili tomb painting, a definite relation of them to the fiery nature proper to Dionysus results. If in the red the highest force and purity of light is recognized, then in blue and sulphur yellow a deeper, more material stage of its embodiment is brought to representation. In all three, however, lies the idea of the earthly generation called forth by the sinking of light into matter. The highest degree of this power of light resting in the sun is shown by the red color, which for that very reason was applied, as to Dionysus, so also to other gods of generative natural force, to Priapus,2) to Pan and the Satyrs, and indeed, according to Plutarch3) and Servius Virg. Ecl. 6, 22, was customary for the gods in general. In this meaning red is preeminently the phallic color, the attribute of male-generative natural force at its highest, the solar stage. From this a peculiarity of the Pamphili painting is now explained, the discussion of which we have intentionally put off until here. To indicate the contrast of the dark and the light color in the representation of the three eggs, it is not the two outermost limits of the whole world of color, the absolute contrasts of black and white, that have been chosen, but rather dark red and white. Thereby the alternation of death and life, which that contrast is destined to bring out, is raised from the limits of sensual-material life into a higher domain, and not only the motion of tellurian organisms between the poles of bodily becoming and passing away, but beyond this the transition from somatic to higher existence of light is indicated. It is not the tellurian but the sidereal egg-birth that is to be brought out by the combination of red and white. Red shows the fullness of natural force in the mortal body, white that which out of it in death

develops as the transfiguration of the initiate, who presses through to communion with his god in the realm of the heavenly stars. Whereas the contrast of black and white indicates the alternation of death and life within the limits of the material world, and therefore symbolizes preeminently the law of the lower, unlamented creation, the combination of red and white shows that higher law which governs the connection of earthly existence with the existence that issues from death, and hence of the this-worldly with the otherworldly, of the tellurian with the uranian, and for that very reason has significance only for the human race, the highest part of earthly creation. In its contrast to the white color, whose high significance in the Bacchic mysteries is placed in the clearest light by the practice of the initiates of painting themselves with gypsum, by the corresponding representation on vases, by the mystery relation of the nivea lana, by the custom of white mourning garments, red now acquires the significance of death. At first the color of the highest, most flourishing life, it now becomes the color of destruction. It designates both at once: it is the fullness of force of earthly existence, governed by the law of matter, by destruction. The same double relation is shown by the red color in connection with Typhon. Here too it passes from the meaning of the fullness of life contained in light into that of destruction and of the annihilating side of nature, so that red is now abhorred as the evil Typhonian color, the scorching, not growth-bestowing, glow of the sun, the red ass, the reddish gold, as a formation hateful to the sun god in his higher majesty, exalted above the limits of the world of becoming.1) Thus the division of the three mystery eggs into a red and a white half is the expression of an idea that itself can be described as the spiritualization of the contrast of white and black. In that double coloration the egg appears as the most sublime symbol of the ancient world of the tombs. The conception of the sensual appearance of our bodily life that is expressed in it is well suited to explain and to justify the expressions of confidence and of consolation in which the noblest of the ancients speak of their mysteries. If the Dionysian religion is rooted wholly in matter, it is raised in the mysteries above its limits, and from a representation of the sensually becoming world it becomes the assurance of a higher existence of light prepared by it. It acknowledges that with the sensual world of this life, which

The red funeral garment of the Lacedaemonians in Plut. Instit. Lacon. in Hutt. 8, p. 252.

surrounds us, another, otherworldly one stands in indissoluble connection, and that the eternal becoming and passing away that forms the essence of material life has its purpose not in itself but above itself, so that eternal motion itself may be regarded only as a birth into eternally motionless being. In this combination of becoming with being, of the tellurian world with the uranian, of motion with immutability, of the this-worldly with the otherworldly, of the sensual with the supersensible world lies the highest spiritual content of the ancient nature religion, and this spiritualization is to be credited to it the more highly, the more closely related to matter it itself was. Always in danger of succumbing to the weight of matter and of granting sole existence to the appearances of the this-worldly world, it nevertheless knew how to escape the one-sidedness of those physicists to whom Aristotle in the Metaphysics 4, 5, 22 points out that eternal becoming and passing away, which they made the last and only principle of all things, belongs after all only to the this-worldly sensual world that surrounds us, and that, if of the two spheres, the this-worldly and the otherworldly, one had to be sacrificed, it would obviously have been better to have acquitted this world for the sake of the beyond than to have condemned the beyond along with it for the sake of this world. In all of antiquity there emerges an effort toward the overcoming of matter, toward personal sanctification,1) and toward the spiritualization of a religion material and sensual in its innermost core, which redounds to its credit the more, as it found in the foundations and in all forms and expressions of cult not only no support, but the greatest hindrance and the most dangerous adversary. Such a striving toward dematerialization deserves recognition even when the masses, unable to grasp and hold fast the higher content of the mysteries, remains at the purely sensual basis of the doctrine, and so become ever more completely the prey of matter and its lust. To the Bacchic mystery egg, which in the midst of all this corruption attests the continuance of the belief in a sidereal birth issuing from the decaying tellurian organism, and presents this view through the picture of the Vulcian lecythus as an object of the deepest meditation, there applies what Aristotle remarks in the Metaphysics 12, 9 on the star cult that leads to the contemplation of the highest moving, yet itself unmoved, divine principle. “From the ancients and from hoary antiquity it has been handed down to posterity in the garment of myth that the stars are deities, and that the divine encompasses

Ocnus the Rope Plaiter.

A Tomb Painting.

Plates 1 and 2.

[p. 1]

The subject of the following account is furnished by the picture which we present on the second plate. It comes from the same tomb chamber to which the three mystery eggs belong. Composition and execution show the utmost simplicity. In an open landscape, his back turned to a farmstead consisting of various buildings, a bearded old man sits on a massive block of stone, his bearing expressing repose after work accomplished and a lofty, solemn earnestness. The garment, which veils the head, falls in wide folds down over the back and, as it is gathered together over the legs, leaves the breast, the arms, and both feet bare and uncovered. In the old man’s right hand is a long rope, which an ass, lying at a short distance, gnaws. The left rests idly on the knee. Peace lies over the whole scene. It is the repose of evening that flows around everything, the old man, the animal, the farmstead. A deep silence reigns. The soundlessness of the grave seems to have been transferred into the picture. What heightens the interest of this painting is the peculiar conception in which it sets before our eyes a subject known to us from elsewhere as well. The aged Ocnus appears here not, as elsewhere, wholly given over to his eternally vain labor, but resting from the work. Idly there lie on his lap the hands that are otherwise busied with twisting the rope. Every thought of toil, of penance and punishment has been deliberately removed. The surroundings, too, are quite different from the usual ones. In a peaceful landscape the old man has sat down to rest. The farmstead, shaded by trees, seems to have just been left by its owners. Creation with all its delight surrounds the old man, who is otherwise banished to Hades and the sunless depths of the earth. The great penitents of the underworld would not fit at all the representation which the Pamphili picture shows. The Danaids, Ixion, Sisyphus, Cerberus belong indeed to the laboring Ocnus, but not to the resting one, to the penitent of Hades, not to the dweller in the realm of the sun. A decisive contrast separates the Pamphili representation from the others. Not artistic play, but conscious intention, has abandoned the traditional conception and set itself in opposition to it. The suffering Ocnus has become a liberated one. Indeed, the more closely the concept of punishment and

[PDF 314]

— 302 —

penance was bound up with the rope-plaiting old man, the more energetically the idea of redemption and rest now confronts the beholder. As a rope-plaiting old man Ocnus was known; here he appears idle. The idea of eternally vain labor formed his innermost nature; here repose and freedom from care have fallen to his lot. As an inhabitant of Hades he was often named; here he dwells in the realm of the living. How decisively the idea of liberation and redemption had to stand out against such a background, how emphatically in the light of the contrast the idea of the Pamphili picture reveals itself! Thus the attention is justified which we claim for it. The ethical idea that lies in it constitutes the highest spiritualization of a symbol that by its foundation belongs to the purely physical-material life of creation. I make it the task of this account to investigate the original meaning of the picture of the rope-plaiting Ocnus, and to indicate the various transformations and reshapings that led our hieroglyph from purely physical to ethical, from material to immaterial, abstract meanings. In order to gain a secure foundation for the whole work, a compilation of the surviving monuments and written testimonies is first undertaken here. Among the former, the tomb painting which we present on our plate 1 holds the first place. In the year 1832 there was brought to light at Rome, close to the Porta Latina, now walled up, by Campana, one of those great tomb buildings to which it has been agreed to give the name columbaria. Of the small tomb niches that are found in the interior of the building, the one that contains the Ocnus representation first meets the visitor. It lies directly opposite the stairs by which one descends into the tomb chamber. Its form is that of an aedicula, crowned with frieze and pediment. On both, remains of ancient paintings have been preserved to this day. In the pediment, filling its center to its full height, Chiron appears instructing the boy Achilles in lyre playing. The son of Peleus gives his full attention to the word and example of the wise Centaur. The frieze was adorned with pictures along its whole length, which amounts to over 20 Roman palms. Most of them have vanished. Only the two outermost pieces have been preserved, on the right the Ocnus picture, on the left the three-headed Cerberus. Surrounded by tall reed plants, the bald, bearded old man, wrapped in a sleeved garment, plaits the rope, whose finished end, falling to the ground, is greedily gnawed by a she-ass. In the kneeling posture and the attention of the old man, directed exclusively to his work, lies the expression of the utmost exertion, and in his whole appearance an underworldly

[PDF 315]

— 303 —

character that recalls the gloom of a Charon. The nude, youthfully female figure, who holds fast with her fingertips her garment, lightly swelled by the wind, belongs to a second group, independent of Ocnus and his she-ass. One has hardly any other choice than to assign her to a representation of the myth of the Danaids, although nothing points to participation in the never-ending labor of the youthful penitents. Still slighter is the piece preserved at the left end. The three-headed Cerberus, however, gives us the certainty that the whole frieze contained a continuous representation of Acherontic pictures, and that Ocnus was depicted here in the company of the great penitents of Hades. The first publication of the pictures described took place in the year 1841. To the merit of the discovery Campana added that of publication and explanation. The work appeared under the title: Illustrazione di due sepolcri Romani del secolo di Augusto, scoverti tra la via Latina e l’Appia presso la tomba degli Scipioni, dal Cavalier G. P. Campana, Roma, presso Monaldi 1841. The scenes of the Ocnus tomb are found on the seventh plate. An examination of the original undertaken in the year 1856 has demonstrated the accuracy of Campana’s illustrations, but has also convinced us of the progressive decay of the tomb.1) Concerning the technique of the pictures, the following results from a closer examination. The figures of the frieze, whose height measures five inches, are not painted al fresco, but rather applied as relief on the smooth ground surface. This was saturated with red color, and the surface of the relief figures likewise painted. The colors of the latter, however, have almost completely vanished, so that the stucco for the most part emerges again in its original whiteness. The red ground color of the frieze, on the other hand, is only bleached, not effaced; indeed, in the places that the reliefs covered it still appears with more freshness, and lets the original contour lines of the figures be recognized here and there. — Besides the Campana tomb painting, other monumental representations of the same subject have been preserved. On a marble round altar of the Museo Pio- Clementino Ocnus appears in connection with the Danaids. The reliefs have suffered so much from time that only long contemplation reveals their outlines with full certainty. The illustration is found in Visconti, Museo Pio-Clementino vol. 4, tav. 36, 36ᵃ, the explanation on pp. 264– 269. After Visconti the copy on our plate 2 was made. The representation of the Danaids is so little separated from that of Ocnus that the gnawing she-ass and the first of the Hydrophoroi appear spatially joined. As regards the

1) Thus today of the three heads of the dog only two are still visible.

clothing, the artist of this monument conforms most closely to that of the Pamphili tomb. Ocnus, like the Danaids, is wholly given over to his hopeless labor. The malice of the animal is quite vividly brought out by its position behind the back of the industrious old man, and thereby recalls a festal custom of the Apaturia, at which people called out to one another: the man with the black goatskin stands behind you. — The Vatican round altar was without doubt dedicated to deities of chthonian nature, an ara, not an altare.1) — At the time of Hermolaus Barbarus there seem to have been still other representations of our subject. According to Visconti’s testimony, the author named speaks in his Castigationes Plinianæ 35, 10, 31 of two marble works that are said to have been located at that time on the Capitol and in the Vatican gardens. De Ocno Græci et Latini scriptores fere certatim, sed et in marmore cælatum id argumentum Romæ duobus locis visitur, in Capitolio et Vaticanis hortis. In the complete lack of a more exact description it must remain undecided how far Visconti’s assertion, that the round altar described must be regarded as the one of those works, and O. Jahn’s, that the illustration contained in the Codex Pighianus must be regarded as the other, is well founded. In order to unite all the surviving Ocnus representations, the last-mentioned picture has been repeated on our plate 3 after O. Jahn’s communication. This painting is important in that it brings together more completely than any of the others the torments and terrors of Hades, and ranks the rope-plaiting Ocnus with the great penitents of the underworld, an Ixion, a Sisyphus, and the blood-dripping Danaids. Accordingly the gap in the Campana tomb frieze can be filled with certainty. In the picture of the Codex Pighianus Ocnus appears sitting on a chair or a mensa, the animal behind his back, swallowing the rope into itself. The chiton with the short sleeves and the trousers are wholly peculiar to this picture; for the Campana Ocnus wears a long-sleeved, coarse, and heavy garment, which covers his legs as well and leaves only the feet bare. Of trousers no trace was found on exact examination of the original.

To these monuments a series of written testimonies is joined. It is noteworthy that most of them refer back to artistic representations of Ocnus. Most famous was the Polygnotan picture in the Lesche of Delphi. To the pictures of the underworld belong, from the wider surroundings, Eurynomus, colored like a bluebottle fly, with bared teeth, squatting on the outspread skin of a vulture, and two female figures, the one young in appearance, the other already older, both carrying water in perforated hydriae, with a common inscription to the effect εἶναι σφᾶς τῶν οὐ μεμυημένων. The rest all still carry water, but the old woman’s hydria seems to have been shattered. What has remained in the vessel she pours out into the pithos. We should like to express the opinion that those are meant to be represented who held the Eleusinian ceremonies in contempt. For the elder Hellenes held the Eleusinian initiations to be holier than all the others, in the same proportion in which the gods stand higher than the heroes.1) Beneath the cask Tantalus is depicted, surrounded by all those torments which Homer describes, but besides this terrified by the threatening fall of a stone hovering above his head.” — As a penitent of the underworld Ocnus was further depicted in a painting which Plutarch describes, περὶ εὐθυμίας 14. — — Ὁ ἐν ᾅδου ζωγραφούμενος σχοινοστρόφος ὄνῳ τινὶ παρίησιν ἐπιβοσκομένῳ καταναλίσκειν τὸ πλεκόμενον. A self-contained representation, without connection with Hades, seems to have been contained in the painting mentioned by Pliny 35, 11, 40. Piger qui appellatur Ocnus, spartum torquens quod asellus adrodit. He who first invented the art of fortifying a camp with a rampart, he says, deserves the punishment of Ocnus:

Dignior obliquo funem qui torqueat Ocno,

Aeternusque tuam pascat, aselle, famem. The concept of penance and punishment recurs here too. Indeed, as a crime that is to be atoned for by such eternally vain labor, there appears here that pigritia which is also emphasized in Pliny as the essence of Ocnus (Piger qui appellatur Ocnus). To lie quiet and inactive behind rampart and ditch forms the contrast to that bold, never-resting spirit of enterprise which appears to Propertius as the highest distinction of the general, and which can be opposed, as rectus, adversus, to the timorous obliquus (Ovid. Rem. amor. 121). To this conception the meaning of the word Ocnus gave the readiest handle. Hesitation, delay, scruple, inactivity form its real content. Upon the slothful, then, eternal, never-interrupted, ever-frustrated labor is imposed as punishment. We find the same idea of hesitation and delay again in Menandros περὶ ἐπιδεικτικῶν 1, 2. IX. p. 133. Walz., where as an example of the ὕμνοι πεπλασμένοι is cited: ὥσπερ Σιμωνίδης τὴν αὔριον Δαίμονα κέκληκε, καὶ ἕτεροι Ὄκνον. Ἡ αὔριον and Ὄκνος have their connection in the idea of the sluggard, who always says tomorrow, tomorrow, and bases his conduct on eternal postponement. A character of this kind lent itself particularly to theatrical treatment and representation, and that Ocnus in this sense formed a typical figure we can infer from Pollux 4, 144, where among the ἔκσκευα πρόσωπα are also enumerated Ἀπάτη, Μέθη, Ὄκνος, Φθόνος. This conception deserves particular emphasis because it stands in decisive contrast to the account of Pausanias. For here Ocnus is called not piger but ἀνὴρ φίλεργος,

and compared with the industrious head of the household, whose unwearied diligence a spendthrift wife frustrates. Indeed, even in the idea which the Ionians connect with their proverbial expression, to plait the rope of Ocnus, there lies the idea of diligence and exertion, even if of an exertion that brings in no profit. Two relations of an entirely opposite kind are therefore connected with Ocnus, that of the utmost sloth and that of the most unwearied diligence. We content ourselves at this point with emphasizing the phenomenon as such. The explanation of the connection between the two meanings will be attempted later. Now it is our task to investigate the original meaning of the rope-plaiting Ocnus.

2.

This must by its foundation necessarily be a physical one. The rope-plaiting Ocnus is a symbol of nature. As the history of individual words always begins with the sensual-natural meaning, and only in the further course of development proceeds to abstract, figurative applications, as in religion, in the development of the individual and of humanity generally, the same progress from matter and the material to the psychic and the spiritual is to be observed: so too the symbols in which earliest humanity was accustomed to lay down its views of the nature of the world surrounding it have a purely physical-material fundamental meaning. Nature has taken symbolism, like language, upon its lap. It will be shown later how justified the juxtaposition of language and symbolism is precisely with regard to Ocnus. Between the rope-plaiting old man and the various meanings of the word ὄκνος there obtains so exact a connection that the two form a single series of development, in which the meanings of the word present themselves as the later unfolding of the Ocnus symbol. The explanations and relations with which we have become acquainted in the course of the first section appear as relatively very late interpretations, and as attempts of a time to which the original view, out of which the symbol itself had emerged, was no longer present. Derived and wholly secondary is the idea of Pigritia, tardiness and sloth. No less secondary is the interpretation of the Ionians, the idea of an industrious husband, a spendthrift housewife, of a labor without profit or yield; just as little original are the idea of punishment and penance, and that opposite one of redemption and liberation, as it emerges in the representation of the Pamphili picture. All these ideas

[PDF 320]

— 308 —

deserve consideration, because they were recognized by the ancients in the picture of the rope-plaiting old man: they themselves, however, did not create the symbol, but attached themselves to it afterward. — The original natural meaning emerges from a cult practice of the land of the Nile. Diodorus 1, 97 describes it in the following words: Πολλὰ δὲ καὶ ἄλλα τῶν μεμυθολογημένων διαμένειν παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίοις, τηρουμένης ἔτι τῆς προσηγορίας καὶ τῆς ἐν τῷ πράττειν ἐνεργίας. Ἐν μὲν γὰρ Ἀκανθῶν πόλει πέραν τοῦ Νείλου κατὰ τὴν Λιβύην, ἀπὸ σταδίων ἑκατὸν καὶ εἴκοσι τῆς Μέμφεως, πίθον εἶναι τετρημένον, εἰς ὃν ἱερέων ἑξήκοντα καὶ τριακοσίους καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ὕδωρ φέρειν εἰς αὐτὸν ἐκ τοῦ Νείλου. τήν τε περὶ τὸν Ὄκνον1) μυθοποιΐαν δείκνυσθαι πλησίον κατά τινα πανήγυριν συντελουμένην, πλέκοντος μὲν ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς ἀρχὴν σχοινίου μακράν, πολλῶν δ᾽ ἐκ τῶν ὄπισθεν λυόντων τὸ πλεκόμενον. This passage is all the more important since it belongs to a larger exposition on the connection of Greek and Egyptian religion, and proceeds from the idea that much that Greece knows only as myth continues in its home country, Egypt, as cult practice and forms part of the practice of religion. Should this relation of descent now also seem unreliable, the fact reported by Diodorus itself cannot be called in question. The historical connection may be rated low, or even rejected outright, as the individual opinion of the Greek historian: the cult act of rope plaiting itself is presented as a fact and must be accepted as such. Its meaning cannot be doubtful for a moment. The plaiting of the rope is a symbolic act which recurs not infrequently, and rests on one and the same way of viewing as the spinning and weaving of the great nature mothers. Thus we find Aphrodite weaving, so Penelope,2) so Circe, so Maia Proserpina, so the tres anus textrices of the underworld, who perform their work without looking up;3) spinning the Parcae, spinning Tanaquil-Gaia Caecilia,4) spinning Eileithyia,5) the priestesses of Diana,6) spinning the Syrian goddess,7) and Aphrodite Urania at Athens,

the image of spinning and weaving is represented the activity of the shaping, forming force of nature. The work of the great material primal mothers is compared to artful plaiting and weaving, which gives articulation, symmetrical form, and fineness to raw matter. Fully formed, the organisms all emerge from the lap of the earth. From the mother they have the artful web of the body, which she prepares with unattainable mastery in the dark lap of matter. Therefore Terra deserves above all others the designation dædala, πολυποικίλη κούρη, artifex rerum, therefore the primal mother the name μήτηρ πλαστήνη.1) From this too stems the high significance of the hand, especially its relation to natural generation and to the maternity of matter. As the seat of all skill, it is the hand that gives to raw matter its articulation, and together with life also bestows beautiful form. Demeter’s χειρόμακτρον corresponds, in conception, to the name of the wise, artful Chiron, to the chthonian Ἐκεχειρία (Tzetz. Lycophr. 480) and Χειρογονία, which, itself sprung from the hand, lets everything arise from it again. The artful fingers of the Lydian maiden retain all their skill even after the transformation; Arachne will never cease to present, in the symmetry and fineness of her net, the beauty of the web of nature.2) In the articulation of the hand lies its capacity for the making of the most perfect work. Therefore, according to Suetonius, the cloven hoof by which Caesar’s horse was distinguished counted as a presage of supreme power; therefore, conversely, according to Plutarch, the lack of such articulation counted as a confirmation of the demonic, destructive nature of the ass. If the Greek representations of the Ocnus symbol show the creative principle in as priestess, and be buried beside her; καὶ πέπλων ἄγαλμά σοι θήσουσιν εὐπήνους ὑφάς, ἃς ἂν γυναῖκες ἐν τόκοις ψυχορραγεῖς λείπωσ᾽ ἐν οἴκοις.” Likewise one now sees what significance it has when, according to Euripides in the Ion 1145, Heracles dedicates to Apollo a beautifully woven peplos from the spoil of the Amazons. As the work of the priestesses of Diana he designates quite clearly the nature of their goddess as a weaving nature mother. — Many another trait of ancient myths, which might otherwise seem meaningless, now gains sense, as when in Hygin fab. 66 Periboea finds the exposed Oedipus while washing clothes; when, according to Schol. on Pindar Pyth. 4, 450, Simonides has the Argonauts hold contests for a garment; but especially when, according to Servius on Ecl. 6, 48, the Proetids draw the golden threads out of Juno’s peplos and shun the plow. They are conceived as Amazons, who withdraw from the male aratrum and from natural generation, especially the conjugal kind, but are then led back by the Bacchic Melampus to the destination of their sex. — Apulei. Met. 11, p. 260: Simia pileo textili.

human form, the destroying one under the image of an animal, the significance of the hand emerges still more sharply in this contrast. Creating is skill, annihilating a work of crude force. The former rests in the human hand, the latter is assigned to the demonic animal nature. If, then, in spinning, plaiting, and weaving the activity of the force of nature, its artful forming and shaping, came to representation, one recognized in that labor still other connections with the work of tellurian creation. In the working together of two threads one could recognize the duality of force, and the interpenetration of the two sexual potencies required for every generation. Still more clearly this union emerged in the technique of the loom. The crossing of the threads, their alternate emerging and vanishing,1) seemed to offer a perfectly corresponding image of the eternally continuing labor of the life of nature. When in his underground game of dice with Demeter Rhampsinitus now loses, now wins, and then on his return is presented by the goddess with the golden hand towel, this is itself a representation of the web of nature, in which light and shadow, emerging and vanishing appear as equally necessary factors. When, further, Arachne on her web represents preeminently the amorous adventures of the gods and their mingling with mortal women, when Hephaestus’s net entangles Aphrodite’s bed with Ares, when especially Eileithyia, the good weaver, appears as midwife, lets herself be moved by a cord nine ells long to assist Leto in labor, and receives from the Delian maidens before the wedding spindles wound round with locks of hair as a gift:2) then it is shown most clearly here what erotic significance belongs to the work of weaving and to the crossed interlacing of the threads. As a crossing, as we showed earlier, the meeting of the two sexes is conceived, and by the hieroglyph of the cross sexual mingling was represented in many ways by the ancients, so that not only the Dioscuri, but especially the Ephesian Diana too, frequently carry the cross. On this rests the significance of the Egyptian tau, that of the cloak clasps, — in the myth of Damia and Auxesia and in that of Oedipus, — which women present to the great mothers and goddesses of marriage, on this that of the Dokana and of the sororium tigillum corresponding to them, on this no less the significance of the crossroads and their relation to the chthonian Hecate. In

ὁδούς, an expression that has a double significance for the nature of the Amazons, hostile to men and to love.

like manner meet the geminæ telæ of the woman weaver; from their union arises the spun fabric whose many-colored images represent the variegated carpet of the earth’s surface. In continuation of the same fundamental view, a single word designates the μορίον γυναικεῖον and the weaver’s comb, whose teeth separate the individual threads. Κτείς unites these two meanings, and in the name Circe (from κέρκις, pecten)1) the concepts of weaver and nature mother likewise converge. It is highly probable to me that the ladder-like implement furnished with rungs, which appears on so many initiation vases, derives its mystic meaning from the same foundation. Originally intended for lanificium, it comes, according to Eusebius, to be taken into the Bacchic mysteries, and can have here no other relation than the one that belongs to wool working and weaving in general, the physical-erotic one of mating and of natural generation generally. In this rests, further, the idea of Fatum and πεπρωμένη. Into the web of which every tellurian organism consists, the thread of death is woven as well. Destruction is the supreme natural law, the Fatum of material life, before which even the gods bow, and which they cannot boast of mastering. Thus the web of tellurian creation becomes the spun thread of fate, the thread the bearer of the human lot, Eileithyia, the midwife, the good spinner, the great Moira, who surpasses even Cronus in age.2) The thread appears as saving in its connection with the Dionysian Ariadne-Aphrodite, as destructive the one that breaks in two at the sanctuary of the Erinyes and delivers to the fury of the people those who after the Cylonian disturbance had entrusted themselves to its protection. On this view is founded that which recognizes in the veil of Helen and Eriphyle, no differently than in their necklace, likewise in the poison-soaked garment with which the woman brings destruction to the woman-hating Heracles, the destructive cloth of fate, which dedicates the fillets preeminently to the tombs and the subterranean powers, which ascribes to the uranian deities in their sidereal nature the loom, the bearer of the supreme law of creation written in the stars, and finally presents, as the structure of the world generally, so especially human life as a great web of fate.3) All these conceptions go back to one fundamental view, namely to that first, purely physical idea of spinning and weaving birth-giving mothers. From this now the

rope plaiting at the panegyris of Acanthus its telling significance.1) Here too the creative and shaping labor of nature is symbolically represented. The raw matter receives artificial form in the hands of the rope plaiter. It assumes form and individual formation. From two cords the rope is plaited together. The duality of the sexes, the dualism of the two poles of life, which as twin brothers sweep along the team of creation with unattainable swiftness, comes together into unity and gives to visible creation, to the ὁρατὸς κόσμος, its first origination, its constant renewal and eternal rejuvenation. But this web is still a quite crude one. No fine thread, no artful spun fabric goes forth from the hand of the industrious man. Diodorus speaks of an ἀρχὴ σχοινίου μακρά, Pausanias and others of σχοινίον, θώμιγξ, funis. As a coarse, crudely twisted, mighty rope Ocnus’s spun thread appears on all our monuments communicated in illustration. This peculiarity is anything but indifferent or insignificant. As, according to the oldest, especially the Orphic, theology, a development of matter takes place from the formless to form, from the imperfect to the perfect, from the chaotically crude to ever finer articulation and organization, and only in the course of a cosmic development advancing from below upward does the beautiful come to representation: so too the births of tellurian matter show a sequence of becoming in which a gradual unfolding from the crude to the artful, from the imperfect to the finer articulation becomes noticeable. Upon the simple crude rope follow finer webs, until in the transparent garments interwoven with artful images of the earth and of the world of the gods the highest artistic perfection of the divine hand attains to revelation. In the song in which the Lesbian Leukos sings of Aphrodite’s contest with Athena for the prize in the art of weaving, this difference between the coarse, artless and the fine, delicate spun fabric is represented in a very significant manner. Aphrodite, the primal mother of crude tellurian generation, is unable to attain Pallas’s perfected skill. Her hands show themselves inexperienced in such work. The threads which she produces reach the thickness of those ropes plaited of willow with which the aged shipbuilder fills the interstices of the badly joined beams of his vessel. work arouse Athena’s mockery. With her work unfinished Aphrodite hastens back to Cyprus, and under her influence the work of tellurian generation begins anew. Nonnus, Dionys. 23, 234–334. It is clear that two stages of the creative activity of nature are distinguished here. Aphrodite weaves from the cruder matter of tellurian formations a coarse plaiting, Athena finer garments of perfected beauty. The former belong to the earth, are a likeness of Aphroditean generation of the earth, as it presents itself in the sappy willow thickets of the moist depths; the latter attain a higher stage of perfection, the heavenly. The former remain unfinished, and are dissolved again (l. 255: ἔργον παλίλλυτον), whereas what proceeds from Athena’s hands is perfect. There material fecundation, joined with the pains of birth, lies at the foundation of the work (ll. 295. 306. 328.). On Pallas’s side is purely Olympian existence, free from all material desire (ll. 287–295), free from the pains of birth, as the goddess herself knows only one father, her Zeus. In this whole representation the significance of the rope plaiting emerges quite clearly. Aphrodite’s work resembles an artless rope. In connection with the primal mothers of tellurian generation the rope becomes the representation of material birth, a symbol of the fertility of the earth, a symbol of the chthonian formations put together out of the coarse matter of the earth. In such a significance it could with equal right be ascribed to all primal mothers of Aphrodite’s kind and nature. If these are instead mostly represented as weaving, there is nevertheless by no means any lack of examples of the rope as attribute. Key and rope we see in the hands of a three-formed Hecate,1) whose illustration Causseus communicates in the Museum romanum sectio secunda tav. 20–22. Both symbols find their explanation and justification in Hecate’s well-known tellurian maternal nature, through which she enters into the closest relation to birth, care of children, and every material blessing, and into the most intimate connection with Artemis, Eileithyia, and Hestia.2) The pairing of key and rope in the hands of the same figure is well founded. Though results of two different views, they are nevertheless designations of the same property, namely the maternity proved in the fruitful opening of the female womb. In this sense more than one of the material primal mothers bears the key. So, besides the nymph in Pausanias 5, 20, 1, also Artemis, from whom the expression κληδουχεῖν has passed to the

priestess placed on a level with her.1) So Eileithyia,2) so Athena.3) All of this primarily in that material sense according to which Ovid F. 4, 87 understands the month name Aprilis from the opening of the lap of the earth. In the same significance the key is also ascribed to Janus and to Hades, to Pluto, who dispenses wealth from the lap of the earth. When Pausanias 5, 20, 1 seeks to justify the connection of the key with Pluto by saying that it is indeed this god who locks the underworld, this explanation belongs to the series of many similar ones which believed they could replace by external connections the fundamental views of the earliest time, which had become unclear. The same reproach applies to those among the moderns who also for Hecate’s connection with rope and key take refuge in similar combinations of ideas. Thus Causseus wishes to recognize in both attributes the expression of the gloomy relation to death of that terrible goddess, and Gerhard § 568 “properly underworldly symbols.” Funes quoque ad pœnas infernales referuntur, clavemque optime comitantur, siquidem, quod ligatum est et clausum, effugere haud facile potest. How far this conception is from the true significance of the rope symbol is shown by its comparison with the view of the ancients, developed above, of nature mothers plaiting, spinning, weaving. Rope and key do indeed have a predominantly chthonian and, if one deems the expression suitable in spite of its double sense, essentially underworldly relation. But this shows us the life of nature first of all in its serene aspect, namely that directed to birth, fertility, and the flourishing of the generation of the earth. In the rope is represented the plaiting, shaping activity of the great Mother Earth; the idea of a strictly ruling fate, leading everything that has come to be to destruction, joins as a necessary complement to that first idea of the mother, and shows the life-giving potency of nature also in the light of the great Moira, who weaves into the web of every earthly existence the thread of death.4)

3.

doubt. We may regard it as completely assured that in that hieroglyph the creative and shaping activity of material force found its expression. Thereby an inconspicuous detail of the Campana picture attains great significance. The illustration given on plate 1 shows that the old man performs his never-ending labor in the midst of tall-shooting swamp plants. One might recognize in this detail an allusion to the swampy depths of the Acherontic stream. For Ocnus is, after all, associated on that tomb frieze with the great sufferers of the underworld, and thus himself represented as an inhabitant of the terror-filled Hades. In the Lesche at Delphi, indeed, Polygnotus, according to Pausan. 10, 28, 1, had sought to make the Acheron recognizable likewise by the reed thicket shooting up abundantly from its muddy waters,1) and by the shadow fish. But with this the significance of that accessory for the representation of Ocnus is not yet exhausted. For this, the proximity of the subterranean muddy depths and their swamp vegetation has quite special importance. It shows us the material from which the rope is plaited, and in this way brings the crude plaiting of the rope into a necessary inner connection with the lowest stage of natural generation. Pausanias calls the plaited thing σχοινίον, Pliny spartum. Σχοινίον is a rope plaited from the σχοῖνος (ὁ and ἡ). Σχοῖνος itself bears the epithet ἐλεία. Dioscorides Περὶ ὕλης ἰατρικῆς 4, 52 Περὶ σχοίνου ἐλείας divides the whole genus into two main kinds: the one ὀξύσχοινος, which runs to a point at the top, the other ὁλόσχοινος, fleshier and thicker than the former. As the corresponding Latin name for the whole genus Dioscorides gives Juncus marinus. The working of this Juncus into ropes is attested by Pliny 19, 2, 19: Junco Græcos ad funis usos, nomini credamus, quo herbam eam appellant, oxyschœnon, holoschœnon. As σχοῖνος and σχοινίον belong together, so they stand beside each other on the tomb painting. — The material and the work made from it are embraced in a single glance. Indeed, in the Latin word Juncus a further relation of the two objects shows itself. The jungere in which the work of the rope-plaiting Ocnus consists has given the swamp plant its name. Juncus is derived from jungere. The view out of which this linguistic connection has arisen rests, now, not on the fact that Juncus is vinciendo jungendoque utilis; still less on the fact that excellent rope work can be made from it. Rather it is the conception of the activity of nature itself that gave to the σχοῖνος ἐλεία the name

painting τὰ ἕλη. Imag. 1, 9.

juncus. To this the Ocnus symbol bears witness, to this the general assumption of plaiting, spinning, weaving powers of nature. As the old man produces the rope by plaiting together and joining two cords, so the swamp plant has come into being through an activity of nature conceived in like manner. The expression Juncus rests on the same conception which has found its artistic and pictorial representation in the rope-plaiting old man, and which recurs also in ἄνθη τὰ πλεκτά in Aeschylus, Persians 719. — Instead of σχοινίον Pliny uses spartum. This word too designates not only the rope but equally the material from which it is made. Spartum occurs as the name of a rush-like reed plant. Dioscorides 4, 158 gives a description which corresponds particularly to the appearance of the plant on our tomb painting: θάμνος φέρων ῥάβδους μακράς, ἀφύλλους, στερεάς, δυστραύστους. Pliny 19, 2, 7 devotes to spartum a detailed description. Herba et hæc sponte nascens et quæ non queat seri juncusque proprie aridi soli, uni terræ dato vitio; namque id malum telluris est, nec aliud ibi seri aut nasci potest. Its use came into practice first among the Carthaginians. Spain supplied it in excellent quality. The Romans followed the example of the Carthaginians.1) The expression spartum too deserves attention. It rests on σπείρειν, just as much as Σπαρτοί, sporium and spurii, Spercheios, Spermo, the name of the Lydian adulterer. But what connection of ideas links spartum and σπείρειν? Have we not just learned from Pliny’s statement that the kind of juncus called spartum belongs to those plants that are not sown, that shoot up out of the earth without man’s contribution, ultro, injussa, ἄσπαρτα, expressions by which Virgil distinguishes this lower stage of the generation of the earth from the laborata Ceres.2) Are plants that sprout freely without plow and without sowing supposed to be named sparta from σπείρειν? The surprising element that lies in this may already have been removed by individual hints laid down in the first treatise. In the reed cult of the Ioxids we recognized the connection of swamp generation with the exclusive emergence of motherhood.3) The sexual mingling of the two great natural potencies, to which rushes and reed thickets owe their origin, is that hetaeric mating in which the fruit knows only a mother, whereas the active male potency, as an individually indeterminate sower, has its activity conceived quite generally as σπείρειν. Swamp generation

itself appeared to us as the prototype of human hetaerism, the illegitimately begotten being conceived in many ways by analogy with swamp plants. The name Spurius and Σπαρτός, which designates one begotten by an unknown sower, can accordingly be used of swamp plants as of human beings, and of every ultronea creatio generally. By this connection of ideas the concept of σπείρειν can very suitably be applied to the wild reed thicket, and raised to the foundation of the designation spartum. What is expressed by it is the hetaeric character of the sexual union taking place in the depths of the swamp. Spartum and Σπαρτοί are named according to the same conception, and Spurii join them both. An external connection is wholly lacking among the objects linked by these three words. What have Spartoi, illegitimate sons of the mother, and reed plants in common? Can three things be conceived from which every kinship is absent in an equal degree? Externally, to be sure, no one can think of a juxtaposition. But etymological kinships rest very often on relations lying much deeper. In the present case it is the fundamental view of the nature of tellurian generation which brings the most heterogeneous things closer together and has guided the formation of the word. We shall soon find occasion to give still further elaboration to the idea developed. For the Ocnus conception it becomes instructive and consequential in more than one respect. — As one sought to explain the connection of juncus with jungere quite externally, so too the connection of spartum with σπείρω has been mediated in the most arbitrary manner, for lack of deeper insight. Hardouin on Pliny conceives the matter thus: Spartum a σπείρω, non qua serere significat, quia spartum non seritur, sed qua conserere, innectere, quia nectendis funibus maxime inservit. To such sham explanations a science arrives that never takes pains to approach the world of ancient thought itself.

4.

If we now bring the relation just developed of the rope-plaiting Ocnus to swamp and swamp plants into connection with the significance, established earlier, of the rope and of the plaiting work, the symbol of nature which was represented pictorially every year before the whole people at the festival assembly at Acanthus gains an ever more telling meaning. The idea that recognizes in the industrious old man a symbol of the creative force of nature now receives a more exact determination. The stage of tellurian generation to which the Ocnus symbol primarily corresponds is not that of the laborata Ceres, but the lower

[PDF 331]

— 319 —

vegetation mediated by no human assistance, as it flourishes most luxuriantly in moist lowlands, above all in swamp countries. If agriculture appears as a higher development of the human race, and Demeter’s golden fruit as the noblest yield of the maternal lap of the earth, the reed and reed thicket of the swamp nevertheless have special significance in that in them the work of natural generation presents itself to the human eye in its full independence and originality. When in Nonnus 11, 370 f., in a beautiful description, Calamus, son of Maeander, and Carpus contend for the victory, and Carpus carries it off at last, when Atalanta, daughter of Schoeneus, the rush man, the Schœneia virgo, is deprived of the victor’s wreath by the magic of the golden apples and becomes the prey of Hippomenes:1) so in these two myths the triumph of the agricultural life, which conditions all higher culture, over the lower stage of generation, of conjugal union over the maiden’s Amazonism, given over to merely hetaeric sexual mingling, is represented in the most beautiful way; the significance of swamp life and of the independent vegetation of the earth for the ancient nature religion nevertheless remains standing beside it in its full importance. It lies in the entirely independent activity of the great material force, which keeps all human participation at a distance and, without anything being plowed, sown, or reaped, in an eternal cycle performs by itself the work of generation, increase, and continued preservation. In the spectacle which swamp life offered to the astonished gaze of the first humanity, the whole omnipotence of tellurian creation stepped forth. No seed has fecundated the maternal womb of the earth, no plow opened the furrow. Out of its own force matter sends up, perfectly formed, into the light of day what it prepares in the dark depth. The stalks grow, attain their highest development, age, die off, and are replaced by newly shooting ones, for which the same cycle of development is in store. The prototype of all earthly life seemed to be placed before the eyes in this, as Hippocrat. Diæt. 1, 5 compares plants and human beings. In the vegetation of the swamp and in its eternal cycle was revealed the law to which the world of animals and of humans is also subject. The same origination from the maternal womb of matter, the same return into its darkness, the same preservation of the eternal youth of the race through the eternal dying away of the individual. This rich fullness of thought is what the ancient world has laid down in the image of Ocnus eternally plaiting his rope from swamp plants. How much the

physical nature of the Nile land had to promote precisely this conception and the symbolism that issued from it is obvious. Under the influence of those phenomena to which Egypt owes its existence and all its fertility,1) there took shape there that view which sees in the chthonian waters the bearer of the phallic force, in the earth the female receptive matter, and in the union of the two, as the annual inundation brings it about, the act of generative sexual mingling.2) The testimonies of the ancients are so numerous that we content ourselves with singling out a few. On Virgil’s words Speluncisque lacus clausos (G. 4, 364) Servius remarks: Hæc autem non sunt per poeticam licentiam dicta, sed ex Aegyptiis tracta sunt sacris: nam certis diebus in sacris Nili, pueri, de sacris parentibus nati, a sacerdotibus Nymphis dabantur: qui cum adolevissent, redditi narrabant lucos esse sub terris, et immensam aquam omnia continentem, ex qua cuncta procreantur. Unde est illud secundum Thaleta: Oceanumque patrem rerum.3) The same tracing back of the Ionian doctrine to Egyptian belief is met with in Plutarch, de Placit. phil. 1, 3, and de Iside et Osiride 34. The priests, we read here, maintain that Homer as well as Thales took over from the Egyptians the principle that water is the origin and beginning of all things, for Oceanus is Osiris and Tethys is Isis, who nourishes and sustains all things. Dionysus, it is said, is called Hyes by the Greeks, as the lord of the moist nature, who coincides with Osiris. Instead of Osiris, Hellanicus writes Hysiris, a designation which, according to Reiske, is doubtless derived from ὕεις or ὑγρεύς, and which certainly also stems from the Egyptian priests.4) Accordingly the Nile in its fecundating force appears as itself the physical foundation of Osiris (c. 33). Its waves roll along with them the generative phallus of the male god (c. 17),5) just as on the Mannheim bronze figure the Ionian Poseidon is represented as phallic and is designated as Ἀρχὴ τῶν πάντων.

As Osiris is recognized in the river Nile, so Isis is recognized in that part of the land which is fecundated by the overflowing waters (c. 30, 53).1) In the union of the two lies the act of tellurian mating, which is completed when the moisture has been taken up into the womb of matter and has vanished. In imitation of this natural process the priests mix earth with water in a golden casket; at Acanthus, too, they pour out the waves of the Nile every day from 360 urns into a perforated vessel (Diodor. 1, 97), a cult act which symbolically represents the filling and fecundation of the womb of the earth with the generative liquid, and so corresponds in idea entirely to the myth of Iphimedea’s love for Poseidon and the use she made of the waves of the sea.2) If in these views tellurian water appears as the principle of creation, so that even the power of the sun enters into a relation of subordination and dependence to it,3) and, according to Cicero, de nat. deorum 3, 16, the whole world of the gods itself issues from the river, then, in a consistent development of the idea, the swamp mud is raised to be the seat and bearer of all earthly fertility. In the swamp mud appears that intimate union of earth and water which also gives to the moist sealing earth, such as the potter’s daughter offers to Neleus, the significance of the fecundation of woman by man. The ancients stress the high significance of the muddy waters in many ways. Philostratus, in the Life of Apollonius 6, 6, traces the high veneration of the Nile back to the fact that the Egyptians regard it as a mixture of water and earth. Cf. 6, 23. The Indus shares the same nature with the Nile, 6, 1; 2, 18. Like it, it inundates the land every year, carries earth along with it, produces similar animals and plants, and appears as the cause of every blessing of the earth, so that when it begins to rise, bulls and black horses are sacrificed to it and a golden grain measure is delivered over to its floods. 2, 19. Heliodorus 9, 9 follows Philostratus’s statement. In his description of the Νειλῶα, which sets out the view of the Egyptians with particular clarity, special weight is laid on the intimate union of the moist and the dry element realized in that river. A no less noteworthy parallel to the mud-covered Nile god is furnished by the cycle of myths of the Elean Alpheus, so closely related to Egyptian views, whose name recurs in the Plautine eques Aleus as well as in Altis, and which, by its kinship with alere and ἄλφιτα, yields, like Almo, the sense of nourishing stream and explains the name of the people Alfaterni. Artemis, pursued by the god inflamed with love, smears her face, and those of the nymphs accompanying her, with mud, and so knows how to deceive the god who leads the nocturnal round dance with her. Here the Earth Mother, so closely akin to swamp and moist lowlands, appears as the representation of the mud formed by the stream, which bears within it the germ of all generation. Therefore she shares with Alpheus the honor of the same altar.3) As the bearer of material force the fecundating river itself appears as Zeus. In February the ash of the Prytaneum is mixed with water from the Alpheus, and with the mass of mud thus produced the altar of the highest god is smeared. Paus. 5, 13, 5. Therefore Alpheus is united with the highest Zeus by the bond of the closest kinship and everywhere set at his side. Pausan. 5, 34, 1. The river forms the physical foundation of the highest god, who thereby takes on wholly the nature of a Zeus-Achelous. Herein is revealed the most complete agreement of the Nile religion and the Alpheus religion. Like the Elean, so the Egyptian river is identified with Zeus. Ἀναλογεῖ γὰρ τοῖς τοῦ Διὸς ὄμβροις τὸ τοῦ Νείλου ὕδωρ· καὶ ὥσπερ ἀντίστροφόν τινα τοῦτον (τὸν Νεῖλον) τῷ Διὶ εἶναι. To the same thought Heliodorus 9, 9 gives the following expression: θεοπλαστοῦσι τὸν Νεῖλον Αἰγύπτιοι, καὶ κρειττόνων τὸν μέγιστον ἄγουσιν, ἀντίμιμον οὐρανοῦ τὸν ποταμὸν σεμνηγοροῦντες, οἷα δὴ δίχα νεφώσεων καὶ ὑετῶν ἀερίων τὴν ἀρουμένην αὐτοῖς ἄρδοντος, καὶ εἰς ἔτος ἀεὶ τεταγμένως ἐπομβρίζοντος. The same expression, ἀντίμιμον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ γεγονότα τὸν Νεῖλον, is used by Philo, vita Moysis 3, p. 682, and by Apuleius in the Hermes Trismegistus p. 90 Elmenhorst: Aegyptus imago cæli. The fundamental idea is clear. For Egypt tellurian water has the same significance as, for other regions of the earth, the liquid streaming from heaven. The fecundating force rests there in the river, not in the downpours of the rain; it has a thoroughly chthonian, not a uranian, foundation. The ancients not infrequently bring out this circumstance. In the work on the face that appears in the disk of the moon, 26, Plutarch has Theon say: Elsewhere trees and fruits are nourished by rain, but in the region of Thebes and Syene the soil drinks no rainwater, only such as comes out of the earth, whereby the expressions φυσίζωον and γονιμώτατον ὕδωρ1) and the attribute of the cornucopia from which a child emerges receive their pregnant meaning. For religion this purely Poseidonian character of the male generating element, which comes to the fore in the name Eridanus, is of great significance. As the Egyptian religion attaches itself closely to the natural character of the land, so that Cicero’s remark, that the oldest mythologies contain the expression not so much of the gods as of the physical phenomena (non tam Deorum quam rerum natura cognoscitur), has its particular significance precisely for the Nile land, so too the chthonian origin of the fecundating moisture was bound to contribute much to the dominion of that tellurism which finds expression in the idea of an origination of all things, even of the sun and the gods, from the moist element, and in the placing first of the swamp mud as the bearer of all generation from the earth. It is a further representation of the same natural phenomenon when the god celebrated at the Νειλῶα is conceived as androgynous and surrounded with all those cult practices which have their origin in the conceptions of a hermaphroditic divine nature. Eudocia violar. p. 305. v. Νεῖλος uses the expression ἀνδρογύνων τιμαί; her description of the sexual excesses is confirmed by Herod. 2, 90, and by numerous reports which Jablonski, Pars 2, p. 170–174, brings together. 5.

Having thus recognized the divine nature which the Nile land ascribes to the river mud, we find the religious significance of the swamp plants follows quite of itself. While the mystery of generation is accomplished unnoticed by man in the dark depths of the moist deep, the secret is betrayed by the reeds shooting up. In the swamp plants, which grow up from the depths of the mud into the light, the fruit of matter conceiving in self-embrace comes before the gaze of mortals. In what is generated the causal force appears embodied. The plant is the appearing deity. It is held itself to be holy and inviolable. This connection of thought emerges very definitely in individual features of Egyptian mythology. By the lotus wreath which Osiris leaves behind with Nephthys, whom he has fecundated, Isis recognizes the adultery of her consort. So Plutarch, on Isis and Osiris 15. In a later passage (c. 38) the same idea receives the following expression: the mating of Osiris with Nephthys is discovered by the plants that shoot up from it. Among these belongs the Melilotum, which was lost and left behind by Osiris, and so betrayed to Typhon the infidelity of his wife. While Isis therefore bore a legitimate son, Nephthys brought into the world a bastard, the dog-headed Anubis. The view of nature that expresses itself in this is easy to decipher. What we have to note especially in it is the equation of swamp generation with

hetaeric sexual union. The two stand on the same line. Thereby what was adduced above to explain the expression spartum receives its full confirmation. The births of Nephthys are designated as bastards. They are illegitimate generations which have only a mother, but were sown by an unknown father, and are therefore called σπαρτοί or spurii. From Heliodorus’s Aethiopica 3, 14 we cited above, p. 191, the myth of Homer’s illegitimate birth in support of the same conception. As the lotus shooting up betrays the deed of Nephthys, so one recognizes from the long hair that covers the poet’s thigh the infidelity of his mother. Hair and swamp plant are set equal to one another. The likeness of the two lies precisely in that peculiarity in which the ancient religion recognizes the particular holiness of swamp plants. By the mere force of matter, without any human intervention, the hair, like the lotus, comes forth into the light from birth-giving matter, a generation of the moisture that pervades the human body, and consequently a seat of force, as with Samson, Nisus, Pterelaus,1) and therefore to rivers, the bearers of the phallic nature, a particularly welcome gift. The name of Isis-hair, which the ancients gave to a species of plant,2) thus rests not merely on a comparison clinging to the surface of the appearance, but rather on a deeper idea of nature, whose expression we recognize also in the shearing of the hair of the priests of Isis, in Rhea of Hierapolis, in the lock of Harpocrates,3) and in the practice of certain African tribes of shaving bare the left side of the head. From the hair of free Thracian women the Erythraeans plaited that rope with whose aid the ship carrying the Tyrian Heracles was drawn victoriously into the harbor of their city. The details which Pausan. 7, 5, 3 reports about this myth are the more noteworthy for us because they throw light on the religious significance of the rope plaited of women’s hair that was still preserved in Pausanias’s time in the temple of Heracles at Erythrae. The offering of women’s hair ornament to Heracles stands on the same line as that which attaches to the service of Venus Calva, of Hera and Isis, and of the Hyperborean-Delian Apollo.4) To the great powers of natural generation the fairest product of it is brought as sacrifice. that Phormio, to whom the god announces in a dream the demand for the offering of hair, is assigned to the class of fishermen, who win their livelihood from the sea. The conception of the hair as the seat of force shows itself in the fact that the god’s boat, which would yield to no human exertion, followed without resistance the pull of the women’s hair. If the relation to natural generation is thus not to be mistaken,1) on the other hand the hetaeric stage of the same also emerges clearly, so that the equation of hair and swamp plants is confirmed everywhere. From woman Aphrodite demands the sacrifice of chastity. Exclusive conjugal union is hateful to the goddess of all erotic impulse, the φιλομειδής, who pervades matter. To reconcile her with marriage, a temporary practice of hetaerism is made a religious duty for woman. The surrender of the Babylonian women is described to us in detail by Herodotus, and similar views emerge in similar practices of European tribes. In times of threatening servitude the women of Locri, according to the testimony of Justin, have recourse to the vow of hetaerism. Through extramarital sexual union they seek to win the protection and favor of the hetaeric nature mother. But the place of this highest of all female sacrifices is sometimes taken by others. Thus hetaeric girls are offered to the Corinthian Aphrodite, so that the duty may be discharged through them. The offering of hair by women attaches to this. It appears as the equivalent of female chastity. Thus the Roman women, to escape Gallic servitude, offer their hair ornament to Venus. The highest danger demands the heaviest gift. The matrons of Locri vow their bodies, the Roman matrons their hair. Both correspond in the same way to the hetaeric nature of Aphrodite.2) The offering of hair by the Thracian girls at Erythrae has no other meaning. The Ionian matrons refuse it, the Thracian women, on the other hand, offer it gladly. Pausanias stresses that the women from Thrace, although of free birth, had nevertheless sustained their lives in Ionian land by servile labor. Who does not recognize here the fundamental idea explained above, in § 16, in its context, according to which the powers of material natural generation are regarded also as the bearers and promoters of freedom and equality among men? Dionysus and Aphrodite bring elevation and a better lot to the serving classes of the people. So in the Erythraean myth Heracles to the Thracian slave women, who reward him for it with the offering of their hair. To the natural

freedom of purely material life corresponds the equally natural yield of the human head. Phormio, too, to whom the god has revealed his will in a dream, is assigned to the lowest stratum of the population. The blindness with which he was formerly afflicted now departs from him. As Helen avenged herself on Stesichorus by inflicting the same,1) so Heracles rewards the pious fisherman by the restoration of his sight. All these features unite in the fundamental idea of the generative and healing natural force, whose symbolic representation is the wonder-working rope plaited of women’s hair in the temple at Erythrae. We now recognize how exactly this attaches itself to the rope of Ocnus. Both rest on the conception of a plaiting divinity of nature that bears within it all the force of tellurian generation. The material of which the fabric consists is the free gift of matter, whose primal force alone brings it forth: there the plant of the swamp, here the hair. Through this we are also introduced to the understanding of a phenomenon which Babylonian hetaerism presents. With a rope around the head the Babylonian women sit in the enclosed space, awaiting their being led away. It has its ground in the relation of the rope plaited of swamp plants to hetaeric sexual mingling, which in the same way governs both the lower and the higher domain in which Aphrodite holds sway.

6.

The preceding remarks attached themselves to the significance of the lotus as hetaeric swamp generation. The holiness which the Egyptian religion ascribes to this water plant is heightened by many natural properties and relations. The first foundation of it, however, is the swamp nature of the Nymphaea, which the Nile mud brings forth out of itself, and whose annual
