being has also climbed to its highest stage of purity, as in the wise Chiron the Dionysian centaur puts on perfected Apollonian luminous nature. Now the meaning of the representation in the pediment of the Roman tomb, and its relation to that on the lower-lying frieze, is presented in all its fullness and beauty. The antithesis appears moving through its simplicity and depth. Below, the dark abyss of Acheron filled with reeds; above, the eternal clarity of the realm of light. There the idea of death and destruction, here that of life. There penance and torment, here the prospect of the reward of a blessed existence. Below, purposeless life and vain toil; above, higher striving with the prospect of the fairest reward. Below, tellurism with all its terrors; above, the Apollonian height of light with all its calming clarity. What overcomes the terrors of Tartarus is represented by Chiron’s Apollonian cithara. If we beheld there the hopeless future of uninitiated human beings given over to a purely material life, then Achilles, listening to the instruction of the wise teacher, shows what is able to surround death with better hopes and to break the dark power of the tellurian forces. Chiron stands beside the penitents as the higher resolution, in contrast to them, just as in the Pamphili tomb Niobe’s grief is set in parallel with the deliverance of Prometheus.1) The tones of anguish of those who suffer have found their resolution in the harmonious sounds of the heavenly lyre. In the representation of Hades and its torments we recognize, then, the intention of setting the benefit of the initiations emphatically before the eyes, and of making visible in a picture the so often repeated doctrine of the ancients about their blessing. The sight of so many hopelessly penitent souls is meant to recommend the choice of the higher life, as the mysteries demand it, as the better portion. With this intention the torments of Tartarus were depicted by the ancients no less frequently than the fire-torment of the damned is in Italy today.2)

Tales of terror avail

To exalt the glory of the heavenly ones; forgetting them, you

Slay your husband, co-begetter of noble children.1) Not without struggle is the palm granted to man. Initiation alone does not lead him to participation in the changeless existence of the heavenly ones. Should the thief Pataecion be dearer to the immortals because he was initiated than Epaminondas, the uninitiated?2) Achilles shows in what way this question was answered by the ancients. Only through the excellence of his life does he press through to that bliss which is prepared for him on the sea-washed, shining lunar island in eternal spring. For since it had been prophesied to the son of Peleus that if he slew Hector he would die, but if not, would reach old age at the hearth of his home, he chose the former, and preferred not only to avenge Patroclus but to die after the dying man.3) Chiron’s teachings are the commandments that everyone must fulfill, Achilles’ example that which everyone must imitate. Promethean suffering must be steadfastly endured if the much-tried man is at last to find admission with Heracles into the company of the immortals. “Great, and by no means slight, is the struggle whether one becomes good or bad; all guilt is the chooser’s, god himself guiltless.”4) Achilles has wholly the Promethean nature. Among the ancients he even bore this name itself.5) And he is Prometheus not only according to his physical foundation, not only as the bearer of the united force of fire and water, in which, as a shining lightning flash, he cleaves the moist aether, enters into the closest relation to bronzework and to Euboean Chalcis, and in the Cretan name Pemptus ranges himself with the Idaean Dactyl-Corybantes;6) he is so also in the spiritual relation, as the bold bearer of the spiritual spark, which he knows how to preserve through all the struggles of life, and which through his untiring wrestling and enduring he at last leads to victory. Thereby he has become, like Heracles, the spiritual redeemer of the human race and has risen higher than Chiron himself, who, struck on the foot by the poisoned arrow, falls in Heracles’ stead, as Menoeceus for the Cadmean-Erechthid line, as the last great sacrifice to the victoriously overcome tellurism. Over his father Peleus, too, he has raised himself.

To him all good fortune comes through the favor of the gods. As εὐδαίμων θεῶν γάμβρος he gathers in a long life a fullness of goods, as Il. 9, 393 f., Hesiod in the Epitalium Pelei et Thetidis (Tzetz. Prol. in Lycophr. p. 261) present it. Neither Acastus nor the ravening beasts of Pelion can do anything against him. Achilles, on the contrary, has won everything himself, and has preferred the multa vita to the longa. Always to be the first and to strive ahead of the others, that is the watchword of a race whose late scion weeps over the multitude of worlds because he has not yet subdued even one. Precisely in this significance Achilles reveals his highest Samothracian mystery nature, by virtue of which he also possesses the power of expiation and ranges himself with the saving Corybantes, the lyre-playing Dactyls.1) In this he enters the world of the tombs, in this he appears on the pediment of the Roman columbarium as the great conqueror of Hades and its terrors, as the embodiment of the mystery idea in its highest perfection.

23.

According to the conception developed, the two pictures of the Campana aedicula appear as the representation of two stages of life, a lower one without the benefit of initiation, and a higher one, to which the initiations grant those better hopes that are realized in a future life. The same contrast takes on yet another shape. It coincides with the difference between the material-tellurian and the immaterial-solar stage of religion. The former belongs to a lower, the latter to a purer conception of the divine nature revealed in the life of nature; the former to a more original, the latter to a more developed degree of formation. The religious development of the human race follows the same law that reveals itself in the development of the individual. It proceeds from below upward, from the material to the psychic and the spiritual, from the formless to form, from the impure to the pure, from darkness to light. According to the oldest Orphic conception2) there takes place an ever more perfect presentation of divinity, and in the

Thus an ascent from matter to the immaterial, from the φύσις ἐν γενέσει (10, 3) to the world of immaterial being, which 5, 18 at the end is compared to a ladder. ever greater perfection of the created, the creative principle too comes to revelation in ever-growing beauty. Like that stepped pyramid joined to so many funerary monuments, the religious development of our race builds itself up on the broad base of the purely material conception in such a way that, in gradual elevation out of matter, it strives ever more heavenward. Tellurism with its materiality yields to the higher solar principle, the chthonian conception of force to the recognition of its uranian nature. Above the Poseidonian-Plutonian rises the Apollonian principle of light. Over against this, the former appears not only as a more impure and lower stage of divinity; it also often takes on the meaning of a demonic power hostile to man, which can be turned again to blessing for the mortal only through its subordination under the new, higher law of light. Thus the bloody law of the Erinyes has yielded to Apollo’s atoning divinity and in the end been reconciled. Tellurism with all its dark violence has bowed before the higher heavenly law of light of the Pythian, and subordinated its older claims to those of the new god. In a similar position Ocnus, too, and the Danaids, and everything that belongs to the tellurism of the draconteum genus, fall back. If all these figures banish the generative force of nature into the dark depths of the moist matter of the earth, then above them Apollo rises in the purer incorporeality of heavenly light. Over against him those appear as conquered powers, whose Delphic connection is destined to glorify the power and glory of the victorious god. To Apollo are traced back Oedipus and the destruction of the Sphinx completed through him, and likewise the overcoming of the dark, hopeless existence of the dragon seed. Through him Orestes escapes the pursuit of the Erinyes, and the law of fatherhood is led to victory over the bloody one of the maternal earth law. To his sanctuary, as to that of the Gaditan Heracles, woman may not approach. With his principle of light the predominance of maternal matter is incompatible. If the Danaids nevertheless find admission into the Delphic Lesche, they are meant here to set off still more brilliantly the benefit of the Apollonian nature, which brought destruction to that dark time of hopeless tellurism. The same idea is joined with all those pictures which Polygnotus emphasis that the Egyptian religion indeed has a physical foundation, but that it was the effort of the priests to lead from it to the immaterial divinity, as fire always flames upward toward heaven. 5, 11, 12. p. 214–216. The contrast of heavenly being and of tellurian becoming, caught in constant flux, is developed very beautifully 10, 5, p. 291, the ψυχῆς κάθαρσις as the last goal of religion 10, 7, p. 293.

transferred from the Greek world of Hades into the Delphic hall. Above them the beneficent, purer nature of the Pythian god shines forth all the brighter. Ocnus and the she-ass take up over against him the same position that is assigned to them in the Roman tomb by their subordination to Chiron’s lyre playing. The sight of them shows the victorious power of the Pythian, who rescued the human race from the cheerlessness of earlier views, such as the Sphinx represents and Silenus laments, and raised its gaze from the figures of suffering in subterranean spaces to the calm clarity of his eternally youthful, changeless heavenly being.1) In connection with Ocnus the ass, too, now appears as an animal hateful to the god of light and banished to Hades. Formerly the joy and delight of the Hyperborean, it is now little agreeable to the purer nature to which the Delphian has risen. Belonging wholly to the phallic nature of tellurian matter and bearing within it its unregulated sensual lust, the ass now represents the nature of impure matter, hostile to Apollonian purity. It is the negation of everything that initiation gives and demands of man. With this significance it forms the center of the mystery tale presented by Apuleius. It appears here as the embodiment of the purely sensual life, of all the errors and sufferings into which that life leads. With the reception of the initiations the animal form vanishes. Risen from the chrysalis of matter, man recognizes his beauty and the conditions of an untroubled happiness. To the nature of the ass the initiations form so deep a contrast that the proverb Asinus mysteria vehens can represent, in this sense too, the incompatibility of the two things.2)

24.

If we have thus recognized in the picture of the Delphic Lesche the same idea that dominates the contrast of the penitent Ocnus and the Apollonian Achilles on the aedicula of the Roman tomb, then it will now be an easy task to appreciate, in its occasion and significance, the particular turn that the artist of the Pamphili columbarium gave to the representation of Ocnus. In the departure from the other representations, as writers and monuments alike show them to us, lies the particular interest of the painting communicated on our Plate 2. It surprises through the resting posture

— 410 —

that it lends the old man. Given up here is that labor of rope plaiting which we found to be the most essential feature of the Ocnus representation. The deep rest to which the old man abandons himself brings out quite deliberately the contrast with the traditional conception. It has received in the reclining posture of the animal a no less conscious continuation. Vanished from the surroundings are all those penitents of the underworld who lead the beholder into the terrors of Hades. As Ocnus himself by his inactivity excludes every thought of torment and punishment, so too the landscape, in whose midst he has settled down, breathes only rest and peace. The stillness of the evening seems to have lured the old man out before his farmstead. Here he rests from the labor of the day, and grants the animal, which shared his rural toils, the play with the rope. Thus the Delphic model is wholly given up, and everything deliberately turned to its opposite. What idea could have determined the painter to this procedure? It would be impossible to find any explanation or justification for it if we were to take our departure from the natural-symbolic meaning of the Ocnus picture. For this, the act of rope plaiting is so indispensable that rather everything else could be given up, if only it found its expression. Thereby we are compelled to betake ourselves to an entirely different field of explanation, and to bear in mind the meaning that Ocnus assumed in relation to the mysteries. Now everything receives a satisfying solution. The idea of the Pamphili picture appears in all its beauty. By the simplest means a turn of ideas is brought forth such as would be unattainable for written expression in equal brevity and concise clarity. Out of the penitent Ocnus the liberated Ocnus has come. Where the idea of punishment and eternal torment reigned, rest steps forth, and an equally eternal peace. If the former is the lot of the uninitiated, the latter forms the hope of the initiated. Both parts of the great contrast lie here united in one representation, whereas the picture of the Campana tomb brings them to representation separately. The resting Ocnus arouses at one stroke two ideas: that of the lot of the uninitiated, and that of the liberation which initiation brings. The curse of profane life and the blessing of the life consecrated to god is the double language of a single pictorial expression. In this turn the identification of the deceased with the image of Ocnus has its occasion and its justification. The bearded old man shows us the initiate himself. The figure has the same double reference as the whole representation. It calls before the soul at once the mythological Ocnus and the owner, nameless to us, of that farmstead which he left in dying, and sets before the eyes, for the former, the final liberation from his torment, for the latter the

[PDF 423]

— 411 —

beginning of eternal rest, for both the victorious force of the higher mystery powers that overcome the terrors of death. That is the last form that the natural symbol of the rope-plaiting old man has assumed. From a representation of tellurian life, and of the law that governs it, it has at last become the symbol of the highest stage of human existence. At first wholly restricted to the material cycle, it now leads the gaze beyond its limits into the realm of the life that begins with bodily destruction. At first the expression of the world of becoming, it is now the image of the world of being. At first akin to the idea of transience, it now shows the hope of a changeless future, which may calmly and indifferently leave the coarse tissue of the body to the gnawing she-ass. With religion itself Ocnus has risen from the dark swamp depths into the heights of light. He designates the lowest and the highest that the earth offers, the whole weakness and the whole greatness of the perishable creature, man’s subjection to the law of death and his sublimity above it. The higher existence prevails. Two worlds stand side by side, a sensual and a supersensible. Foolish it would be, as Aristotle expresses it in the Metaphysics, to sacrifice the latter to the former.

For all is affliction on earth

And we find no rest from our sufferings.

Whatever is sweeter than this life, that conceals

Enveloping night from the gaze of mortals.

We love only this with such ardent longing,

Because here on earth it shines upon us,

And the other no one ever explored.1)

If in this way the two poles between which the riddle of all earthly existence moves come into immediate contact, then the distances in time and space too seem wholly removed. The Ocnus symbol, native to the land of the Nile, returns at Delphi and in Roman tombs, and while its origin is shrouded in the darkness of primeval states, it accompanies the ancient peoples down to those times to which, on the lonely high seas, the destruction of the great Pan was proclaimed,2) and above the hut the new star appeared.

Tiberius had the event investigated. It falls, then, in the time when the new light appeared, and attests in any case how deeply the conviction of the decay of the old religion, and of the beginning of a new age of the world, was rooted.

[PDF 424]

— 412 —

That is what lends the ancient world of the tombs so high a significance and makes its contemplation so fruitful on every side: that in it the inner unity of the ancient world of thought emerges more strikingly and tangibly than elsewhere, and hastening centuries are unable to carry through their transforming power. Unchanging as death is the world of the tomb. Every innovation passes it by without a trace. The oldest symbols and conceptions of mankind find here their last but secure place of refuge. A wealth of spiritual treasures lies hidden in the necropolises. The earth gives back what it received thousands of years ago. Most of it is still unintelligible; the study of the ancient world of the tombs has hardly been introduced at all into the circle of our research. If the present attempts have been able to awaken even only an intimation of its importance and significance, then surprising successes will not be long in coming, the tomb finds of our century will be recognized in their true value, and Sigalion, like the mute son of Croesus, will at last find his speech.

Appendix.

The recently published catalogue of the Museo Campana furnishes some important contributions to the points discussed especially in our first treatise. A belated mention of them forms the main content of this Appendix. The color combination of white and black, like that of white and purple-red, whose meaning and relation to the Bacchic divine nature we have explained, appears on a larger number of funerary vases of decidedly Dionysian relation. I call attention to a few. Classe I, serie quarta, vassellame dipinto, n. 335 shows as its main scene Bacchus and a satyr. Tutto il fondo è coronato di tralci di vite con grappoli. Nel collo è un frigio di edera con corimbi e nell’ orlo sono alternati i colori nero e giallo. — No. 391: Il collo ha un frigio di edera e la parte superiore di esso è ornata di dadi alternati gialli e neri. Cf. further 396, 400. — Classe I, serie 9, 10. Sala G. 55. — No. 302 of the same section shows, beside the Bacchic eyes, a wreath of alternating white and black color. I, ser. 9, Sala H, 273: corona formata di una larga tenia a color bianco e purpureo. In this opposition purple-red takes on the significance of life and divinity, as black belongs to death and to the idea of transience. Lucian, veræ hist. 3, 12. For the combination of white and purple-red a new conception results from this. It shows in its two components the idea of apotheosis, and is thereby preeminently suited to indicate the divine nature with which Asia clothed its kings. The antithesis then lies in the degree of purity of the two colors. If red bears the materiality of the sun as a generative natural potency, then in the white color the principle of light appears in its highest purity and complete immateriality. We can call the former the Dionysian, the latter the Apollonian stage of the luminous nature. Nothing stands in the way of attributing the same meaning to the red-and-white double color of the Bacchic egg. The antithesis of a higher and a lower stage of being, which we emphasized above, p. 294 f., as the fundamental meaning of that color combination, remains in this conception too wholly

Above, p. 128. — Finally the significant and especially frequent emergence of the number five deserves attention. Thus we meet five warriors, five dancing figures, five horses’ heads, five Ionic columns, five winged sphinxes, five flowers, and objects of various kinds too are combined with one another in the number five. For the application of the Pentas, moreover, Alexandria quinquevertex is significant. The city of the united cult of Sarapis and Isis (Arr. 3, 1.) is the city of five hills, as Rome is septemplex. Above, p. 281. Jul. Val. Res gestæ Al. M. 1, 18. 29. To the five hills correspond the first five letters of the alphabet, which bear the walls of the newly founded city and its five quarters (Philo in Flaccum ed. Here we have again the E of Delphi as the highest number, and this agrees with the Pythian oracle, which calls the god of Sinope Apollo- Father. Tacit. Ann. 4, 83. 84. It is the Hyperborean god in whose stations the Pontus city is also listed. His phallic nature is matched by the Dionysian Pentas, not by the perfect seven of uranian-spiritual nature. — With the number five Alexander’s ἑτεροφθαλμία, corresponding to the ἑτερημερία of the Dioscuri, whom Alexander also especially venerated (Itinerar Al. 90), stands in connection. of the phallic formation with old age (p. 367), Origenes, philosophum. ed. Miller p. 144. On the myrtle wreath in the mysteries Tzetzes on Cass. v. 1328, p. 1006 Müller. — Wieseler treats the Delphic omphalos in the Ann. dell’ Instit. 1857, p. 160–180. This essay gives me occasion for some remarks. The omphalos is referred in it to Hestia and called the symbol of this deity. Two concessions lie in this. First, the Delphic omphalos is detached from Apollo, and moreover the female connection with the material primal motherhood is substituted for the male bond with the θεὸς πατρῷος. These two propositions agree completely with the conception carried out above, pp. 106–108. The divergence of our views begins only with the further question, in what personification we are to conceive that motherhood? W. decides for Hestia, the above consideration for Themis- Gaea; to the latter opinion I still hold fast. It is supported by various circumstances already indicated by Ulrichs, Reisen und Forschungen in Griechenland, pp. 78, 93. Orestes’ atonement at the omphalos, over which the blood of the piglet runs off, shows that the latter belongs to the earth, for through the matricide the earth is violated, hence the atonement and consequently the omphalus can apply only to the earth. Further, it is said in Euripides, Ion 5, Plato, Republic 4, 5, that, seated on the omphalos, Apollo proclaims his oracles; since now, according to Aeschylus’s Eumenides, the oracle passed from Themis-Gaea to the male god, the conclusion is inescapable that the Apollonian omphalos must originally have belonged to the great mother Themis-Gaea, and not to Hestia. Third, the expression Γῆς ὀμφαλός is entirely constant, as the passages in Ulrichs, p. 93, n. 61 show, Ἑστίας ὀμφαλός without example, although Hestia’s connection with Delphi cannot be denied, but is rather as firmly established for the Pythian sanctuary as for any other whatever. Hymn. Hom. in Vest. et Mercur. 1. 3. Γῆς ὀμφαλός is, to be sure, finally used as a designation of the center of the earth. But this meaning presupposes an older one, from which it was derived. In the original sense Γῆς ὀμφαλός designated the cult image of Mother Earth. From this the idea of the center of the earth develops in the following way. In motherhood lies the generative significance. The female κτείς belongs in this sense to the symbols of the Themis mysteries. But the generative forms the center, and takes this place locally as well. Varro. L. L. 7, p. 303 Spengel: Neque hic locus est terrarum medius, neque noster umbilicus est hominis medius. Itaque pingitur qui vocatur ἡ χθὼν Πυθαγόρα, ut media cœli ac terræ linea ducatur infra umbilicum per id quo discernitur, homo mas an femina sit, ubi ortus humanus similis ut in mundo; ubi enim omnia nascuntur in medio, quod terra mundi

[PDF 431]

— 419 —

media. For the same reason the mundus lies in the center of a newly founded city. It is therefore the maternal κτείς that lends the omphalos the significance of the center of the earth. In consequence of this the Aphroditean omphalos at Paphos too becomes the center of the earth. Hesych. Γῆς ὀμφαλός. Cf. Tacit. H. 2, 3. Serv. Aen. 1, 724. Themis-Gaea as well as Aphrodite have the earth as their material foundation. Their κτείς appears accordingly as the center of the whole surface of the earth, and hence the omphalos erected to the γυναικεῖον μόριον appears as μεσόμφαλος γῆς. In the face of these phenomena the connection of the Delphic omphalos with Themis-Gaea, the original oracle mother, can admit of no doubt. But the egg form too, which is so wholly certain on the Ruvo vase painting, now appears fully justified. To the birth-giving μόριον γυναικεῖον nothing corresponds so perfectly as the egg, which can be designated not only as uterus expositus, but lets birth issue from itself just as the tellurian organisms spring from the womb of the earth. Since now the maternal womb of the earth not only cherishes birth and sends it to the light, but finally takes it back again into itself, and through the cooperation of both activities keeps generation eternally young, the egg must unite in itself the same double significance of giving and taking, of life and death. In fact the Delphic stone is regarded as the burial place of the dragon Pytho. The omphalos itself is held to be his μνῆμα, as Pythonos βουνός or tumulus. Hesych. Τοξίου βουνός. Varro L. L. 7, p. 303. Sp. Alexandria too, the urbs quinquevertex, has its Draconis sepulcrum or heroon, to which the omphalos form may be ascribed all the more surely since Zeus Ammonius, the Alexander-father, possessed an omphalos especially venerated by the matrons. Curtius 4, 31. Strabo 6, 1, 1. In the connection of the dragon Pytho with the omphalos there shows itself again that union of serpent and egg which we have demonstrated in a larger number of cases. To the examples named on p. 131 ff. others may still be added. An Etruscan tomb relief in Raoul-Rochette, monum. inédits pl. 26, fig. 2 shows, set up on the altar, the egg girdled by the serpent, in the same form in which we found it on the coin in Lajard, culte de Vénus pl. 14. H, 11. The sacrifice of Iphigenia, which forms the subject of the whole representation, leaves no doubt that the serpent egg was here conceived in the same relation to Artemis as the Delphic one to Themis-Gaea, others to a Cerealian Fortuna and to Hygieia. Set up in a sacred shrine the ovum anguinum appears again on a second Etruscan ash chest in Gori, Mus. Etrusc. 1, tav. 170. Müller, Archeol. § 361, 5, to which Wieseler, p. 167 adds as a third example a sarcophagus in

[PDF 432]

— 420 —

Wicar, tableaux statues etc. de la gallerie de Florence et du palais Pitti T. 4, pl. 11. On the walls of Pompeian houses Mercury is joined with the serpent-entwined half-egg. Avellino, bulletino Napoletano, serie antica 1, p. 11. On others we see it surrounded by the two Lares, as at Delphi by the two eagles (Museo Borbon. T. 9, tav. 20), on the denarii of the gens Eppia and Rubria by a double herm. Eckhel, Doctr. T. 5, p. 296. Wieseler, p. 168. It is the dualism of force according to its creative and its destructive, its light and its night side that occasions and governs the connection of these double figures with the maternal omphalos. Thus Leda’s sons issue from the mother egg in the number two, as two dragons too appear as serpent guardians. In face of this fundamental idea the personal identification of the mother goddess to whom the serpent-girdled omphalos of the Pompeian wall paintings cited belongs is of only secondary importance. Besides Vesta, other rival claimants can be thought of (above, p. 149), if we do not prefer to attribute to the symbol an independent validity. If the maternal relation of the Delphic omphalos is indisputable, its elevation to Apollonian significance must not on that account be denied. In the transfer of the oracle from Themis-Gaea to the paternal god there is revealed the progress from the principate of the maternal-material principle to that of the male principle of light. The former appears as a surmounted stage of religion, which finds recognition only in a subordinate position. Above the tellurism of the omphalos there now rises up the founder of a higher law, the power of light Apollo. His power derives from the highest Zeus (Aen. 3, 251. Serv. Aen. 1, 24. Aesch. Eum. 19. Soph. Oed. R. 151), not from the primal mother Themis, although he too in body sprang from woman and is significantly reminded of this his maternal origin by the Erinyes in Aeschylus. Hence the omphalos appears at times beneath the feet of the god. Müller, Archeol. § 361. 5. But in union with Apollo it now itself passes over into Apollonian nature. The mark of the primal mother Earth becomes the attribute of the male god, like the Ammonian omphalos of Zeus. The originally maternal relation of the Delphic cult stone is not the only one. If Wieseler presents it in the light of such exclusiveness, he is no less in error than those who, over the paternal connection with Apollo and Zeus, leave the maternal one with the earth out of consideration. Only by virtue of its Apollonian nature can the omphalos grant the matricide Orestes protection against the pursuit of the Erinyes. The female connection of the egg recedes here wholly into the background. Lifted out of the law of the earth, it is now clothed with Apollonian luminous nature, the eagle pair

[PDF 433]

— 421 —

itself receives a higher Jovian relation. Schol. Pind. Pyth. 4, 6. Schol. Soph. Oed. R. 475. Schol. Eurip. Or. 330. Schol. Luc. Saltat. 38. In this elevation the omphalos is no longer the material primal egg that gives birth to all births into the world of becoming, but that which mediates the passage out of this into that of being. It cannot be mistaken that on the two Etruscan tomb reliefs this latter higher relation has been attributed to the serpent-entwined egg. Iphigenia’s sacrifice, as a sarcophagus picture, can have no other meaning than to serve as pictorial expression for those higher mystery hopes which open to the initiate after death the prospect of nova salutis curricula. One day sees the maiden die and gaze out toward the light. Mourned as lost by her mother, she has yet, saved, penetrated to a higher union. Death itself mediates birth into a more divine existence. What we call life is death, what we call dying is life. The same idea lies in the egg, which just thereby enters into the closest union with the sacrifice of Agamemnon’s daughter. Symbol and myth join and illumine each other. The archaeological explanation has been content, with the sarcophagus picture just discussed as well, to establish the subject of the representation itself, and to assign to all details the right relation to the whole. The sepulchral meaning has been left wholly out of the question, and the archaeological task therefore only half solved. In that the monuments were detached from their original destination, the funerary significance receded wholly into the background. Art archaeology has thereby deprived itself of the best fruits of its labor. A field still little trodden opens before research. The difficulty of the task must not deter us. The goal is set, the prize worth every effort.

The egg on three Pompeian wall paintings. — Its relation to Fortuna and to the guardian pair of serpents. — Position of the male-generative to the female-receptive principle. Antithesis of rest and motion. § 13. pp. 159–165. Demonstration of the same antithesis in the concepts sanctum — sacrum, ἱερόν — ὅσιον. § 14. pp. 165–184. Connection of law with the female natural principle and with the motherhood of matter. — Demonstration of this connection for a series of mother goddesses, especially for Isis, Dea Syria, Aphrodite. — Significance of the hand, the fingers, the dice, the left and the right side. § 15. pp. 184–200. Continuation of the consideration of law in its connection with the female natural principle. — Law as material natural law. — Jus naturale of the Aphroditean stage of nature. In particular of libertas as law of material life, of the hylic gods, of the Dionysian religion. § 16. pp. 200–216. Continuation of the consideration of the maternal principle of law. — Law as Cerealian law. — Its connection with Ceres, Demeter, Moneta, Bona Dea. — Nature of praetorian and aedilician law. § 17. pp. 216–220. Continuation of the consideration of the maternal principle of law. Gynecocracy presented in its fundamental features and in contrast to the potestas of the Roman father and to the state imperium. § 18. pp. 221–228. The eggs of the circus. Elucidation of their connection with the significance of the games. Cassiodor, Var. 3, 51. § 19. pp. 228–243. Continued. — The sanctuaries and the cults of the circus in their connection with the significance of the eggs. Especially of the connection of the games with water and with funeral rites. — Significance of their representation on the sarcophagi. § 20. pp. 243–254. Continuation of the consideration of the circus games. — In particular the odd numbers prevailing in them: three, five, seven. Elucidation of the number three. — Application of the result obtained to the Pamphili tomb painting. § 21. pp. 255–269. Continuation of the consideration of the circus numbers. Significance of the number five. — Application to the funerary scene. § 22. pp. 269–278. Continuation of the consideration of the circus numbers. The antiquity of the introduction of the Hebdomas into the circus games. — Its sanctity, its connection with Apollo, its application to the celebration of the day.

[PDF 437]

— 425 —

§ 23. pp. 278–287. Continuation of the consideration of the circus numbers. — Development of the Hebdomas in its various meanings. § 24. pp. 287–292. Application of the results obtained to the number seven of the circus eggs, and to the funerary significance of the games in general. § 25. pp. 292–297. Significance of the colors of the Pamphili tomb painting. — In particular the combination of white and red in its relation to white and black and in its validity in the mysteries.

Second Treatise. pp. 301–412.

Ocnus the Rope Plaiter. § 1. pp. 301–307. Compilation of the monuments and testimonies. § 2. pp. 307–315. Determination of the significance of plaiting and weaving, of spun threads and of the rope. § 3. pp. 315–318. Significance of swamp plants in the ancient nature religion; the ultronea creatio and its sanctity. § 4. pp. 318–325. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants with particular reference to Egypt, the homeland of the Ocnus symbol. § 5. pp. 325–328. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants. — Their equation with human hair and the relation of both to hetaeric sexual mingling. § 6. pp. 328–341. Continuation of the consideration of swamps and swamp plants. — Demonstration of their sanctity in myths, in cult practices, and in connection with individual deities. — Application of these views to the rope of Ocnus. § 7. pp. 341–347. The Mantuan Ocnus. — Proof of the identity of his divine nature with that of the rope plaiter. — Consideration of the name Vianor and of its relation to the sanctity of the swamps. § 8. pp. 347–349. Historical connection of Boeotia with Mantua; the Cadmeans in the north of Italy. § 9. pp. 349–354. Ocnus-Aucnus. — Etymology and meaning of the word. — Various transformations and turns of the meaning according to their inner connection. § 10. pp. 354–361. The augural significance of the king heron Ocnus. — Connection of the same with that of the rope plaiter. — Religious significance of swamp birds, in particular of herons and storks. — Their names as names of peoples, in particular Pelasgians, Tyrrhenians, Rutulians, Ardeates. § 11. pp. 361–370. Continuation of the consideration of individual features of the Ocnus pictures. — The old age of the rope plaiter. — Significance and connection of the same with the fundamental idea of the Ocnus symbol. § 12. pp. 370–373. Transition to the consideration of the second main part

[PDF 438]

— 426 —

of the Ocnus representation, the gnawing she-ass. — Antithesis of the creative and the dissolving principle. Significance of the visible end of the rope.

§ 13. pp. 373–374. The significance of the ass.

§ 14. pp. 374–377. Continued. — The phallic significance of the animal.

§ 15. pp. 377–379. Continued. — Connection of the ass with Priapus, Silenus,

Dionysus, Vulcan, Midas, Vesta.

§ 16. pp. 379–382. Continued. — Connection of the ass with Apollo Hyperboreus

and with Artemis. — The ass among Scythians, Carmanians, Indians.

§ 17. pp. 382–386. Continued. — The religious significance of the ass among

Phoenicians, Jews, Assyrians, Egyptians. — Its Typhonian-evil nature.

§ 18. pp. 386–389. Continued. — The Typhonian significance of the ass demon‐

strated in a series of mythological formations.

§ 19. pp. 389–392. Application of the view obtained to the Ocnus symbol. —

Significance of the female sex of the gnawing she-ass.

§ 20. pp. 392–394. Antithesis of the plaiting and the devouring principle. — The

eternal flux of the phenomenal world brought forth by the united labor of both.

§ 21. pp. 395–400. Admission of the Ocnus symbol into the tombs. — Sepulchral

meaning of the same. — Ocnus as penitent of the underworld. — His connection

with the Danaids. — Elucidation of the myth of the Danaids and of the mystery

idea contained in it.

§ 22. pp. 401–407. Antithesis of the scene of the tomb frieze with that of the

pediment of the aedicula, of Ocnus doing penance in the underworld with the boy

Achilles instructed by Chiron in lyre playing, of uninitiated with initiated life.

Sepulchral meaning of Achilles.

§ 23. pp. 407–409. Further development of this antithesis. — The subjugation of

tellurism by the Apollonian luminous nature.

§ 24. pp. 409–412. The resting Ocnus of the Pamphili tomb. — Antithesis of the

penitent and the liberated old man. — Juxtaposition of the original physical signifi‐

cance and the highest spiritualization of the Ocnus symbol.

Addenda. Emphasis on some funerary vessels described in the Museo Campana. —

On the Delphic omphalos. — The egg in connection with the sacrifice of

Iphigenia.
